Topic:Cyber Security

The ads appear to be a generic image that says "SALE" and shows a picture of miscellaneous products from Ugreen, a Chinese consumer electronics company. (X: John Scott-Railton)

Highly sensitive government agencies have been targeted by a sophisticated, foreign bad actor.

Online ads were used to install spyware on some systems, researchers say.

An Australian spyware researcher said it shows the need for more oversight of the online advertising industry.

Australia's nuclear science agency and other highly sensitive government and critical infrastructure organisations have been targeted by a sophisticated, foreign bad actor that secretly weaponised online advertising to track millions of devices and install spyware on some systems, according to researchers.

Research group, The Citizen Lab, said it found proof that an Israel-based company exploited digital advertising technology to install back doors onto devices, merely by the victim viewing an advertisement on a website or in an app.

It said millions of devices were targeted in the unprecedented attack, including those on networks belonging to Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation (ANSTO) and a number of other Australian government agencies, critical infrastructure and major media organisations.

A spokesperson for ANSTO said it had not identified any impact to its systems as a result of the techniques identified by The Citizen Lab.

Deakin University associate professor Diarmaid Harkin, who has researched the spyware industry, said it was a novel case revealing how bad actors were using online infrastructure to compromise their opponents.

The Citizen Lab is a University of Toronto research lab that has uncovered numerous high-profile examples of cyber espionage targeting governments, businesses, non-for-profits, media outlets and political organisations.

Last week, it published a report, Exposing AdFection: How Discover-Tech Turned Targeted Ads Into a Pipeline for Zero-Click Mercenary Spyware, that identified what it said were bad actors using online advertising to infect devices using spyware.

Dr Harkin said normal online advertising technology runs a "little bit" of code in browsers and apps to show an ad.

"That's normally something innocent, but this time, it wasn't the case," he said.

A screenshot highlighting the Discover-Tech ads. (X: John Scott-Railton)

Instead, this exploit — called ''zero-click mercenary spyware" — allowed bad actors to run code on devices that installed software that acted as a back door to the device, allowing them to access things like passwords, emails and details of internal systems.

The Citizen Lab claims that a company, Discover-Tech, acted as the go-between for online advertising platforms like Google and spyware and hacking companies. At least one of those, Candiru, has been placed under US export controls because of its "malicious cyber activities".

As part of normal online advertising practices, Discover-Tech "bid" against other prospective advertisers to show ads on websites and apps like Duolingo, the BBC and New York Times.

When they won the online auctions, they showed seemingly benign ads to users that secretly included code that could infect their devices.

"This report shows that this ecosystem is being weaponised at a massive scale to profile millions of users, then silently infect targets with zero-click mercenary spyware," the report said.

Spanish authorities say the mobile phones of the country's Prime Minister and Defence Minister were infected with Pegasus spyware last year.

The Citizen Lab verified that bad actors were able to use these advertisements to infect devices belonging to international news network Al Jazeera.

The research group traced the moment from Al Jazeera devices first seeing the infected ad, to the initial contact between its devices and servers spyware maker Candiru, to files being installed on the Al Jazeera computers that would hijack the device.

Merely viewing the ad didn't guarantee the devices were successfully infected, only that it had been exposed to the exploit.

However, researchers said the company was also able to exploit the online advertising technology to profile devices so it could identify them, track their web activity and find their geographical location.

This information would be enough to reveal a person's name or suggest where they worked, and was used to help target the subsequent spyware attacks, researchers claim.

Public records from online advertising show that Discover-Tech carried this out against millions of devices.

Among numerous international defence forces, cyber agencies, and international organisations including NATO, The Citizen Lab highlighted a "substantial cluster" of impressions in Australian critical infrastructure, government, university and media networks.

The report does not specify most of these, however it does say many Australian targets were working on nuclear research, and named the ANSTO and its Australian Synchrotron research campus.

A spokesperson for ANTSO said it was aware of the reports but said its systems had not been breached.

Digicel Pacific's network resources are likely being used by private spy firms to track unsuspecting people on the other side of the world and steal their call, message and location data, according to an expert cybersecurity analysis.

"We are following standard response processes and have not identified any impact to our facilities, systems, and information from the techniques described in the reports," they said.

The Department for Home Affairs directed the ABC's inquiries to Australia's cyber intelligence agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, which declined to comment.

The Citizen Lab report said Google removed Discover-Tech from its platform once the researchers had shared their findings.

Dr Harkin said the report showed how the size and ubiquity of online advertising offered a unique opportunity for bad actors

"What this demonstrates is how zero-click exploits need to find information about who to target with that particular exploit and vulnerability. And what allows them is using the ad tech," he said.

Dr Harkin said it raised questions about how a company was able to gain the trust of major advertising players, like Google, and use them to distribute their exploit without being caught.

"If these ads are being delivered to our devices, our browsers, are they going to do anything malicious once they reach the user? That's the question that needs to be handled upstream by those who are running these ecosystem and by who's regulating them," he said.

"Who's acting as a watchdog for these digital advertising systems?"

Google was approached for comment.

vance_gop_midterm_2026_cnn:
For the next two weeks, Vice President JD Vance’s job is to save Congress for Republicans.

But then he’ll turn to another political project — himself.

Vance’s 2026 closing arguments on the Iran war, high energy prices and immigration are becoming an early test of whether and how, as a 2028 presidential contender, he might handle the tumultuous legacy of his boss, President Donald Trump.

It’s not an easy task.

Vance’s performance at a CBS town hall that aired this weekend showed he’s finding it tough to navigate the grim midterm environment set by Trump’s unpopularity and policy choices. His inability to promise imminent relief on gas prices; his pleas for more time for an economy that voters hate; and his fuzziness on an end to the Iran war highlighted why the odds seem to favor Democrats two weeks out.

“Fundamentally, we are where we are,” Vance said. His comment specifically responded to Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s critique of Iran policy, but it also captured the helplessness of GOP candidates caught in Trump’s political undertow.

The tough questions also foreshadowed a momentous decision looming for Vance over whether to run for president in 2028. A GOP drubbing on November 3 would hand whoever becomes the president’s heir the task of reinventing the party’s message and appeal in two years — with Trump peering over their shoulder.

Vance rather gingerly grappled with how to defend Trump’s immoderate approach on key issues such as immigration that might please the MAGA base but that often seems to alienate a more general audience.

“We’re trying to strike the right balance,” Vance said when asked by a nun why Immigration and Customs Enforcement separation policies appeared to lack compassion and were traumatizing children.

And another of Vance’s flexes — blaming former President Joe Biden — figures to be an even more questionable strategy in two years than it’s proving in the midterm campaign.

Yet Vance is also an intriguing political figure.

At the town hall, he came across as articulate and intelligent. He was more conventional, courteous and empathetic than Trump. And after a decade of presidential leadership by elderly men, his youthfulness raised the possibility of a generational shift in American politics.

Vance, who has a young family and tales of a hard-knocks upbringing, seems more relatable than many in the gilded bubble of billionaires and millionaires that surrounds Trump at the White House and Mar-a-Lago.

The vice president also made apparently sincere efforts to connect with audience members, including one whose wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, was killed in the Iran war and who poignantly wanted answers about what he said were operational failures before her death.

But Vance is not yet Bill Clinton when it comes to feeling others’ pain. He sometimes betrayed the clumsiness of a politician who in his lightning rise has run only a single campaign in his own right — for the Senate in 2022. This could become an issue in the always-on glare of a presidential election race.

Vance’s greatest challenges came in explaining Trump’s decisions on the war and the economy, which are deeply unpopular and have created a tangible link with voters’ own economic struggles, according to almost every opinion poll.

His answers were a study in miniature of the entire midterm season.

“I recognize that gas prices are too high right now,” Vance said, showing more candor than Trump normally does and exemplifying his more direct rhetoric on the economy in general. But his explanation that Iran had held the Strait of Hormuz hostage didn’t account for the fact that this was an obvious outcome of Trump’s war of choice that the White House seemingly failed to anticipate. And Vance’s warnings that Iran must not have a nuclear weapon might have hit home more had Trump tried to make that case to the nation before launching the war.

After Vance blamed Biden for high gasoline prices, CBS anchor Tony Dokoupil jumped in to point out: “It’s almost been two years. At a certain point, it becomes your economy, not Joe Biden’s economy.”

Vance also struggled to square Trump’s repeated declarations of victory early in the war with an opaque reality nearly eight months later. “I would say in some ways we have won decisively, but the Iranians, the enemy gets a vote here,” he said.

Neither of these answers seems likely to appease voters angry with Trump’s administration. A Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll on Sunday put the president’s approval rating at only 33%, weighed down by deeply negative perceptions of his policies on the economy and the Iran war.

Polls two weeks out cannot predict the results of elections. But Republicans have been pouring money into red states in a way that supports the perception that Democrats have a good chance to win back the House. The Senate is a tougher ask, however. Democrats would need a net gain of four seats on a tough map featuring key races in states that Trump won easily in 2024.

Vance is hardly alone in laboring to make a strong election message. Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers showed Sunday on “State of the Union” how hard it is for candidates to deal with Trump’s looming shadow.

Asked about Trump’s controversial sanctions-busting diesel deal with Russia that shocked even many Republicans last week, Rogers replied: “Well, that’s just not where I would be.” He told CNN’s Dana Bash that Trump had made investments that would benefit his state when the war ends. But he implicitly admitted that talking to voters about the long term doesn’t help much now. “Most people I talk to are frustrated with the costs, you bet. Who isn’t when you’re paying over four bucks a gallon?” Rogers said.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright had little help for Republican candidates facing voters’ wrath over high gas prices. Back in March, he predicted that it would take weeks, not months, for prices to come down. Asked about that assessment by Bash on Sunday, he said, “Of course I’m not comfortable, but I’m happy they’re coming down. They have gone down the last few weeks, as have diesel prices, and they will continue to come down.”

Drivers, however, are still paying an average of $4.30 nationally for gasoline and up to $6.32 a gallon for diesel. Handed this bleak reality, Republicans can do little but warn that things would be worse if Democrats win control of Congress. Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson claimed on Fox News’ “Sunday Morning Futures” that Democratic climate policies would raise prices. “You have to keep the grown-ups in charge, steady hands at the wheel,” Johnson argued.

But calling for continuity when angry voters want change is a tough sell.

And unless Trump somehow slays the affordability curse in the next two years, any GOP presidential candidate will confront the same issue.

Vance, as vice president, is widely seen as Trump’s likeliest successor. But he told CBS he hadn’t decided whether to go for it. “You know, anything can happen, man. Anything,” Vance said. Another supposed contender, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, has repeatedly said that he’s not planning to run and that he’d back Vance.

But CNN’s Donie O’Sullivan reported Saturday that he found little enthusiasm for Vance among a couple of hundred members of the president’s base he spoke with over the last six months. The alternative name he heard most frequently was Rubio.

Successful election campaigns are usually about the future. So the next Republican standard-bearer must conjure a vision that is more compelling than the one Vance offered in the town hall.

At one point he was asked by a small-business owner why Trump’s promise of a “golden age” for the economy hadn’t panned out.

After a lengthy reply stressing a long-term dearth of investment and the positive potential of Trump tax cuts and factory-opening projects, Vance concluded: “I’ll be the first person to tell you that just as this country wasn’t broken in one presidential term, it’s going to take more than 18 months to fix things and turn them around.”

That’s not going to cut it in 2028.

Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin presented Vladimir Putin with “proposals for a number of personnel changes in the government,” the Kremlin’s press service said. The two discussed the changes at a meeting held the morning of Monday, October 19.

Mishustin proposed making Finance Ministry head Anton Siluanov a deputy prime minister as well (Siluanov held both posts from 2018 to 2020). He also nominated Primorsky Governor Oleg Kozhemyako for deputy prime minister and presidential envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District, a post currently held by Yuri Trutnev.

Mishustin has also nominated Transport Ministry head Andrei Nikitin for deputy prime minister. He is proposing Dmitry Yadrov, head of Rosaviatsia, as transport minister.

Mishustin has also nominated First Deputy Finance Minister Irina Okladnikova for deputy prime minister and head of the government’s staff, a post currently held by Dmitry Grigorenko.

“These proposals have received the support of President Putin,” Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov said.

Under the Russian Constitution, candidates nominated by the head of government must be confirmed by the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament.

Anton Siluanov previously served as deputy chairman of the Russian government, holding the post of first deputy prime minister from 2018 to 2020.

By ELIOT FORCE, US NEWS REPORTER

Published:  01:49 AEDT, 19 October 2026   |  Updated:  16:01 AEDT, 19 October 2026

Just days after she was ousted from her five-day tenure as White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia is facing fresh scrutiny for posting pictures of herself with Trump that may have contained sensitive information.

Zacharia stepped into the role on Monday, but was quickly asked to resign on Friday, following a shaky performance during her first press briefing and revelations that she never passed the bar exam despite describing herself as an attorney.

The day she was ousted, Zacharia shared a gushing farewell post about Donald Trump on social media that included a picture of herself standing next to the president who was seated at his desk in the Oval Office.

On the desk was a conspicuously blurred map. Then, in a second post on Saturday picturing Zacharia and her family with the president, the map appeared to have been edited out of the photo.

The first picture drew questions and speculation, and the second photo only added fuel to the fire as people wondered why the map was digitally removed if it was insignificant.

Observers pointed out that the shape of the landmass on the map appeared to resemble East Potomac Park in Washington DC, which Trump has been eyeing as part of his goal to overhaul landmarks and federal properties in the nation's capital.

Trump in late June announced his intention to renovate the park's 'dilapidated, worn out, and very dangerous and outdated Golf Course' on Truth Social, but the plan has since been challenged by a lawsuit filed by the DC Preservation League.

The administration has said that there is no final design for the golf course, but critics have perceived the map on Trump's desk as evidence to the contrary.

Katie Zacharia drew scrutiny for this photo she posted with Trump that shows a blurred map on his desk. Observers said it appeared similar in shape to East Potomac Park in Washington DC

In the second photo Zacharia posted, which included her husband and children, the map appears to have been edited out. People questioned why it was removed if it was insignificant

Zacharia served as White House press secretary for just five days after a shaky performance during her first press briefing

The advocacy group Save East Po, which is opposed to the renovation plan, retweeted Zacharia's post on Friday and wrote: 'FYI to anyone paying attention – that blurred out map on the PRESIDENT’S DESK is East Potomac Park'.

A follow-up tweet that included Zacharia's second photo with the map edited out said: 'Nothing says “we have no plan” like a photo of plan-shaped map on the President’s desk, followed by a second photo where that map has been digitally removed.'

Alex Rosen, the founder of Save East Po, told The Washington Post that details on the blurred map resemble previously circulated renderings of renovation plans for the park.

After more than 400 trees in East Potomac Park were felled, US District Judge Ana Reyes, earlier this week blocked the National Park Service from cutting down any more.

Trump administration lawyers have contended that the tree removals were not part of the president's golf course renovation initiative but instead part of a 2019 plan to restore the course to its original design.

Reyes, who is presiding over the lawsuit challenging the renovation, appeared sceptical of the government's argument in a court memorandum issued on Tuesday.

'It is a coincidence, the government seems to suggest, that DOI [Department of the Interior] cut down hundreds of trees at the course weeks after the President asked DOI to cut down trees at the course, and not, say, any other time in the last seven years,' the judge wrote.

Those opposed to East Potomac Park's renovation perceive the blurred map on the president's desk as an indication that he intends to move forward with renovation plans despite the court challenge.

An advocacy group against renovating East Potomac Park said the map looked like a rendering of previously circulated renovation plans. The map and park pictured side by side

The National Park Service felled more than 400 trees at the park's golf course, claiming the work was part of a 2019 plan. A federal judge said she was suspicious of the timing

An advocacy group against the park's renovation highlighted the map on Trump's desk and said it indicated he has full plans for the renovation despite claiming the contrary

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung scoffed at those concerns in a statement claiming the Daily Mail was 'breathlessly obsessing over an innocuous photo' and suffering from 'Trump Derangement Syndrome'.

Zacharia similarly told the Daily Mail: 'It is only fitting that the Daily Mail would turn a very sweet picture into something controversial.'

Trump addressed his goal to renovate East Potomac Park in a Truth Social post on Sunday morning. It is unclear whether the announcement was related to the scrutiny surrounding Zacharia's posts.

'Doug Burgum, and the United States Department of the Interior, is very excited about the new Development of a Great Golf Course at the site of the old East Potomac Golf Links. We would like to thank Tom Fazio for his initial conceptual design and ideas, coupled with those of others from within the Golf World and the Department of the Interior,' the president wrote.

'Any variance or changes will be made, depending on site conditions, by the Experts in Parks and Recreation, whose experience and knowledge in Seawalls, Landscaping, and Design are second to none.'

Critics have pointed to Trump's history of pushing through major changes to Washington DC without oversight and have said they are concerned that the park is just the latest example.

The president demolished the White House East Wing to build a ballroom without Congressional approval, advanced plans for a 250ft arch on Columbia Island without final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission and added his name to the Kennedy Center.

All of those initiatives faced legal challenges. The Supreme Court ruled that construction of the White House ballroom can temporarily move forward, but the other two plans are currently in limbo.

Economy

October 18, 2026

Syria and the World Bank have agreed to establish a multi-donor trust fund to support the country's recovery and reconstruction following more than a decade of civil war.
The World Bank estimates Syria's reconstruction will cost $216 billion, making it one of the most expensive rebuilding efforts in history.
Infrastructure accounts for 48 per cent of total war damage, with residential and non-residential buildings each representing $33 billion in losses.
Syria has secured significant investment commitments from Gulf partners, including a $2 billion Saudi Arabian package and Qatari financing for electricity, water and airport rehabilitation.
"An important milestone in Syria's recovery and reconstruction journey," Syrian Finance Minister Yisr Barnieh said of the newly established trust fund.

Syria and the World Bank have agreed to set up a multi-donor trust fund for the country's recovery and reconstruction, the two sides announced in a joint statement on Sunday.

Damascus is continuing to rebuild after a civil war that lasted for more than a decade and had destroyed the country's infrastructure.

Interview:Syria 'pressing on accelerator' to attract US investors

The Syria Recovery and Reconstruction Trust Fund – or “Start” – is a multi-donor fund that aims to provide concessional financing, investment guarantees and technical assistance, and build trust, the statement said.

The agreement comes after Syria took part in the International and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. The gatherings were the latest to be attended by Syrian officials since the fall of president Bashar Al Assad's regime in December 2024.

Syrian Finance Minister Yisr Barnieh said the agreement helps to set the foundation for a new phase of co-operation with Damascus's international partners. Partners in the US, Europe and Middle East expressed their support for the initiative, the statement said.

“An important milestone in Syria’s recovery and reconstruction journey,” Mr Barnieh wrote in a post on X.

The World Bank in 2025 estimated Syria's reconstruction would cost about $216 billion, making it one of the most expensive rebuilding efforts in history. The World Bank classified this as its best “conservative” estimate.

The World Bank said infrastructure accounted for 48 per cent, or $52 billion, of total damage from the civil war, followed by residential buildings at $33 billion and non-residential buildings at $33 billion.

It said the multi-donor trust fund will help to support the delivery of basic services, strengthen institutional capacities and expand economic opportunities.

“We look forward to working with all partners to support a comprehensive and sustainable recovery path,” said Ousmane Dione, World Bank vice president for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan.

Syria's transitional government has been racing to secure investment commitments to help rebuild the country's infrastructure. Some of those pledges have recently gone to the implementation phase, including DP World's $800 million towards Tartus Port.

The country has secured deals with its other Gulf partners, including a $2 billion Saudi Arabian investment package to develop two airports in Aleppo, as well as other projects involving energy, real estate and telecommunications.

At this week's gatherings in Thailand, Mr Barnieh also held discussions with Qatari Finance Minister Ali Al Kuwari on supporting recovery and development work, the state-run news agency Sana reported. Norway also expressed interest in contributing to the trust fund, Sana reported.

Qatar has also offered financing for projects to rehabilitate Syria's electricity grids, water networks, public services and the Damascus International Airport.

Baker Hughes, Caterpillar and Visa were among a delegation of about 50 US companies that visited Syria last month to explore and deepen economic ties, which came weeks after the US delisted Syria as a state sponsor of terrorism.

Syria will also return to the Arab group at the International Monetary Fund beginning on November 1, leaving the Russian-led group it joined in 2012, the Finance Ministry said in a post on Telegram.

The IMF restarted communications with Syria in 2025. The fund said in August it had agreed on a technical assistance programme for the country after a staff-level visit in July.

The IMF has not had an Article IV consultation with Syria since 2009.

A former Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) scientist won a legal victory this week after losing his position following sexual misconduct allegations made by a female colleague.

Dr. David Sabatini, a former MIT biology professor and prominent biomedical researcher, was awarded $6 million in damages Friday after a jury found that his former colleague, Dr. Kristin Knouse, had defamed him.

At the time of the allegations, Sabatini had led a research lab at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for approximately 24 years.

His work focused on cell biology and its connections to neurodegenerative diseases, diabetes, aging and cancer.

In 2021, Sabatini lost his position at Whitehead following an internal investigation into allegations made by Dr. Kristin Knouse, a younger colleague who worked at the institute.

The pair met in 2012 and began a sexual relationship in 2018, which ended the following year, according to court documents obtained by Fox News Digital. Knouse later alleged the relationship was coerced.

According to records from the investigation, Whitehead also found that Sabatini had fostered a sexualized atmosphere in his lab. He subsequently resigned from the institute.

Following his departure from Whitehead — and amid an ongoing investigation at MIT — Sabatini filed a defamation lawsuit against Knouse, “alleging claims for defamation, tortious interference with contractual, prospective, and advantageous relations,” according to court documents.

Knouse subsequently filed a counterclaim against Sabatini, alleging sexual harassment.

Throughout the legal battle, Sabatini maintained that he had never fostered an improper atmosphere in his lab and that his relationship with Knouse was consensual.

During the trial, his attorney, Lisa Arrowood, cited text messages between the pair that she argued showed Knouse willingly participated in their relationship.

In one 2020 exchange, Knouse lamented that she was “pouring a lot of energy and emotion into a game I’m destined to lose” and wondered “if it’s best for both of us to cut all but work-related ties for the foreseeable future.”

She concluded the message by writing, “But most times I feel at peace and want to do everything and anything I can to help you.”

Sabatini and his legal team argued in court that the relationship was consensual. They also presented evidence they said showed that Knouse had become jealous of another woman in whom Sabatini was interested and had sought to have him fired.

A day after a Suffolk County jury awarded him $6 million in damages, Sabatini told Fox News Digital that hearing the verdict was “overwhelming.”

“It was done,” Sabatini said. “We had won everything, lost nothing. It was like a complete sweep.”

Five years after filing his lawsuit, Sabatini emerged from the trial with a favorable verdict after the jury rejected Knouse’s counterclaims, including her allegation that he had coerced her into a sexual relationship.

“The sad reality of our time is that society still has a difficult time believing women and appreciating the difficulty they encounter with men who too often control their fate,” Knouse’s attorney, Ellen Zuker, said in a statement to the New York Times.

Knouse’s attorney did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

Despite the legal victory, Sabatini is now attempting to pick up the pieces of his career.

The allegations seeped into every aspect of his life, and many of his loved ones — including his parents, nephew and high school-aged son — began receiving threats shortly after Knouse’s claims were made public.

“Everyone who came out and tried to defend me got attacked every which way,” Sabatini told Fox News Digital.

Shortly after his departure from MIT and Whitehead, Sabatini discussed a potential faculty position at New York University (NYU). But after students and faculty members protested his possible hiring in 2022, the university ultimately did not offer him a job.

Sabatini said protesters also appeared outside his parents’ home, drawing his family further into the controversy.

One year later, in 2023, Sabatini landed a job at the Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry in Prague after receiving several offers from foreign countries — including China. He later opened a Boston branch of the institute, and he splits his time between Prague and the United States.

“It was a necessity,” Sabatini said. “There were no options [in the United States]. So there was no choice.”

Following Friday’s verdict, Knouse’s attorneys said they planned to appeal, while Sabatini’s legal team also prepared to challenge the dismissal of his claims against the Whitehead Institute.

“I think institutions don’t care about due process,” Sabatini said. “They care about having a certain conclusion. And for whatever reason that one could discuss, at that time the conclusion was, ‘Get this guy out of here and make an example of him.’”

Sabatini said he hopes to rebuild his life and career following the verdict and eventually return to working primarily in the United States.

“But ultimately for me, it’s just being able to be close to my son before he goes to college,” Sabatini told Fox News Digital. “That’s really number one through 100.”

Fox News Digital also reached out to the Whitehead Institute and MIT for comment.

PARIS — Police arrested at least 1,800 people across France after violent groups clashed with officers and looted shops during nationwide demonstrations that drew hundreds of thousands of people who denounced rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.

Authorities said masked groups on Saturday set fires and attacked public buildings, including city halls, in several cities.

In Limoges, a city in central France, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall, causing its roof to collapse. Haute-Vienne prefect Maurice Barate told LCI television that the fire was deliberately set and nearly destroyed the building. The fire was under control Sunday.

French President Emmanuel Macron will hold an emergency meeting with top government officials on Sunday afternoon, before addressing the nation at 8 p.m., according to his office.

"The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not," Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote on X, pointing to the lootings of hundreds of businesses in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Rennes, Strasbourg, Grenoble, Nice, Limoges and other cities.

coral-bleaching-reversed-stanford:
Coral bleaching has been reversed at record speed using a new method developed at Stanford University.

Corals that were ghostly white returned to full health in their lab in a mere seven weeks—the fastest documented recovery to date.

It is the first time scientists have observed bleached corals on the brink of death fully recover through brief contact with healthy clones.

They say the breakthrough, published in the journal Science Advances, opens new possibilities for restoring coral reefs damaged by the intense heat of climate change.

Coral reefs, which protect coastlines and communities from storms and flooding, expel beneficial algae living within their tissues when ocean waters warm.

The loss of their algae partners leaves corals pale, starving, and vulnerable to the invasion of harmful algae.

But, the lead study author Danny Collins says that while bleached corals may be dying, “they are not dead yet”.

In a lab setting, corals fully recovered from bleaching within weeks through brief contact with healthy corals. By fusing tissues, healthy corals sent enough life-giving algae and nutrients to their bleached counterparts to kickstart the recovery process in three days.

Collins, a PhD student at the University’s Doerr School of Sustainability, explained that all corals are animals that can multiply by producing clones that grow together to form vast, reef-building colonies of the same genetic make-up.

In 2025, study coauthor Professor Steve Palumbi observed something curious about coral biology in his research lab. Two coral fragments—one bleached, one healthy—sampled from the same colony had tipped over in a tank and were now touching.

Where they made contact, color returned to the bleached fragment, signaling the return of beneficial algae.

Around the time of the observation, Collins was considering the origins of coral disease—the possibility that bacteria lurking on plastic debris is settling onto the coral.

“Harmful bacteria enter corals through physical contact, (so) we were curious about what would happen if we used contact to reintroduce something good—the beneficial algae from healthy corals,” explained Collins.

Collins arranged five pairs, close enough to touch, and left gaps of just a few millimeters between the remaining pairs—and the bleached fragments in touching pairs fully recovered within seven weeks, while those without contact died.

“Genetically identical corals recognize one another when they come into contact, and their tissues fuse,” said Stanford Prof. Palumbi.

“We see something similar in humans. Organ transplants are often successful if the donor is your identical twin.”

Microscopic channels in coral tissues align shortly after contact, creating a pathway for transport between corals, allowing beneficial algae and the nutrients they produce to flow through those channels.

They also tested how different contact durations influenced recovery rates and found that after one week of contact, and in some cases after just five days, bleached fragments received enough beneficial algae to complete recovery on their own.

After separation, recovery took just seven weeks, matching the recovery time of coral pairs left in continuous contact.

That led the team to realize that algae replicating within the bleached fragment—rather than traveling from the healthy fragment—primarily drove continued recovery.

“Once beneficial algae enter bleached corals, they don’t just spread out,” said Prof Palumbi. “They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals.”

During the second week of contact with healthy corals, algae within bleached fragments doubled every four days, around ten times quicker than the rate observed in wild corals.

Researchers have been trying for years to develop tools and approaches that can protect corals from bleaching, disease outbreaks, and increasingly acidic waters, despite bleached corals often being considered ‘a lost cause’.

Solutions being explored include selectively breeding heat-tolerant corals, cultivating coral nurseries to restore degraded reefs, and even transplanting coral microbiomes.

In the coming months, the researchers plan to explore alternative ways of delivering beneficial algae to bleached corals that don’t require continuous contact.

“These new insights into how corals can naturally recover give us hope for the future,” said Stanford Prof. Fiorenza Micheli. “They open the door to what’s possible and may lead to the breakthrough we need to accelerate reef restoration.”

The developing phenomenon is already among the strongest on record by several measures, with forecasters warning it could intensify further as winter approaches, climate scientist Daniel Swain wrote in an Oct. 12 analysis for Weather West.

The warning signs are already playing out along the Southern California coast.

In Long Beach, city leaders on Friday outlined a recovery plan after powerful surf from Tropical Storm Rachel tore apart homes and infrastructure on the Peninsula. Seven homes remain red-tagged, down from eight, and officials still don’t know how many will have to be demolished.

With king tides expected around Thanksgiving and a strong El Niño pattern developing, officials are racing to reinforce the battered coastline before the next round of dangerous surf arrives.

“We’re now shifting into preparing for the next storm while we recover from the impacts of Rachel,” Mayor Rex Richardson said.

The developing El Niño pattern, along with powerful oceanic Kelvin waves, is contributing to the threat. The waves can temporarily raise sea levels by up to 12 inches, increasing the risk of coastal flooding when powerful surf and high tides hit vulnerable communities.

“I think that this year’s El Niño event is likely to be the strongest in 1,000 years if the latest models of its peak prove accurate,” climate scientist Zeke Hausfather told The Daily Mail.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a statewide emergency last month in preparation for what officials warn could become the strongest El Niño on record.

“The emerging El Niño event is already breaking records, and forecasters expect it to continue to strengthen, potentially becoming the strongest in recorded history,” Newsom’s office said.

The designation does not mean California is guaranteed to be battered by storms. But stronger El Niño events increase the chances of weather typically associated with the phenomenon, including heavy rain, flooding, powerful waves and coastal erosion.

California officials previously said they hope early planning will negate some effects of the powerful weather system.

“We are not waiting for this season’s storms to be on our doorstep,” California Office of Emergency Services Director Caroline Thomas Jacobs said.

“By planning early and coordinating resources ahead of El Niño, we are working to ensure communities and first responders have the personnel, equipment, and support they need to prepare for severe weather, respond quickly when conditions change, and protect lives and property across California.”

Paris protests turn to looting as Louis Vuitton, Dior, Goyard and Hermès stores are hit across France.

Paris protests turned into a night of fires, tear gas and looting Saturday as hundreds of thousands of people flooded the streets of France and some of the most expensive stores in the world were ransacked.

Video:

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez put the turnout at 550,000 nationwide, including 110,000 in Paris. The CGT labor union, which helped organize the marches, said the real number was closer to 800,000. Either way, it was one of the largest days of protest France has seen in years.

The fashion capital’s priciest addresses took the hit. Demonstrators broke into Louis Vuitton, Hermès and Apple stores in Paris and Bordeaux. Video circulating online appears to show a Christian Dior store on Rue Saint-Honoré being looted, and videos shared from the same luxury strip show Goyard, the French trunk maker whose flagship has sat on Rue Saint-Honoré since 1853, caught up in the chaos too. A post viewed hundreds of thousands of times claims Dior brought in its own private security team to guard its flagship as the night went on.

More than 300 protesters also tried to push up the Champs-Élysées, the avenue lined with flagship luxury stores, before police blocked them with tear gas.

At Place de la République, where the Paris march began, the scene turned violent by early afternoon. Protesters threw fireworks and rocks at officers, who answered with tear gas and water cannons. A car went up in flames in the middle of the square, along with bicycles, a newspaper kiosk and trash bins. Looters forced their way into a nearby Monoprix supermarket on Boulevard Saint-Denis, and a toy shop was broken into, with people parading the stolen boxes down the avenue while filming themselves.

It was not just Paris. In Marseille, dozens of shops were looted, including a Hermès boutique, and rioters stormed city hall. Protesters smashed into the town hall in Lille, where an Apple store was also cleaned out. In Lyon, the tourist office was set on fire.

The Paris protests did not start with luxury stores or politics. They started at a high school. On September 17, students at Lycée Saint-Exupéry, an underfunded public high school in the Paris suburb of Créteil, walked out over a chronic shortage of teachers, run down facilities and the declining quality of their education. Within weeks, students at hundreds of schools across France had joined them, demanding more teachers, smaller class sizes and buildings that are not falling apart.

Saturday was the biggest day yet because the students were joined by workers, unions and the Yellow Vests, the movement that first took over French streets in 2018 over fuel prices and the cost of living. Their anger now is over the same thing: rising prices, fuel costs and public services they say are crumbling while the country’s money troubles deepen.

The crackdown on this movement has been heavy, and much of it has landed on kids. As of October 6, France’s Justice Ministry reported 5,060 arrests since the protests began, and 87 percent of the people arrested were minors. Nuñez told the French Senate that 248 students and 149 school staff members had been injured, the highest number ever recorded by the country’s Education Ministry. A 15 year old lost his hand to a police stun grenade during a protest in the city of Lens on October 5. On Saturday, another demonstrator lost a hand.

Nuñez said nearly 400 people were arrested on Saturday alone, with more arrests coming in the days ahead, and 60 officers were injured.

President Emmanuel Macron responded on X late Saturday. “No room for violence in our Republic. Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished,” he wrote. Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said the overwhelming majority of demonstrators wanted to march calmly and that acts of vandalism were tarnishing their protest.

The students who started all of this asked for teachers and classrooms. A month later, the Paris protests have half a million people in the streets, Rue Saint-Honoré covered in broken glass and a government promising more arrests.

If you’d like to live near the water along the spectacular California coast at some point in your life, you have a number of options.

You can settle in, say, Culver City, which is several miles inland, and wait for rising tides to arrive.

Or, if you just can’t wait that long, I saw a listing you might be interested in. It’s in Capitola, near Santa Cruz, right next to the wharf. The three bedroom, two bath, 1,850-square-foot condo, one of a string of Venetian, pastel beachfront homes, is listed for $3,995,000.

“The beach is your backyard, the cool ocean is your pool,” says the promo.

Given what’s happening right now along the California coast, you might not have to leave that condo to go for a swim. But UC Santa Cruz oceanographer and geologist Gary Griggs, who has seen the thrashing of that row of homes in previous years, is not going to make an offer.

“I’ve got a number of photos,” he said, “that show waves breaking over the top.”

Someone will buy the place, eventually, despite the chance of it becoming a fish tank. California is flush with dumb money and bad judgment, and an insatiable romance with an epic 1,200-mile shoreline.

But it’s time to rethink the relationship.

Climate & Environment

Overwhelmed by El Niño forecasts? An expert explains how a confluence of high tide cycles could peak around Thanksgiving and Christmas along coastal California.

Last weekend in Long Beach I said a few words at the 50th anniversary of the California Coastal Act, which has kept our shoreline from looking like Atlantic City or Miami Beach by balancing sensible development with conservation and public access.

“The coast is never saved, it’s always being saved,” I said at the 50th, borrowing as I often do from the late Peter Douglas, hammering home the need for constant stewardship, from one generation to the next.

But in an ironic twist, part of the parking lot was underwater, a tractor had raised a berm to hold back the ocean, and just to the south, homes were being thrashed by waves. The coast wasn’t being saved, it was being reclaimed by the sea.

From there I headed south for a friend’s planned birthday party on the sand in Newport Beach, but city streets had been flooded and beaches were closed. The party was moved indoors.

We have not seen the worst of it, with a fall forecast that includes the possibility of an epic Super El Niño that could coincide with king tides, Kelvin waves and a peak lunar nodal cycle, all of which my colleague Rosanna Xia laid out a couple of days ago.

It’s not going to rain hammerheads and sea horses, I don’t think, but coastal destruction could be dramatic.

“We’re likely going to break a number of water level records,” said Timu Gallien of the UCLA Coastal Flood Lab. “It’s not implausible to see some of the piers wiped out, or breakwaters or jetties.”

“This is a glimpse of our future,” said former California Coastal Commission Director Jack Ainsworth. “This is it. It’s here.”

Some low-lying communities have been warned for years to prepare for rising sea levels, Ainsworth said, but have put off the inevitable.

In some areas, the only sane maneuver is what’s called “managed retreat,” meaning relocation of structures farther inland. But that is fraught with legal and political challenges and resistance.

Look, if you want to live on the sand and can afford to do so, good for you. But the general public should not be on the hook for your losses. Along the entire coast, public infrastructure that we all benefit from is under threat, including roadways, parks and railroad tracks, and that’s where any public investment ought to go.

Among the tools available are sand berms, cobble berms (sand on top of small stones), jetties, dredging and relocating sand, and below-surface breakwaters. Living shorelines, such as those along the Orange and San Diego county coasts, involve piling sand atop boulders or smaller stones and covering the berms with vegetation.

But these projects don’t happen overnight, Gallien said. “Right now we’re seeing reactive responses. OK, let’s throw up some sandbags and plywood.”

Kelsey Ducklow, coastal resilience director for the Coastal Commission, said the agency has awarded millions in grants for local planners to study the threat to their communities and come up with plans. Some locales are further along than others, Ducklow said, but there’s no single strategy that will work everywhere, and one typical response is, “Yeah, we know we need to do something. But where’s the money to do it?”

The three choices we have are mitigation, adaptation and suffering, Griggs said. We’re likely to do some of each, but on the mitigation end of things, sea walls, rock revetments and armored cliffs are temporary fixes.

“In the long run, there’s nothing we can do to hold back the Pacific Ocean,” said Griggs, 83, who has been teaching for 59 years. “Everything we do is a Band-Aid, and comes with different price tags and lifespans.”

Griggs was featured in Xia’s award-winning book “California Against the Sea: Visions for Our Vanishing Coastline,” which explores the impact of sea level rise and community responses that range from denial to respectful intervention.

Climate & Environment

The human-built world keeps getting in the way of the rising sea. But this current story of our coast does not have to end in disaster.

Precious ecosystems are under threat, Xia wrote, “trapped between rising water on one side, pavement on the other.” And multiple Southern California beaches that are “so deeply tied to the state’s heart and soul” could be lost.

I asked Xia what she thought about the rising threat this year.

“So many people think about the coast as a place — a place that doesn’t move,” she said. “But the coast in reality is a living dynamic process that changes every time a wave crashes ashore. That’s the heart of the issue — we’re fundamentally trying to impose permanence onto a space that is meant to be constantly changing.”

We haven’t been the best stewards of the planet, and maybe what’s happening now is a bit of a reckoning. From the first time I saw the California coast as a young lad on vacation from the hot interior, I think I understood that the truest way to love the sea was to fear and respect it.

I now have more fear and more respect.

And maybe, too, a deeper love.

The Sunshine Coast artist said she hoped Pride Round would help queer people relish and celebrate their identities.

"There is a world that still exists where people would rather not be here than be themselves, and that's so sad to see," she said.

Her work has won the endorsement of Mitch Brown, who last year became the AFL's first past or present player to openly come out as part of the LGBTQIA+ community.

Gold Coast Suns AFLW players Lily Mithen and Katie Lynch worked with Ms Peters to develop the guernsey.

Mithen said the team wanted the design to reflect their individual personalities.

"Katie and I are a bit loud and fun and silly and we wanted that to be felt through the jumper," she said.

Mithen said helping design the guernsey was an important way to honour the LGBTQIA+ community, which she said had been "woven into the fabric of the AFLW from the very beginning".

"[The AFLW has] always been a place where people have been really free to be themselves," she said.

Lily Mithen says Pride Round celebrates everyone’s individual strengths. (Supplied: Gold Coast SUNS)

For Lynch, her connection to football began playing with "the boys" at the age of four and grew into an enduring love of the game and a place where she felt accepted.

She said many in the AFLW had grown up knowing they "maybe did see themselves doing things a little differently", and that shone through in their sport.

Lynch said it was important to acknowledge a "very brave and courageous group" continuing to challenge perceptions of the LGBTQIA+ community in sport, including in the men's competition.

Head of AFLW at the AFL Players Association Julia Chiera said she could remember feeling like the "odd one out" as the only young girl playing football in her community, before finding a sense of belonging at Melbourne's Darebin Football Club as an adult.

Chiera said women's football had provided a welcoming environment for many queer people at the community level well before the national competition began.

She said football had historically attracted many queer women and gender-nonconforming people because of their "fearlessness" to challenge social expectations.

"It felt empowering to be amongst women who loved football and didn't really care if it was not socially acceptable for women to play sport," she said reflecting on her time at Darebin.

Julia Chiera says the AFLW’s culture of authenticity and acceptance extended beyond sexuality and is celebrated year-round in the women’s league. (Supplied: AFL Players’ Association)

However, Chiera said more work was needed to improve inclusion in the men's game, which did not have a dedicated Pride Round.

She said meaningful support for the LGBTQIA+ community required clubs, players, administrators and supporters to demonstrate genuine inclusion throughout the season and behind closed doors, rather than relying on a single round.

Ms Peters said she hoped the guernsey would bring the Gold Coast side the same good luck for their second and final game of Pride Round 2026 after the Suns won their first match last week.

"I knew it was lucky. I put lucky vibes into it," she said.

The Gold Coast Suns will wear the Pride guernsey for a final time against the Adelaide Crows in Adelaide on Saturday afternoon.

FBI Director Kash Patel said this week that the bureau has cleared a backlog of DNA samples that once topped 1.8 million and reduced it to zero in under a year and a half.

The backlog covered DNA collected from federally convicted offenders, arrestees, and non-citizen detainees under the DNA Fingerprint Act of 2005, which requires the samples be sent to the FBI Laboratory Division for processing. Patel joined the Lab Division team over the weekend to mark the milestone, according to the FBI’s Office of Public Affairs.

In a statement provided to Breitbart News, the director tied the backlog to prior leadership and credited his team with clearing it.

This was yet another example of institutionalized bureaucracy from prior leadership that left crimes across America unsolved. When we got here, there had been a backlog nearly 2 million samples  — literally breaking statutory requirements and hindering the FBI’s work — and we immediately got to work.

The FBI receives roughly 50,000 samples a month, the office said. Those samples are processed for entry into the Combined DNA Index System, or CODIS, where investigators compare them against DNA recovered from unsolved homicides, mass shootings, and sexual assaults.

The director said the bureau attacked the problem with new resources after he took over.

“This FBI dedicated more resources, more equipment, improved IT systems, and used business analytics for DNA processing — and thanks to incredible work from our Lab team the backlog is officially at zero,” Patel continued.

In a separate statement posted online in August, the director put the figure at more than 1.81 million samples and said the pile had been growing by roughly 75,000 samples a month. “DNA profiles belong in CODIS helping law enforcement solve crimes — not stalled in a government backlog,” Patel wrote.

The bureau’s own fiscal year 2027 budget request states the CODIS processing backlog reached 1.8 million by the end of fiscal 2024, saying sustained volume increases outpaced DNA program resources.

Patel repeated the figure in September during the Senate Judiciary Committee’s oversight hearing, telling lawmakers the Lab Division had carried a backlog of more than 1.8 million samples for years before his confirmation and that it now stood at zero. Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-IA) cited FBI data showing criminal arrests up 80 percent and violent crime arrests up 90 percent during the director’s tenure.

The announcement comes as the FBI touts a record drop in violent crime. The bureau reported in August that murder and non-negligent manslaughter fell an estimated 18.1 percent in 2025, the largest year-to-year decline in violent crime since the agency began national estimates in 1936.

nhs-england-biological-sex-ward-guidance:
NHS England is facing criticism for new guidance, which Trans+ rights advocates fear "may even lead to [trans patients’] deaths".

NHS England has published new guidance on same-sex accommodation in NHS hospitals. It sets out that, due to its interpretation of the 2025 Supreme Court ruling on the Equality Act and the subsequent EHRC Code of Practice, trans patients should be put on wards that align with their 'biological sex', which the court determined to be their sex assigned at birth.

The guidance emphasises that all decisions must be "clinically appropriate" and determined through individual assessment. But it gives little guidance on how to consider this. Critically, it sets out that while trans patients' priorities should be considered, so should other patients'.

Because of the clinical risk focus throughout, it does not set out that trans patients should automatically be offered single-bed rooms. However, it does say that this should be done to maintain "privacy, dignity, and safety for all patients", and adds that this will also be based on wider needs for 'side rooms', which are usually reserved for infection control and end-of-life care - QueerAF

"Exclusion should not be the default. The priority should have been patient safety - instead, this policy will mean trans patients are left stranded in corridors without proper care," Good Law Project’s Trans Rights Lead Jess O'Thomson tells QueerAF.

"Trans patients have been treated on gendered wards for many years without complaint or incident. This new policy is not just a potential violation of trans people's human rights - in some cases, it may even lead to their deaths."

The policy comes as the NHS continues to struggle with the rising breaches of its existing mixed-sex guidance, with a rise every year since 2021. The most recent figures show that in August 2026 there were 5,520 breaches, which count as each patient being held on a mixed-sex ward. This compares with 3,853 in June 2025. - BBC

The NHS also launched new guidance on how Trans+ staff members should be treated in the wake of the Supreme Court and EHRC Code of Practice.

It set out that single-sex changing and toilet facilities on NHS properties now must be offered on the basis of 'biological sex' too. It says alternative provisions, like accessible and lockable cubicles, may need to be created for trans people.

It follows multiple cases brought by gender-critical nurses, including Sandie Peggie and the Darlington Nurses, that have pressured NHS England to change its approach.

Notably, however, in both cases the rulings were not simple anti-Trans victories. In the case of the Darlington Nurses, the employment tribunal exonerated a trans woman who faced accusations of harassment and discrimination for using a women's changing room at the County Durham and Darlington NHS Trust. But it did so while concluding that the Trust had harassed the group of eight nurses by allowing Trans+ people to use the changing rooms and bathroom of their choice.

In Sandie Peggie's case, which she is now preparing for another tranche of action about – this time against her union – ruled that the Supreme Court’s ruling on the Equality Act does not require Trans+ people to be segregated from single sex bathrooms and changing areas. Both cases have now been superseded by the EHRC Code of Practice, which aligned with the gender-critical arguments in these cases.

Speaking to Trans+ organisations in the wake of the publication of this guidance yesterday, as well as the clear sense of yet another "unworkable" policy, many expressed concerns that Trans+ people simply would not get access to care because of these additional requirements. That’s why some say it will lead to deaths.

More broadly, this decision will further affirm a growing sentiment peddled by media, politicians and anti-trans actors that it is fair game to challenge people's gender for ever-narrowing ideals of what men and women should look like. The hospital ward, which should be about care and recovery for people struggling with their health and disabilities, will instead become another playground where culture wars will play out.

As a disabled immunocompromised person who's spent at least three years of my life in NHS beds, I've seen first-hand how few resources NHS staff have, a situation that's got increasingly worse in the 17 years I’ve been accessing it for my condition. I know that there are not enough private rooms for the most clinically vulnerable, let alone anyone else. The idea that Trans+ people can be put in side rooms is a fallacy; I could rarely get one despite my clinical needs.

On top of this, whose job is it to navigate claims that people are being placed on the wrong wards? As a statement by TransActual and Trans+ Solidarity Alliance set out, "Doctors and nurses need to be able to prioritise looking after the person in front of them, not juggling scarce side rooms and writing breach reports to keep trans people safe."

"This guidance will not survive contact with reality in resource-strapped hospitals and will create unworkable operational challenges. The government failing to get a grip of this legal mess is sadly putting politics over patient care.

Segregation has already begun - with signs appearing across even spaces that might feel like progressive bastions - pointing Trans+ people to gender nuetral bathrooms.

Despite claims 'sex questioning' will be rare, forms of gender policing have been on the rise since anti-trans movements gained a foothold in the public sphere.

We're aware of all kinds of attempts to undermine Trans+ rights taking place at businesses, in government and in civil society. But we simply don't have the resources to investigate them all.

A Florida man is facing charges after deputies say he shot his girlfriend and then proceeded to run her over with his vehicle while his child was in the car.

It happened after the couple allegedly got into an argument across the street from a bar in Safe Harbor, Florida.

The Pinellas County Sheriff’s Office said Christopher “Dodge” Smith, 40, is the man behind the attack.

Deputies named his girlfriend Jessica Antolini, 30, as the victim.

According to a criminal complaint, Smith showed up at a bar on Tuesday just before 9 p.m. and appeared to be “hunting” the victim down, witnesses said, adding he looked “possessed.”

The complaint says once the suspect found his girlfriend, they got into an argument outside the bar where he allegedly shot her in the face.

After gunning her down, deputies say he ran her over with his SUV and sped off from the scene with his 5-year-old child also in the car — leaving the victim behind.

“Detectives say multiple 911 calls reporting the shooting were received from witnesses who also provided information about Smith’s vehicle,” the report says.

Responding to those numerous calls, deputies arrived on scene and later located Smith’s SUV and tried to pull him over.

He did not comply, deputies say, to which his “vehicle was immobilized.”

Bodycam, dashcam and aerial video released by PCSO appear to show a deputy vehicle successfully pulling off a PIT maneuver of his SUV.

He was arrested on charges of attempted first-degree murder and child abuse following the pursuit.

His girlfriend is still in the hospital in critical condition; the child inside the vehicle was not injured in the incident and was reunited with family.

Smith is sitting inside a Pinellas County jail cell with no bond due to the charge of attempted first-degree murder.

But behind the red lights, thumping playlists and punishing treadmill sessions, the company is now facing uncomfortable questions about staff morale.

The Daily Mail has approached Barry's Australia multiple times for comment.

In September, veteran trainer Nicole Swift (née Christey) announced in an Instagram Story that she was leaving Barry's Australia 'for good', adding a cheeky 'for real this time lol'.

But it was her explanation that really caught the attention of fellow instructors.

'I cannot continue to align myself with a brand that has allowed certain behaviours and actions to take place,' she wrote.

'After a lot of thought, I've realised that I can't continue to be part of a business when I no longer feel that alignment exists.'

Swift did not name anyone or specify the conduct she was referring to. However, the Mail understands her concerns about the company were linked to Ruscoe's hiring.

Her post was subsequently circulated among fellow trainers, prompting speculation about what had led her to walk away.

After the Mail reported on her departure, Swift took to Instagram to criticise the article, describing it as 'trash' and questioning why the publication had contacted her for comment.

Days later, another popular instructor delivered a blow to his loyal Saturday-morning following, revealing he would no longer be teaching the weekend sessions after more than seven years with the business.

'Unfortunately I won't be teaching anyone ever again on Saturdays for a @barrysaustralia session,' he wrote.

Another trainer announced their sudden departure with this Instagram post

Barry's trainers are elevated to near-celebrity status in the brand's marketing

Back in July 2023, Ruscoe did her best to keep a low profile after she was charged with assault

'This is due to "management and business needs".'

'Wild to me seeing as I've done the same Saturday classes for over seven years.'

The trainer, described by one longtime fan as 'a legend', has since landed a new gig at buzzy Pilates studio Body by Berner, where he is set to become its first male instructor.

The departures have intensified concerns about the atmosphere inside Barry's Australia, although neither instructor has publicly detailed the full circumstances behind their exit.

Meanwhile, Barry's Melbourne operation has been attracting attention of its own, with its South Yarra studio at the centre of questions about staff dynamics.

The studio is managed by Ariel Kaplan, the former Neighbours and The Saddle Club actress who swapped Ramsay Street for the Red Room.

Kaplan has faced questions from the Mail about concerns reportedly raised by staff over the appointment of a trainer who has since left Barry's and moved to another gym in Perth.

We understand the recruitment decision was among the issues discussed by staff, although the full circumstances remain unclear.

When contacted earlier last month, Kaplan was not willing to discuss the matter.

'I have nothing to say,' she said before abruptly ending the call.

South Yarra studio manager Ariel Kaplan has faced questions raised by staff over the appointment of a trainer who has since left Barry's and moved to another gym in Perth

There is no suggestion Kaplan has been accused of any personal wrongdoing, nor is there any indication the issues at the Melbourne and Sydney gyms are connected.

In a recently deleted Reddit thread discussing the behind-the-scenes drama at Barry's, one user wrote: 'There is one trainer in particular that has a little posse of clients / loyalists who thinks she's top s*** because she has an almost monopoly of peak times slots. [She] brags about how full her classes are to members and tries to benchmark herself to other trainers who have less desirable slots that their classes "should be as full as hers".'

Founded in Los Angeles in 1998, Barry's Bootcamp has become an international fitness institution, with its signature combination of high-intensity treadmill work, strength training and nightclub-style lighting attracting a devoted following.

Its Australian studios have become a favourite among influencers, socialites and the well-heeled fitness crowd.

But with longtime instructors walking away and concerns mounting over staff morale, the brand's carefully polished image is beginning to crack.

Supercars will return to Phillip Island for the first time since 2019 as part of a five-year deal with the Victorian government.

The first Supercars event will be held on Phillip Island in 2027.

Supercars will return to Phillip Island next year, helping plug an economic gap left by MotoGP's move to Adelaide.

Victorian Major Events Minister Anthony Carbines today announced a five-year deal to host a Supercars Championship final series round.

It will be the first time since 2019 that the island has hosted Supercars.

"We know Supercars fans are wrapped with this news. We know our drivers are wrapped because they love Phillip Island, they love the circuit and they can't wait," Mr Carbines said.

"It was critical that we got back out there and made sure we locked in something that was going to make a big difference to the community of Phillip Island and the vast coast, but also to bring Supercars back to the Island."

Phillip Island will host its final MotoGP from October 23 to 25.

The track has hosted the event since 1989, but lost it to South Australia after the Victorian government rejected a request to move it from Phillip Island to Melbourne's Albert Park.

It later lost the Australian round of the FIM Superbike World Championships, which will be held on Phillip Island for the last time in 2027.

The loss of the two events has created anxiety in the local business community, which relies heavily on event-driven tourism.

Local tourism body Destination Phillip Island says racing is worth $80 million to the local economy.

Phillip Island will host a Festival of Motoring in March next year, with Labor and the Coalition both promising to back the event.

Opposition major events spokesperson David Southwick today said the Coalition would provide $100,000 to fund the event if it wins November's state election.

Keith Mortimer says motorsport connects many visitors to Phillip Island. (ABC Gippsland: Madeleine Stuchbery)

by-the-past-standards-nidal-hasan:
Betrayal, dishonor, cowardly violence, willful cruelty to defenseless victims: rapid and certain execution upon discovery. This is the American military norm.

To understand the upcoming execution of Nidal Hasan, understand Plot E at Oise-Aisne.

At the beginning of June 1943, American soldiers searching for a missing nine-year-old girl in Algeria found her body face down in a field. An army doctor examined the body and concluded that the child had been sexually assaulted and suffocated, probably several days earlier.

A soldier, Pvt. James Kendrick, had been seen with the girl. He told a series of shifting stories that ended with the claim that the sexually aggressive child had come on to him and asked to have sex, after which she suddenly and inexplicably just started to choke. Kendrick’s court-martial opened on June 12, quickly convicting him and sentencing him to death. He was executed by hanging on July 17.

Pay close attention to the timeline: crime in very late May, discovery in early June, trial in mid-June, execution in mid-July.

Later, the army dug up Kendrick’s body in Algeria and transferred it to a new cemetery plot, Plot E at the Oise-Aisne American Cemetery in France. That hidden plot, locked away behind tall walls, is where the American military relocated the bodies of 96 soldiers executed in Europe and North Africa during World War II. The graves in Plot E are marked only by a number, the names of the dead denied to them in shame. Visitors are rare, and need special permission for brief and supervised entry.

The army quickly executed soldiers who shamed their uniform and betrayed their brothers-in-arms, then took the trouble to relocate the bodies to a place where they couldn’t be honored, visited, or mourned.

You can find the stories of the army’s 96 hidden bodies in Col. French MacLean’s detailed history of Plot E, The Fifth Field.

Those stories tend to go about the same way. Pvt. Fred McMurray and Pvt. Louis Till raped a pregnant woman in Italy, causing her to miscarry, and raped a second pregnant woman, then shot and killed a third woman who resisted as they tried to force their way into her home. The crime took place on June 27, 1944. Administrative delays slowed the opening of the court-martial – because the US Army was kind of busy in Europe in the summer of 1944 – so the executions by hanging weren’t carried out until July 10, 1945. By the prevailing standards, a year was a long wait. Soldiers who murdered a pregnant woman could expect to be executed.

Betrayal, dishonor, cowardly violence, willful cruelty to defenseless victims: rapid and certain execution upon discovery. This is the American military norm, though it began to shift after World War II as the military justice system was steadily reformed to look more like civilian justice.

For an example of the way the military has treated American soldiers who kill other American soldiers, consider the ending of the St. Patrick’s Battalion during the Mexican-American War. Irish immigrants enlisted in the US Army, sometimes at the docks as they arrived in the country, but then rebelled against nativist officers who applied harsher discipline to Irish Catholics. Many deserted and fought for Mexico, firing at their former colleagues in battle.

Captured, dozens were executed. On September 13, 1847, thirty were hanged in a group as the American flag was raised at Chapultepec Castle, signaling an American victory. The Irish deserters to the Mexican army watched the Mexican flag come down, then watched the American flag go up, then felt the drop.

Supervising the mass execution, Col. William S. Harney declined to have the executed men cut down and removed from the gallows. As he said, he had orders to hang them, but no orders to unhang them. Their bodies were left to rot, hanging where the men died. They were regarded as traitors who had worn the uniform of the U.S. Army before turning against it, and the intensity of that sentiment transferred to their lifeless bodies.

Compare all of that to the example of Maj. Nidal Hasan, who chose to take an officer’s commission in the U.S. Army, then killed other men and women who wore the same uniform. Pvt. Francheska Velez was pregnant, and screamed, “My baby! My baby!” as Hasan started shooting. He killed her as she begged for the life of her unborn child. Hasan attacked his fellow soldiers in 2009, wearing their uniform as he fired.

In the context of American military history, the anomalous fact of the execution is that it has taken so incredibly long to be scheduled. The man has been treated with far more restraint than any American soldier should ever have expected after so consequential a betrayal.

The Trump administration has desperately searched for evidence that Rep. Ilhan Omar committed fraud, alleging she or her late father are liars for changing her age from 18 to 17 years old on her citizenship application.

According to what US officials and other people with knowledge of the federal government’s investigation told the Wall Street Journal, the goal is to construct a case to strip the Minnesota congresswoman of her American citizenship and deport her from the US. Early Monday morning, the Journal reported, Homeland Security agents took Omar’s phone, notebooks, personal computers, and her passport during the raid on her DC home. Authorities have also reportedly handed out more than a dozen subpoenas, which the New York Times wrote Wednesday include Sahra Noor, Omar’s sister, and “at least one other member of her family circle.

On Monday evening, the crowd at an Ohio Republican rally chanted “deport” as President Donald Trump yet again hurled racist rhetoric at Omar, people from Somalia living in Minnesota—whom he called “Somali bandits”—and Michigan Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed (Trump called him “a jihadist”).

On Tuesday, the president suggested on Truth Social that Omar had also committed financial fraud: “Could it be that her highly paid accountant actually reported the money that was stolen from her fraudulent account activities in Minnesota?”

The same day, Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney in Washington, said she is looking into Omar’s financial disclosures.

“There are several investigations going on,” she said Tuesday on Fox News. “If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted.” The US attorney also asserted it “doesn’t matter” that a nonpartisan, independent body found Omar blameless of wrongdoing and recommended the House Ethics Committee withdraw misconduct allegations when she substantially overstated her wealth in documents she submitted to Congress.

All of this is happening just three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is favored to win reelection.
