zelensky-urges-unity-more-money-for-ukra:
EUobserver

Europe today

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Brussels with two main requests for his meeting with EU leaders on Friday (16 October): more funds for Kyiv for defence and more sanctions against Russia.

“All of us in Europe want this war to end. And for that to happen, strong signals are needed – more real pressure on Russia and more defence support for Ukraine,” he said on X.

“It is especially important now to act together to protect lives,” he added.

Zelensky’s plea comes days after US president Donald Trump announced a deal to bring Russian diesel to the US and global markets, raising questions about the consistency of Western efforts to restrict Russia’s energy revenues that are feeding the Kremlin war machine.

EU leaders are expected to “regret” the Trump-Putin deal in their summit conclusions, where they also mention more financial, humanitarian and diplomatic support to Kyiv ahead of what many predict to be one of the most difficult winters for Ukraine.

Dutch PM Rob Jetten said the diesel deal was “not a good step”, adding that “Europe has to show that we are not only dependent on the US”.

But he also appealed directly to the US, calling for more support: “Do what is necessary to support the Ukrainians. They need not only sufficient weapons to defend Ukraine, but also the information they need to repel Russian attacks.”

Despite the diesel deal, Estonian PM Kristen Michal, whose country hosts a US military base, also said the US is still a “partner” of Europe in the war in Ukraine.

“We will see what happens in the midterm elections. But I will never give up trying to talk to and convince … our transatlantic partners that we are better off united than divided on this issue,” European Parliament president Roberta Metsola said during a press conference on Thursday after meeting EU leaders.

And in a warning to Moscow about Nato’s unity, US top military commander Alexus Grynkewich also said earlier this week in Warsaw that any “foolish” attack on the Nato alliance would be "utterly futile".

In December 2025, EU leaders failed to agree to use over €210bn in Russian frozen funds sitting in Europe and instead decided to go for a €90bn loan, aimed at covering about two-thirds of Ukraine’s external financing needs.

“The remaining third is the problem,” Tetiana Shevchuk, from the Kyiv-based Anti-Corruption Action Center, told EUobserver, referring to commitments by other countries like Canada and Japan coming only for 2026. “2027 is the real gap”.

The €90bn loan is split into €45bn for 2026 and 2027, but recent reports point to about a €23bn financial gap amid an expected Russian escalation ahead of the winter.

Zelensky has asked Brussels to bring forward part of the loan to cover this gap in the defence ministry. But Brussels fears this advance “could unravel the compromise on gradual instalments and leave a hole later in 2027,” Shevchuk also said.

The global war on terror beat back organized terrorism significantly in the 25 years since American forces invaded Afghanistan, but by most measures, that 20-year war and subsequent U.S. war in Iraq were costly failures in ways that left the region and its people worse off.

Clearly, the United States is safer from attack than it was on Sept. 11, 2001, when members of al-Qaida who trained in Afghanistan carried out the horrific suicide terrorist attacks that slaughtered 2,977 people at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and in a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Credit goes to successive Republican and Democratic administrations.
But the conduct of America’s longest war and the chaotic withdrawal of U.S. forces in 2021 let the Taliban return to power and revive its repressive Islamic regime, bringing an uneasy peace but also a heavily armed extremist government, economic hardship, a loss of freedom and a deplorable ban on girls over 12 getting an education. The recent U.S. withdrawal from Iraq, another endless war, left the region more perilous and empowered Iran to claim success there.
“I think the threat to the U.S. from Afghanistan is much lower than it was in 2001,” said Adam Weinstein, deputy director of the Middle East Program at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft in Washington, D.C. “Is it zero? No, but we can’t be everywhere at once.”

“We didn’t have another 9/11, and there was a lot of work that was done quietly to prevent more terrorist attacks,” Weinstein, a former Marine who served in Afghanistan, said in an interview. “But I don’t think it’s necessary for Americans to be deployed all over the world to prevent terrorism.”
Former President George W. Bush launched the war on Oct. 7, 2001 that ousted the Taliban from power. Almost 10 years later, then-President Barack Obama dispatched Navy SEALs to storm a compound in northern Pakistan on May 2, 2011, and they killed al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden, mastermind of the 9/11 attacks. Joe Biden as president authorized a CIA drone strike in Kabul a year after the U.S. pullout that killed bin Laden’s successor, al-Qaida leader Ayman al-Zawahri, co-conspirator in conceiving the 9/11 attacks and global terrorist plans.
Al-Qaida has “declining relevance as a global movement,” according to one United Nations monitoring group, but U.S. and Western intelligence officials assess it still has training camps and safe houses in Afghanistan under Taliban protection. Thankfully, for now, it is said to be focused more on regional activities than planning grand, far-away attacks on the U.S. and its allies.
At the end of last month, American troops withdrew from Iraq following the deadliest war of the 21st century for U.S. forces. That war, launched in 2003 as part of the war on terror, is widely considered a disastrous strategic mistake, because Iraq had no significant links to al-Qaida and no terrorist weapons of mass destruction. Most experts agree the U.S. mishandled post-invasion planning.				
					
				
The courageous work of U.S. and allied ground troops from 37 countries toppled Sunni Muslim Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein and installed a Shiite-led government to help fight an insurgency until the first phase ended in 2009. American forces later returned to Iraq from 2014 to 2017 to put down Sunni Islamic State militants, but the Iraq war severely damaged America’s reputation and emboldened U.S. enemies in the region.
While the terrorist threat to the U.S. is much lower now and over-the-horizon anti-terrorism strategies have been effective, the overall lessons of the war on terror are that military force alone cannot guarantee the success of U.S. policies or the safety of Americans. It must be combined with engagement, economic power and diplomatic leverage. President Donald Trump has learned that the hard way with his ill-conceived war of choice in Iran.
Sadly, bin Laden got some of what he wanted when his monstrous terrorist plot forced the U.S. to dispatch American forces to the region, and thousands were lost in battles. According to one study by Brown University in 2021, the cost of the U.S.-led global war on terror was an estimated $8 trillion and some 900,000 deaths of military and civilian casualties on all sides. Of that total, estimated cost of operations in Afghanistan and Pakistan was $2.3 trillion, and another $2.1 trillion was committed for Iraq and Syria.
More than 7,000 U.S. service members lost their lives in the Afghanistan and Iraq conflicts, and more than 53,000 were wounded. And $2.2 trillion of the total cost is designated for future medical care and disability payments over the coming decades. The war on terror and counterterror operations continue in more than 80 countries today, the Brown study said.				
					
				
Terrorism remains a significant global threat, according to the Global Terrorism Index compiled by the Institute for Economics and Peace, headquartered in Sydney, but there are some positive trends. This year, the GTI reported that the largest declines in terrorist activity by percentage since 2007 have been in Iraq (99%) and Afghanistan (95%). In fact, deaths from terrorism have fluctuated significantly since 2007, when records started for the GTI, peaking at 10,882 in 2015 and reaching a low of 5,582 last year. Most global terrorism incidents have shifted from the Middle East and South Asia to Africa, according to the U.N. committee charged with monitoring the sanctions regime for terrorism.
Yes, things are calm from Kabul to Kandahar, but al-Qaida and other terrorist groups still operate in Afghanistan. The U.S. needs to shift its strategy to reengage there in more meaningful ways than hostage negotiations. The real policy disaster was less the chaotic pullout of American forces in August 2021 but rather the polices that led to it with the fall of the Taliban in December 2001, when the U.S. started pursuing a war without end that America could not win.
The Trump administration and its successors should focus now on cleaning up the mess America left behind and making small gains where possible through targeted diplomacy, not nation building, for now, as the Quincy Institute’s Weinstein advocates.

That means engaging with the Taliban’s de facto government and using humanitarian aid and economic leverage to make progress — picking up where military victory proved impossible. America still needs a regional, over-the-horizon counterterrorism strategy to protect the homeland. That might be difficult, sure, but it’s a must.

California parents are furious at a school district after four teenage girls posted a TikTok in blackface last month.

The girls were disciplined, but parents claimed their conduct is part of a pattern at Santa Barbara Unified School District.

Parents sat with signs decrying racism at a school board meeting on Tuesday night. Signs read things like, “Don’t be a bystander, stop ignoring racism,” and “What was the reason it took two weeks and some to notify parents?” and “racism doesn’t disappear when it’s swept under the rug.”

Most of the signs were made because of an organized protest in favor of black students and demanded action from the district.

Most of the discourse surrounded the girls’ TikTok video in which the girls are seen mimicking an AI-generated image of four young black boys in various poses. “Meet the gc🥷🥷🥷🥷🥷🥷🥷…,” the post is captioned. The ninja emoji is known to be used as a reference to the N-word.

San Marcos High School Principal Dare Holdren previously said the students “portrayed blackface” in the post and noted the school “instituted consequences” for the girls.

Parents wondered why it took Holdren two weeks to notify them of the incident.

“Parents deserve to know,” Leticia Forney Resch, an executive director for Healing Justice Santa Barbara, said. “They had pictures and images going out to students for a week-and-a-half… Y’all didn’t do your job.”

The girls posed for the picture in an African American studies classroom. The teacher who uses the room as his classroom expressed outrage at the racism in the school.

“When black students are harmed, every student is harmed,” Abel Gonzalez, the ethnic studies teacher at San Marcos High School, said. “Black and brown students are very upset and trying to heal.”

Other racist incidents have rattled the school district in the past.

According to the Santa Barbara Independent, a San Marcos High School substitute teacher read the N-word out loud during a reading of “Of Mice and Men” last year after being told not to. The substitute was then removed from campus.

A parent said the district has just watched racism escalate.

“When a nation refuses to confront institutional and structural racism, the harm does not stay contained, it escalates,” Charlotte Gullap-Moore said. “Santa Barbara Unified has watched that escalation in its own schools.”

The local NAACP previously criticized the school for failing to establish protocols to respond to incidents of racism.

“SBUSD has struggled to establish protocols to respond to racial incidents and execute them with humanity. Principals need clear guidance; parents and students need accessible information about district investigations and potential disciplinary actions for racist incidents,” NAACP Santa Barbara President Connie Alexander wrote in an op-ed for the Santa Barbara Independent.

Even teachers say the only way the school district can remedy the situation is action.

“Doing nothing tells this community that anti-Black bias and racism is woven into the fabric of Santa Barbara schools,” Moore, speaking on behalf of Santa Barbara Unified teacher Tahnia Mark, said. “So be honest, do you really care about black students? If you don’t, just say it…Otherwise, show through action.”

Mike Flanagan is a legendary name in the horror genre, and unlike your typical slasher and gore content, his horror stories generally tell very complex stories that play out over a lengthy period of time.

Below are his notable series:

Flanagan reached a deal in 2022 to jump from Netflix to Amazon Studios ("The Fall of the House of Usher" was his final Netflix product), and "Carrie" is his first show for the company.

Now, to be clear, I have never read the book written by Stephen King or seen any of the movies or TV products that were created.

I know the 1976 film is considered a classic in the horror genre, and I understand the basic plot premise of a young woman ultimately terrorizing the people around her.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

I went into the premiere of "Carrie" more or less completely blind outside of the stated facts above, and as you all know, I prefer it that way most of the time.

The series isn't a linear timeline through the premiere episode. It jumps between Carrie's introduction to being forced into a public school following her father's death and people being interviewed in a later timeline after some kind of horrific tragedy.

Amber Midthunder as gym teacher Miss Rita Desjardin in "Carrie." (Robert Falconer/Prime)

In the school timeline Carrie is an isolated and shielded child struggling with her father's death and essentially thrown to the wolves at school. She's completely unprepared for the shift of not knowing much about the outside world to be bullied and traumatized by a school shooting drill.

There's immediate signs of paranormal capabilities that nobody, Carrie included, have a handle on. In the later timeline, viewers don't see Carrie at all.

There are only traumatized survivors, clear indications that a violent event has occurred and confirmed deaths of characters introduced in the premiere.

Personally, I like the creative choice from Flanagan. It sets the stage to see Carrie's arc from innocent child to someone who plays a pivotal role (although, seemingly not alone based on what is shown in the premiere) of a live-altering event.

One of the most interesting choices from Flanagan is that in the later timeline with the interviews, Carrie isn't painted as a villain by anyone.

That would seem to indicate she will continue to be a sympathetic figure throughout season one. It will be fascinating to see that continue to unfold. I will tell you there are some painfully uncomfortable scenes in the premiere, especially one in a locker room, that are a bit difficult to sit through but do provide specific plot purposes.

inflation-jumps-higher-midterms:
Scott Horsley

Rising gasoline and diesel prices pushed inflation higher in September. The cost of living index was up 3.7%, according to a report Wednesday from the Labor Department.
                
                    
                    Isabelle Souriment/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

Nights are getting colder, but inflation is heating up.

A report from the Labor Department on Wednesday showed consumer prices in September were up 3.7% from a year ago. That's a larger annual increase than the previous month.

A spike in energy prices tied to the U.S. war with Iran drove the cost of living higher.  Prices jumped 0.6% between August and September.

"It's not looking good," said economist Brian Bethune of Boston College. "The main problem, of course, that everybody knows is gasoline prices. But also heating oil."

Heating oil is a close cousin of diesel fuel. The cost of the fuel oil has jumped 74% in the last year, which is hard on families in New England who rely on heating oil to stay warm.

Stripping out volatile energy and food prices, what's known as "core inflation" was 2.6% in September. That's also a bigger annual increase than was tallied in August.

The artificial intelligence boom has raised the cost of memory chips, affecting all sorts of consumer electronics. Apple, for example, raised the price of older-model iPhones last month by $100 apiece.

Shortly after the inflation report was released, the Social Security Administration announced that benefits will increase by 3.6% next year.  The annual cost-of-living adjustment is based on prices in July, August and September.

The jump in benefits amounts to an extra $75 a month for the average Social Security recipient.

Advocates for seniors welcomed the increase.

"It helps millions of Americans keep up with rising costs for groceries, routine bills, healthcare and other everyday expenses," said AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan.

Loading...

But critics complain that the cost-of-living adjustment doesn't reflect seniors' actual expenses, which often include higher costs for healthcare.

"It won't be enough for most seniors to even tread water financially," said Max Richtman, president of the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare.

Treading water would be an improvement for most workers, whose paychecks are not keeping pace with today's rising prices.

Average wages in September rose just 3%, so the typical worker's buying power has eroded over the last year.

"People are kind of saying, 'Something isn't right with that,'" Bethune said. "I'm working harder. I'm more productive. And this is not a square deal."

Inflation is not nearly as high as it was in 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. But every time prices start to level off, the economy is rattled by a new supply shock, such as President Trump's double-digit tariffs or the war with Iran.

Beth Hammack, who heads the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank, worries the cumulative effect of these shocks could make inflation more entrenched. Hammack told a group of economists this week about a Cleveland-area retailer she'd heard from who is raising prices not just to cover today's costs but the higher costs that may come in the future.

"This could be a sign that an inflationary mindset is taking hold," Hammack said. "When people expect higher prices, they make decisions with this in mind. It can become a self-fulfilling prophecy that makes it harder for monetary policy to bring inflation back down."

Policymakers at the Federal Reserve will weigh the new inflation data when they meet in two weeks to discuss interest rates. Investors now see about a 50-50 chance the Fed will raise its benchmark rate in October in an effort to combat inflation.

An earlier version of this story said that inflation was higher in 2002, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The invasion and the resulting spike in prices were in 2022.

An illegal immigrant couple dubbed “Bonnie and Clyde” by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) allegedly turned strangers’ kindness into a payday, stealing necklaces from elderly victims in a jewelry theft spree stretching across four states.

Rudi Lacatusu, 28, and Mirabela Lacatusu, 26, Romanian nationals accused of targeting victims on Long Island, are now in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody, DHS announced Tuesday.

The pair allegedly carried out at least 14 jewelry thefts across New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Maryland, according to DHS, which cited local reporting.

The stolen necklaces were valued between $2,000 and $3,000 each.

One alleged encounter began with a seemingly innocent request for directions.

A 73-year-old woman was standing outside her Valley Stream, New York, home Oct. 5, when a gold Mitsubishi with a man and woman inside pulled up, Nassau County police said. The female passenger asked how to get to BJ’s Wholesale Club.

After the woman helped, the passenger stepped out, asked to hug her and placed two gold-colored necklaces around her neck, according to detectives.

A short time later, the woman realized her own gold necklace, worth approximately $2,000, was gone.

Investigators linked the suspects to similar thefts in Franklin Square and East Meadow. Each faces three counts of fourth-degree grand larceny, police said.

DHS said Nassau County authorities turned the couple over to ICE after their arrests. Both entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown time and location, according to DHS.

“This ‘Bonnie and Clyde’ illegal alien couple from Romania has been charged with grand larceny after allegedly carrying out more than a dozen jewelry thefts across four states,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.

“Thanks to local partners in New York, these illegal aliens are in ICE custody and will be removed from our country.”

Mullin also took aim at Democrat New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, arguing that sanctuary policies put Americans at risk.

“If it were up to sanctuary politicians like Governor Kathy Hochul, these criminals would be back on the streets to rob more Americans,” he said.

DHS used the arrests to renew its criticism of New York’s sanctuary policies, calling the state a “hotbed of illegal alien crime” under Hochul. DHS also argued those policies have had “disastrous consequences” beyond New York’s borders.

The announcement follows Operation Rotten Apple, an ICE crackdown that ran from July 27 through Aug. 29.

DHS said officers arrested 2,197 illegal immigrants across New York during the operation, including people the department described as murderers, rapists, child predators, drug traffickers and violent assailants.

Nassau County police initially issued the suspects appearance tickets directing them to court in Hempstead Oct. 20, according to the department’s arrest announcement. DHS’ statement Tuesday did not specify when ICE took custody of them.

The case prompted police to warn residents about distraction scams targeting elderly people, including strangers offering jewelry or gifts, asking to pray together, requesting change or seeking help with a flat tire.

While a victim’s attention is elsewhere, the thieves can remove jewelry directly from their body, police warned.

Authorities urged residents to stay alert in parking lots and outside grocery stores and call 911 to report suspicious activity.

Anyone who has been targeted in a similar theft can contact Nassau County Crime Stoppers at 1-800-244-TIPS.

Apple’s ad introducing its new HomeView smart display is a little unusual. It’s fast-paced and unruly, depicting a family of five as they rush through the morning routine. There’s yelling and mess, misplaced keys and discarded eggshells. Apple’s typical vibe is clean, simple, orderly; this commercial is chaos.

But the spot has parents — those with teen children in particular — feeling seen.

I’ll admit that it stressed me out the first time I watched it, too. Mornings getting my five-year-old out the door are a special breed of chaos, and usually culminate in us playing whatever ad-libbed game will get him to put his shoes on. But it’s not quite as intense as this one, which features dad making french toast, mom losing and finding keys in her pocket, a proxy battle over the thermostat, a teenage boy helping himself to whipped cream from a can, and an unexpected video call. There’s also a microdrama about the daughter’s ride to school with a boyfriend nobody knew about that ends with everyone gathered around the HomeView watching the security camera feed of the two of them departing the porch. It’s a lot for just over three minutes of screen time.

If I know anything though, I know to trust my colleague, senior reviewer and parent to two teens, Jen Tuohy on matters of the home. Her take? “The most unrealistic part of the video is that no one is holding an iPhone.”

Other parents of teens shared similar reactions on Threads. When tech analyst Benedict Evans posted about the ad feeling stressful and confusing, CNET editor at large Bridget Carey chimed in to defend it, saying “It was exactly what my morning is like and it was the most real ad I’ve ever seen from Apple.” Others agreed, calling it “accurately captured” and that it “hit home,” no pun intended, at least I think.

Even if Apple didn’t need to do much to heighten the stakes of a family getting out the door, there is of course plenty of sleight-of-hand at work when it comes to making the HomeView appear so essential. The family has seemingly drilled a hole directly into the middle of their kitchen island to accommodate the charging cable, for one. And what sibling is going to check a text message from a secret boyfriend on the communal kitchen screen with their brother sitting at arm’s length? I don’t believe any teenager trusts Apple’s privacy features that far.

The confusion about the commercial is understandable. This is a far cry from the quiet luxury lifestyle everyone seems to enjoy in Apple’s Vision Pro ads. There’s also Evans’ observation that the HomeView doesn’t really solve any of the problems that come up throughout the coarse of the video. In the case of a spontaneous FaceTime call from the grandparents, the screen in the middle of the kitchen seems to make things worse.

But maybe morning chaos isn’t the problem that’s being solved. If the alternative is five people all interacting with their own phones, then the HomeView presents a different picture where everyone gets the essential information they need from one shared screen and stays more present.

A screen that makes you be more present is a lovely idea, but the real test will come when it’s in in real households. Is the HomeView going to be enough to convince families to put their personal devices down? Will everyone just ignore it and keep scrolling on their own iPhones? These are questions worth answering before you start drilling holes in your kitchen island! In any case, an ungovernable morning routine is probably a feature of a busy household, not a bug. Just ask a parent.

WASHINGTON — The House speaker stood before Donald Trump during his first term at the White House and pointed a finger, declaring that with this president, “All roads lead to Putin.”

The stark assessment years ago from Nancy Pelosi echoed anew after Trump’s surprise announcement last week that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import tons of Russian diesel to the U.S. as a way to ease sky-high prices at the pumps for Americans ahead of the midterm elections.

Trump’s diesel deal with Putin has been criticized by both Republicans and Democrats as fueling Russia’s war against Ukraine, violating existing U.S. laws and drawing the U.S. closer to Russia. It joins a growing list of instances in which the Republican president has sided with Putin, often at the expense of Ukraine — and America’s own standing.

“The harm to the Ukrainians is real,” said William Taylor, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine, now a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, in an interview Monday.

“And the cost to us, the United States, is high.”

It’s not at all clear the Trump-Putin deal will deliver the supply boost the president is seeking to bring down prices. Energy experts have said the flow of Russian diesel is unlikely to lower prices in the U.S., which have escalated largely due to disruptions from the U.S. war against Iran. But the agreement underlines a message at home and abroad that Trump is an unreliable ally as Ukraine battles Russia.

A bipartisan group of six senators urged Trump over the weekend to reverse course, saying the U.S. “should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline.” Trump, however, held fast to his deal with Putin and lashed out, blaming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for America’s high diesel costs and asserting he should step aside — something Ukraine’s leader has no intention of doing.

“Anything that could help our farmers, our ranchers, I like,” Trump said Monday outside the White House.

Asked about Republican criticism of the Russia deal, Trump said they “can’t really be serious.”

Trump also insisted that an energy ceasefire is in place for Ukraine and Russia, despite Zelenskyy saying that Moscow continued to strike his country’s energy sites.

An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices.

Congress swiftly approved legislation at the outset of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in spring of 2022 to ban the import of Russian energy products, which are widely viewed as providing the financial fuel for Putin’s military assault on Ukraine.

The bill passed the House on an overwhelming 414-17 vote and the Senate without a single senator opposed. The law says the president can seek to lift the prohibition if an agreement has been reached to withdraw Russian troops from Ukraine and cease military activity. Such a proposal would need to be reviewed by Congress and to have been “accepted by the free and independent government of Ukraine.”

“Trump is directly violating that law,” said Rep. Lloyd Doggett, D-Texas, the bill’s chief sponsor, in a statement Monday.

He said Trump “illegally rewards his pal Putin while once again blaming Zelensky for not capitulating to Putin.”

More recently, Congress last month approved a sweeping Russian sanctions bill, named after the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would slap tariffs on countries that continue importing Russian oil. Trump signed the bill into law.

The bulk of the law’s provisions go into effect Oct. 18, the end of the administration’s 30-day review period. But such action now appears to be in question since Trump’s diesel deal with Putin will allow the flow of Russian energy.

In a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senate leaders from both parties last week said the most urgent priority for the U.S. must be to tackle the “shadow fleet” of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America’s sanctions.

But that was before Trump announced his deal with Putin, which he said would unleash hundreds of tons of diesel.

Treasury did not immediately respond Monday to a request for comment.

Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who faces a competitive race for the U.S. Senate against Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa, where $6 a gallon diesel prices have become an issue, said, “It makes me a little bit nervous anytime we’re talking about relieving a sanction on Russia.”

Almost seven years ago this week, Pelosi stood before Trump and a roomful of U.S. officials during a heated White House meeting and leveled her accusation, suggesting the president’s policy favored Putin.

The powerful House speaker led the first impeachment of Trump on corruption charges over his administration’s decision to withhold congressionally approved aid to Ukraine in 2019 as it faced Russian aggression at its border. Trump was later acquitted by the Senate.

Since Trump’s return to the White House, he has seesawed between pressuring Zelenskyy to make concessions and showing frustration with Putin’s hard-line stance on the war. Trump often complains that he thought his good relationship with his Russian counterpart would have made it easier to end the war.

A year ago, Trump reversed his long-held position that Ukraine would have to give up land and suggested it could win back all the territory it has lost to Russia — only later to call on Kyiv and Moscow to “stop where they are” and end the war.

In July, Trump praised Zelenskyy and Ukraine for their wartime resilience. But by September, Trump was expressing frustration about strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

Trump insisted Monday the sides agreed to a ceasefire on the energy systems. “They agreed,” Trump said. “Because I said, ‘You agree.’”

When pressed about the attacks by Russia, Trump said he’d have to take a look, “because there’s been violations on both sides.”

Associated Press writers Collin Binkley and Josh Boak, and Steven Sloan in Dyersville, Iowa, contributed to this report.

Statins may be protecting people from more than just cholesterol, suggests new research from the University of California in San Diego.

Patients with glaucoma who take the cholesterol-busting pills appear less likely to need surgery—and have a reduced chance of the condition worsening, according to the findings.

Called the “silent thief of sight” because the vision loss usually occurs slowly over a long period of time, glaucoma may cause blindness if left untreated, damaging the optic nerve, which transmits visual information from the eye to the brain.

The new study, published online in the British Journal of Ophthalmology, found that people who already have glaucoma who are taking statins appear less likely to need stronger treatments, such as extra eye drops or surgery to keep it under control.

“Statins are prescribed to lower cholesterol levels but studies have indicated that they may also prevent or slow nerve cell death,” said study author Dr. Robert Weinreb.

But their potential role in preventing or slowing down glaucoma—a leading cause of irreversible blindness which permanently damages the optic nerve—is poorly understood.

Dr. Weinreb and his team searched a large global database covering 165 million people and compared more than 210,000 patients who had a record of statin use between 2006 and 2026 with a matched control group of 210,000 people who had no record of using statins. People in both groups had to have a recorded ophthalmological follow up.

The findings show that statins were linked to a lower risk of the individual progressing to need glaucoma surgery—or any other treatment.

• Statin use was associated with a 15% lower risk of developing the most common form of the progressive eye disease.

• At five years, statin use was associated with a 36% lower risk of incisional glaucoma surgery and a 55% reduced risk of minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS), a keyhole procedure to lower the intraocular pressure in the eye.

• Statins were also associated with a 60% lower risk of ‘selective laser trabeculoplasty’ (SLT), a procedure that lowers the pressure in the eye by using laser pulses.

• There was also a 12% reduced risk of (needing) eye drops to reduce the pressure in the eye—linked to statin use.”

And after 10 years, statin use continued to be associated with a lower risk of incision glaucoma surgery, MIGS, SLT, and use of eye drops.

RELATED: Dyson Award Goes to First Ever Device to Monitor Glaucoma Symptoms From Home

In a separate analysis, more than 30,000 people with glaucoma who were taking statins were compared with almost 250,000 with glaucoma who weren’t taking the drug.

Although these were observational studies, so no firm conclusions can be drawn about cause and effect, the findings add to the growing literature about the neuro-protective effect of statin drugs.

Aiden Markram, Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood. (Getty Images/AP)

Alex Carey breaks the game open with a spectacular take, Pat Cummins confuses Beau Webster for Muttiah Muralitharan, and Josh Hazlewood's career-best wins it for Australia.

Here are the quick hits from the final day of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

The Australians were worried they might have to push to victory without the fielding brilliance of Smith. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

After not taking to the field after Pat Cummins's tea time declaration on day four, there were serious concerns that Australia would have to push for victory without the fielding brilliance of Steve Smith.

The Australia vice-captain was hit in the helmet by an Anrich Nortje bouncer while batting and was held back over fears of a delayed concussion.

But Australian fans would have been delighted to have seen Smith out on the field and warming up ahead of the final days play, suggesting the slipper supreme was right to re-assume his role in the cordon.

Speaking on Fox Cricket, Mitch Starc said Smith appeared to have "the light back in him" and he certainly seemed to as he snared a sharp chance at first slip, his fifth of the match, to get rid Kyle Verreynne in the 67th over.

Alex Carey's brilliant catch ended a troublesome Wiaan Mulder-Aiden Markram partnership. (Supplied: Fox Cricket)

Australia tried a lot of tricks to break the Aiden Markram-Wiaan Mulder partnership on the final morning of the Test at Kingsmead.

For 154 balls, near misses elicited plenty of "Ooh"s and maybe even the occasional "Aah", but little more despite some sensational bowling.

Then, in the space of four balls, everything changed.

Josh Hazlewood swung one towards the pads of Mulder, facing his 110th delivery, and it kept going down the leg side.

Mulder tried to help it on its way to fine leg as he'd done many times before, but only managed to get a faint tickle on it and that wasn't enough to evade Alex Carey.

Australia's phenomenal wicketkeeper shuffled and leapt to his left, sticking his gloved hand out and plucking the ball out of the air just centimetres off the grass.

The partnership broken, wicket-taking suddenly looked straightforward as Matt Renshaw nicked off Kyle Verreynne just three balls later to allow the Aussies to breathe a little easier.

Webster would have needed to produce some serious turn for it to be a successful review. (Fox Cricket)

With six overs still remaining between lunch and the new ball, Cummins had time to kill.

The Australia captain decided that cycling through his part-time spinners would be the most efficient way to get the 80th over.

But with the pitch offering some substantial turn and the South African tail exposed, the Australian fielders were an in excitable mood.

And in the first over after the break, that excitement was channelled into one of the most questionable reviews of Cummins's captaincy career.

Beau Webster, who has never been a big spinner of the ball to start with, pitched his off break far enough from the stumps that Jansen felt comfortable kicking it away.

Webster would have had to have transformed into a prime Muttiah Muralitharan to have gotten that one back towards the pegs — and he hadn't. The DRS projected the ball to be missing by a considerable distance.

Hazlewood ripped through the South African lower order. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Jansen and Markram made it to the new ball, but things went down pretty quickly after Starc and Hazlewood got their hands on the fresh cherry.

Hazlewood, who had started things off with the first two wickets of the innings on day four, produced a sensational 85th over double strike to all but end the South African resistance.

First, he found some movement off the pitch to castle Jansen, then, he procured some extra bounce to have Simon Harmer dismissed for a three-ball duck.

Mitch Starc then got in on the act to have the brilliant Aiden Markram caught behind on review, before Hazlewood fittingly ended the Test with the dismissal of Anrich Nortje.

The Proteas had lost their final four wickets for five runs and Hazlewood had career-best figures, with his 6-49 eclipsing the 6-67 from Bengaluru in 2017.

Aiden Markram has a habit of doing this to Australia. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Every time Aiden Markram bats in Tests against Australia, many of us find ourselves perplexed by his Test average in the mid-30s.

But all the ingredients were there to turn him into a modern Graeme Pollock.

Markram averages over 60 against Australia, comfortably highest among any of his Test opponents. His fourth-innings average is in the mid-40s — for reference, Steve Smith's run-chase average is 31.65. And, among grounds he's played more than two Tests on, Kingsmead is his best.

Australians may remember him for his fourth-innings 143 in Durban back in 2018, but more recently for a match-winning 136 in the World Test Championship final run chase last year.

And Markram was almost chanceless as he held South Africa's innings together with a marathon 237-ball 75, before his late dismissal spelled the end for the Proteas.

The two women vying to represent Colorado’s easternmost congressional district engaged in a feisty back-and-forth during a televised debate Monday night, touching on topics ranging from tariffs to the Iran war to diesel prices.

The candidates, incumbent Congresswoman Lauren Boebert and retired Navy rear admiral Eileen Laubacher, also waded into more arcane topics like Laubacher’s previous work history and Boebert’s vote against a bill to help veterans.

On the Iran war, which has driven up diesel prices to record levels in recent weeks, Boebert, a 39-year-old Republican, said she hadn’t wanted for the country to be at war but stands by President Donald Trump.

“I will stand by and say the president is commander in chief,” she said. “This was never about regime change — this was about making sure Iran never has a nuclear weapon.”

Laubacher, a 58-year-old Democrat who served in the Navy for 34 years, said the United States and Iran were in negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program when Trump bombed the country on Feb. 28.

“When negotiations are on the table, you do not start a war,” Laubacher said. “We should have given those serious efforts and instead of that, we go to war and we accidentally kill 150 girls (at an Iranian school).”

Boebert and Laubacher appeared together in the 9News studios for the hour-long debate — the only one scheduled in the district this fall. The election is Nov. 3 and thousands of ballots have already landed in Colorado voters’ mailboxes.

Democrats are taking their hardest run yet at the district that covers all or parts of 21 Colorado counties that stretch largely across the state’s Eastern Plains. Pieces of several populous Front Range counties, like Arapahoe, Douglas, Larimer and El Paso, are also in the 4th District.

The district has been reliably red for years, with no Democrat representing it since Betsy Markey left Congress in January 2011 after serving a single term.

But the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added the 4th to its list of “Districts in Play” in August. It’s part of an aggressive play the national party has made this election cycle for House districts once considered out of reach, taking advantage of the president’s plummeting poll ratings over the Iran war and stubbornly elevated prices.

The 4th Congressional District is dominated by farming and ranching, where Trump’s tariffs haven’t always been greeted with enthusiasm. Boebert on Monday insisted that Trump’s tariffs have been a “tool” in trying to secure the best trade deals for the United States.

But Laubacher said many of the Trump administration’s tariffs are not paid by foreign governments, but by Americans.

“It’s hurting our consumers,” she said. “Congress is supposed to be looking after consumers.”

Laubacher was challenged by the moderator as to why she only switched her party affiliation from Republican to Democrat in the last year or so. And whether her decision to do so was solely for the purposes of running for Congress.

Laubacher said her previous Republican affiliation was due to the fact that the party traditionally emphasized fiscal restraint, a strong military defense and support for individual liberties.

“I feel like we’ve gone from that party to a party that is barely recognizable,” she said of today’s GOP.

Boebert was asked about whether she has made a concerted effort to engage in less drama-filled and confrontational behavior, antics that landed her in hot water — and her name splashed across front pages everywhere — when she was tossed from a musical three years ago after fellow patrons objected to her conduct in public.

“I think it’s great to have an approach to disagree better,” Boebert said.

The women agreed on a couple of items: both said the loose border policy under President Biden was a disaster and both said it was a mistake for Trump to import Argentinian beef in an effort to bring down meat prices.

Laubacher holds a massive money advantage over Boebert. According to the most recent contributions and expenditures listed with the Federal Election Commission, which date back to the end of June, Laubacher had nearly 15 times as much money on hand as did her opponent.

The latest fundraising reports, covering the third quarter of 2026, are due on Thursday.

Neither candidate has lived for long in the 4th District.

Boebert moved there last year after leaving her previous congressional district (the 3rd) in a successful move to save her political career. Laubacher moved to Highlands Ranch in 2024, having lived in the neighboring 7th Congressional District, where she still owns a home.

Story and photos by Drew Anderson

Drew Anderson has reported on climate and the environment, with a particular focus on oil and gas and electricity in Alberta, for The Narwhal since 2021. He is based in Calgary.

The parking lot off the highway is busy and there’s a line-up for the outhouses next to a Parks Canada information stand featuring maps from years past. To the left, a wide accessible trail leads to the well-trod bridges and pathways crisscrossing Marble Canyon in Kootenay National Park in southern B.C. just 50 kilometres from the Alberta border.

The walk up the length of the canyon is short, barely a kilometre, with a little detour near its end where the ubiquitous red chairs of the national park system sit on a rise looking back toward the parking lot. It’s about as far as most people venture, but those red chairs don’t mark the end of the trail system through the valley.

A few more steps and walkers encounter a sign warning that the trail ahead — still listed on those yellowing maps — is no longer maintained. The sign doesn’t lie. Heading up through Tokumm Creek valley requires climbing over and under fallen trees, over collapsed log bridges and through overgrown brush.

It’s the sort of trek that eats at Trevor Willson, the president of the Canadian Backcountry Trails Preservation Society.

“I’m an engineer,” he says, driving through the Rocky Mountains toward Marble Canyon one fall weekend. “So if you have a problem, you don’t ignore the problem, you solve the problem.”

His organization is trying to convince Parks Canada to reinvest in trails it says have been abandoned, hindering backcountry access in parks at a time when more and more people are visiting. That’s particularly true for the Rocky Mountain parks of Banff, Kootenay and Jasper.

According to Willson, the cost of his plan to fix the nation’s parks is minimal, approximately $50 million to replace bridges and fix all of the existing trails, plus one-to-two million dollars per year in maintenance. Parks Canada, he says, doesn’t want to spend the money in an era of budget cuts, and doesn’t want volunteers taking on some of the load.

But the question runs deeper than dollars and cents, touching on a philosophical debate about the purpose of Canada’s national parks and whether to prioritize recreation, conservation or some balance between the two.

“Hiking and horseback riding are the classic activities to do in the mountains,” Willson says. “If you want to see the national park, you need to get out of the town of Banff because it’s beautiful, but it’s a very civilized, very well-developed little chunk of real estate.”

It should not be, he says, a “drive-through park.”

Willson has been involved in trail building and maintenance for years, including building bridges and negotiating partnership agreements with governments. He was inspired to start his society when he tried to convince Jasper National Park to replace a bridge along a historic passage across its northern border — and was rebuffed.

The Simon Creek bridge broke around 2015, severing a trail that was once a thoroughfare for First Nations and then the fur trade. Willson says he approached Jasper National Park about fixing it but was told there wasn’t enough money. Not one to take no for an answer, Willson found private funding but says he was eventually told rebuilding the bridge would have a negative impact on the ecology of the area.

Willson and his organization focus their efforts on existing trails and areas where bridges once spanned significant waterways. They do not, as he puts it, campaign to get rid of all obstacles or prevent your feet from getting wet.

“The point is, if you come to a river or creek and it’s impassable — like you can’t get across — and therefore you have to turn back, that bridge should be replaced,” he says, adding the bridge on Smith Creek crosses a section of fast, opaque and boulder-filled water.

Gavin Fitch, a fellow society member and environmental lawyer based in Calgary, says the group had a formal meeting with Jasper National Park officials in April, but still haven’t received a response.

“Our optimism has, I would say, changed to pessimism,” he says.

Not only is the Canadian Backcountry Trails Preservation Society trying to convince the government to make investments in trails and bridges — potentially one of Willson’s own designs — but to allow certified volunteers to help maintain the trails. That’s common in provincial parks, particularly in B.C., but Parks Canada has moved away from the practice and is reluctant to change tact, Willson says.

Parks Canada did not directly answer questions emailed by The Narwhal, but says it regularly reviews investments in the more than 8,000 kilometres of trails in its network based on visitation and conservation priorities.

“These decisions help ensure available resources are focused where they provide the greatest benefit to visitors, Indigenous partners, communities and protected places,” spokesperson Charlotte Bordeleau says in an email.

“In Kootenay National Park, for example, maintenance on portions of the Tokumm Creek Trail above Marble Canyon was discontinued as part of broader wilderness management decisions designed to support conservation objectives and wildlife habitat protection.”

Climbing over trees and scrambling through brush on the hike from Marble Canyon, Fitch says abandoning infrastructure doesn’t just prevent access to the backcountry, it erases public trails.

The trails are not decommissioned, simply allowed to deteriorate, he says. Then they disappear from government websites. Soon, the hiking apps used by modern adventurers downvote them into near obscurity.

It’s one reason Fitch carries around a well-worn trail book from 1990, an encyclopedic guide to routes across the Rocky Mountain region that’s fading in the digital age.

“One of the issues here is — now I’m putting on my administrative lawyer’s hat — these are decisions that Parks Canada makes with zero consultation,” he says.

“And of course, once the decision’s made, as we are finding out, trying to get them to reverse a decision that they’ve made on maintaining a trail is like proverbial pulling of teeth.”

It’s only a matter of minutes up the valley from Marble Canyon and those red chairs before the crowds feel far away. It is quiet and empty and the trees blocking the route multiply as you move farther in. The live trees are short, showing only about 20 years of growth since a fire ripped through this area. Skeletal burnt trunks still hover high amidst the green.

The quiet, even this close to a highway tourist stop, isn’t uncommon in the sprawling mountain parks that hug that Alberta-B.C. border. The vast majority of land in these parks is tucked far away from main thoroughfares. In Jasper, Willson says his own calculations show 83 per cent of the land is more than five kilometres from a highway.

“If you don’t have trails to access that 83 per cent, that’s a huge loss,” he says.

But not everyone would agree.

Bordeleau says Parks Canada has invested approximately $155 million in trail infrastructure since 2015, a figure that goes beyond backcountry trails. But she says the first priority of the agency is protecting the ecological integrity of the parks.

Willson argues that focus is too restrictive and ignores Parks Canada’s commitment to enjoyment of these vast public spaces.

“Ecological integrity is the number one priority in national parks. It’s written into the National Parks Act, and it states that the national park shall be maintained for future generations, which is fine, is great,” he says. “But they interpret that as ‘Keep people out of the back country.’ ”

At the same time, he says, more and more people are crowding into tourist hot spots.

According to data from Parks Canada, more than 11,000 people visited Lake Louise in Banff National Park each day in 2025, and the park itself set a new record with 4.5 million visitors that year.

Nadine Raynolds, the director of communities and conservation at the environmental group Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative, says there are ways to balance human access with ecological integrity, given the proper data and funding.

But that doesn’t necessarily mean maintaining existing or historic routes and will depend on wildlife routes, the specific species that use an area, the impact of human activities and even the time of year.

“What is the information that we need to support decision-making on the landscape?” she says. “Often what that leads to is making choices about where those trails should be and where is a place where we maybe shouldn’t put trails because of the wildlife needs.”

Unlike Fitch and his guidebook, her organization leans into digital apps and technologies to determine what areas are popular among humans and wildlife as it decides where to invest tight budgets. And she argues those tools can be effective in monitoring.

“Land managers that we spoke with in B.C. and Alberta were really keen to explore all these options because they need this information,” Raynolds says, adding those managers don’t have the staff or resources to implement sufficient monitoring programs.

When it comes to underused backcountry trails, the impact of human activity is unlikely to be significant, and it would be easy to manage numbers with trail restrictions and campsite access.

But Fitch acknowledges the calculus could work against them, precisely because the number of people who want to trek in the backcountry is small.

“So I think it would be the bean-counter argument, that the scarce resources which we have should be put to use on essentially front-country infrastructure, so the stuff you can reach easily from the highway,” he says.

In March, the federal government announced $3.8 billion for initiatives it says will protect Canada’s natural landscapes. Of that, $267 million will go to the creation of two new protected areas overseen by Parks Canada. The plan also calls for private partnerships and investments in Indigenous-led stewardship.

It’s unclear if those moves will include a reinvestment in backcountry trails, but Willson and Fitch aren’t waiting to find out. They’re stepping up lobbying efforts, meeting with Corey Hogan, the sole Liberal MP in Calgary, and hoping that one of the doors they knock on opens.

Raynolds says the tools and the research exists to plan trails and parks that benefit both wildlife and recreation. But implementing those plans will take political will and a bit of investment.

Willson hopes there’s more to it than a simple cost-benefit analysis.

“The park is not only the highways and the towns,” Willson says. “The park is the trails too. Walking and hiking on a trail in wilderness is a very quintessential Canadian thing.”

It’s a classic Haines scene in the summer and early fall: fishermen and brown bears dodge each other along the Chilkoot River, while local Sue Rakes watches on.

The rhythm played out as usual around dawn on a recent Saturday. A sow and four cubs meandered toward a packed riverbank. The fishermen scattered, but someone left a black backpack behind.

“Is that your backpack?” Rakes asks the crowd. “Can you get it, please?”

The owner declined, nodding to the advancing sow.

“Well, I’ll go get it,” Rakes said, before she scrambled down to the shore and snagged the bag.

“We can’t give them any rewards at all,” she explained to the seemingly frustrated owner, who said the pack was empty anyways.

Through summer and fall, Rakes spends hours on end at the Chilkoot Lake State Recreation Site. She loves bears, but she’s not really there to watch them. She’s there as an unaffiliated volunteer to watch people and ensure neither they — nor their fish, food or dogs — attract or endanger the bears.

Rakes first visited Haines from North Carolina in the fall of 2022. During her weeklong trip, she saw bears constantly contending with people who were not keeping a safe distance.

The next year, she came back to stay.

"I wanted to move here and try to do something about the bears,” she said. “It was so frustrating.”

She has since become a permanent and sometimes controversial fixture along the river. Her goal is to help educate people about bears and eliminate as many attractants as possible, to minimize the potential for dangerous interactions.

“It literally ramps up in two or three visits from a bear, and then everybody gets afraid, and then everybody gets let’s-kill-bear-fever,” she said.

The recreation site is notorious for being a relatively small area with lots of bears, lots of people, and lots of potential for dangerous interactions between them.

Hannah Manninen, a wildlife biologist with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, said Chilkoot is so popular in part because it’s easy to get to. Many other bear viewing spots in Alaska can only be reached by boat or plane.

But it’s also unique because the area is used for far more than bear viewing alone. It also draws hordes of fishermen, campers and tourists on commercial tours.

“If something is established as a bear viewing location, that’s often one of the only things that’s happening there,” Manninen said. “And so you can have more strict regulations or enforcement policies.”

The Alaska Division of Parks and Outdoor Recreation manages the site but declined to comment for this story.

There are regulations in place for tour operators, and signs advise everyone else where they should walk, park, fish and watch for bears. There is also a ranger who spends some of his time at Chilkoot, and a technician who was hired by Fish and Game this year to educate visitors during peak hours.

“The dream or goal would be that there would be a minimum of two technicians,” Manninen said. “It can be a lot for one person to handle.”

Rakes said her aim has been to support that new program by serving as an extra pair of eyes. In her experience, many people who frequent Chilkoot still largely do as they please, particularly when no one is around. So she’s trying to fill the gap.

“I really just want more people to have eyes out here and have people know they’re being watched,” she said.

Rakes also works as a volunteer host at the Chilkoot Campground, where she checks sites for attractants and educates campers. But she said she’s not speaking in that capacity, and that she does this work as a concerned citizen, not as a camp host.

While a lot of people thank Ranks for her volunteer work, she conceded that not everyone is a fan. She said she is sometimes short and firm with people, and that it’s not exactly uncommon for fishermen, campers and tour operators to get upset with her when she tells them what to do. Some have accused her of yelling.

She said she’s worked on adjusting her approach so it’s more effective, including by learning from the paid educator.

This summer in particular, her goal was to crack down on any attractants and reduce the odds that cubs get accustomed to eating human food. She said she hopes that could prevent dangerous conflicts with humans, which she worries could lead to a park closure — or a dead bear.

“My biggest motivator is those four cubs,” she said, “because they’re going to be on their own next spring.”

Activity along the river is winding down now as temperatures drop. Rakes said she’ll be out there for as long as the bears are.

The True Economic History of Columbus’s Voyage of Discovery

Columbus Day should be a humbling moment for the critics of Donald Trump’s trade policies.

The just-so story Trump’s critics and many of the people who like to call themselves “free-traders”  like to tell is that Europe’s discovery of the Americas and the subsequent boom of overseas trade required the removal of so-called trade barriers such as tariffs, state-granted trade monopolies, and international cooperation. But economic history tells a very different tale.

In a 2002 paper published in the prestigious Journal of Economic History titled “After Columbus: Explaining Europe’s Overseas Trade Boom, 1500–1800,” economic historians Kevin O’Rourke of Trinity College Dublin and Jeffrey Williamson of Harvard University found that commerce flourished in a global market that was dominated by economic hurdles and interventions as varied as import duties, excise taxes, export restrictions, wars, and piracy.

And these were not trivial. If trade barriers were falling during the period, you would expect to see a sustained narrowing of price gaps between continents. Instead, O’Rourke and Williamson found, the price gaps persisted. Indeed, they were so strong that they overwhelmed improvement in shipping technology.

By examining import prices and the incomes of the Europeans buying overseas goods, the authors estimated that rising demand explained roughly half to two-thirds of the trade expansion. Overseas supply dominated the sixteenth century, while European demand accounted for the seventeenth-century boom. As affluent Europeans acquired more money to spend on spices, silk, and sugar, merchants had good reasons to brave the expensive voyages. Their customers’ growing purchasing power supported commerce through conditions that would have horrified today’s trade-policy establishment.

This can be seen as a triumph for the power of markets. Government interventions and high seas piracy were strong enough to keep price differentials high but not strong enough to prevent the growth of global trade. But it also suggests that governments could accomplish public goals such as protecting vital industries with trade policies that would send today’s establishment free traders into fits—without depriving their citizens of the benefits of trade.

This is important because critics of Donald Trump’s trade policies often act like there’s only one path for benevolent international commerce: Either we sign the Trans-Pacific Partnership—or whatever the latest multilateral trade pact is—or we plunge ourselves into economic isolation. Erect tariffs and we’ll never import anything again and spark ruinous trade wars. If not for “globalism,” we wouldn’t have burritos or pizza.

The real-life economic history of trade in the wake of the voyages of Christopher Columbus tells us this is nonsense.

Christopher Columbus taking leave of Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon before setting out from Spain on his first voyage to the New World, on August 8, 1492. (Photo12/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

We saw the effects of the globalist trade delusion in the reaction to President Trump’s Liberation Day tariff announcement. In April of last year, the World Trade Organization projected Trump’s new policies and retaliation from our trading partners would result in a 0.2 percent decline in global merchandise trade volumes, nearly three percentage points below its earlier baseline. A downside scenario envisioned a 1.5 percent contraction.

Instead, global goods trade volumes subsequently grew roughly four percent, U.S. imports increased, and the WTO now expects global merchandise trade to grow 3.9 percent this year.

The tariff collectors, meanwhile, enjoyed a considerably better year than the forecasters, with customs duties generating $195 billion in fiscal 2025, compared with $77 billion the year before. Fiscal year 2025, by the way, ended in September 2025, less than half a year after the tariffs were announced. Many of the tariffs were in place for even a shorter time span than that. The Congressional Budget Office attributes almost all of that $118 billion increase to the administration’s tariff changes. Trump managed to collect substantial additional revenue from international commerce while the trade contraction predicted by his critics failed to materialize.

We also saw a boom in U.S. manufacturing output and productivity. The labor market witnessed a reversal of the decline in manufacturing employment that dominated the end of Biden’s presidency. Business investment is booming. The construction of new manufacturing plants has survived the end of Biden’s subsidies at an elevated level.

One of the reasons trade held up stronger than expected is that businesses building AI infrastructure were ordering semiconductors, servers, and equipment for data centers in quantities that overwhelmed the gloomy forecasts. Trade in AI-enabling goods rose 21.9 percent in value in 2025, accounting for 42 percent of the increase in global merchandise trade value.

This was helped by the fact that the Trump administration’s tariff program preserved access to essential computing equipment while collecting revenue on other imports. Knowing that we are still dependent on imports for many high-tech products—and will be for some time, even under the most optimistic scenarios—the administration adopted a rational approach to facilitate, rather than frustrate, the AI boom.

In other words, the free-trade establishment underestimated the strength of private demand and the power of markets to adjust to tariffs. Just like in the post-Columbus world, markets mattered more. There’s a deep irony that so many self-styled free-traders consistently underestimate the power of markets. The people who profess the greatest faith in markets have spent much of the past two years predicting that a customs bill would bring them to their knees. It’s hard to escape the suspicion that they aren’t really advocates of trade and free markets at all but simply the valets of those who benefited from the particular trade arrangements that dominated before Trump arrived at the White House.

Tariffs are taxes on imports, and in some cases they really do drive up prices of those imports or convince merchants to source production domestically. But profitable investment opportunities keep businesses buying and suppliers competing. On Columbus Day, the expansion of trade through centuries of costly voyages should remind us how powerful those incentives can be.

The Justice Department has launched a formal anti-trust investigation into five major U.S. television networks for their actions during a court battle over whether several news outlets should have access to the White House despite angering President Trump.

While the five networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News — did not comment, press rights advocacy groups denounced the move.

"[S]ummoning antitrust authority, on top of the retaliatory actions the White House has already taken to bar certain outlets, is another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists," said Bruce Brown, the president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press.

Last month, Trump had aides bar CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House after blasting them for what he characterized as unfairly negative coverage. The administration stripped White House press passes from more than 70 journalists. The three news organizations sued in federal court to have their access restored. In court, the Justice Department is citing national security grounds for the decision.

The federal judge overseeing the case issued a temporary stay requiring their passes to be restored and says he will make a more enduring decision by Tuesday evening.

However, the White House also blocked CNN from fulfilling its planned shifts as part of the White House television press pool, which includes the other television networks now under investigation. While the news outlets' decision-making is day-to-day, The five have agreed not to substitute for CNN on the days that the administration blocks the network, though they are handling decisions day-to-day.

As part of a longstanding practice, the members of the pool share the logistical burden and the costs of covering Trump's actions in public appearances that take place in smaller places, such as Air Force One. As a result of the ban on CNN, the networks did not cover an event Trump had with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The Justice Department says it is reviewing whether the coordination of that decision constitutes anti-trust behavior, which is to say, anti-competitive.

"Members of the television press pool have proudly boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act," the Justice Department said in a statement Saturday. "The Antitrust Division is investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws."

Four people with direct knowledge of events affirmed the outlines of the investigation. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the matter. The development was first reported by the New York Times.

Michael Dorf, a professor of Constitutional law at Cornell University's law school, says that political motivation on the part of the president or the Justice Department in investigating the networks does not shield them from legal repercussions in court.

But Dorf says it would be subject to a review of whether the networks' actions were reasonable. These were, he says. And he highlights what he calls another "oddity."

"If the networks agreeing not to cover the White House is illegal, why isn't the press pool itself illegal? Presumably the answer is that the kind of cooperation involved in the press pool is necessitated by the limited space in particular venues," Dorf writes in an email. "But if that's a sufficient justification for the cooperation in coverage, why isn't standing up to protect the free press at least as an important a justification?

The incident highlights the increased tensions between the president and the news media. ABC and its parent company Disney are suing Trump's chief broadcast regulator for mandating an immediate review of whether it should hold all eight of its local TV station licenses — threatening a hit to its bottom line. A judge is weighing whether to intervene in the process.

Trump has frequently called for ABC (and NBC) to lose their broadcast licenses.

Disney calls the review of the ABC station licenses retaliation over content Trump doesn't like on The View and Jimmy Kimmel Live.

Federal Communications Commission chief Brendan Carr says it's all a question of upholding "the public interest." Under Carr, the FCC has also launched investigations of all other major broadcast networks, including NPR, with the exception of Fox broadcast network, owned by Trump's political ally Rupert Murdoch.

Trump is also suing many major news organizations as an individual. Those outlets include the New York Times, BBC News, and the Wall Street Journal (which is also owned by Murdoch but sometimes draws Trump's ire). ABC and CBS settled earlier lawsuits Trump brought against them.

"The investigation is nonsense," said Seth Stern, Freedom of the Press Foundation's chief of advocacy. "Trump may view the presidency as a business venture, but news outlets' standing up for their constitutional rights has nothing to do with antitrust law."

Conservative values, National renewal

“Medicare for All” is enjoying a political resurgence. A KFF poll released last week found that two-thirds of Americans support a national health plan — the highest level since the organization began asking about the idea in 2017.

But enthusiasm falls when Americans confront some of the trade-offs. Just 24% still support “Medicare for All” when told it could mean delays in medical tests and treatments, and 35% do so when told it could raise taxes.

Join Washington Examiner for unlimited access to the news, analysis, and commentary that matter most.

Already a member? Log in

Putting Washington in charge of everyone’s healthcare would not make it free. It would leave government officials to decide how to stretch finite taxpayer dollars across virtually unlimited demand.

Waiting is one way government-controlled healthcare systems make the numbers add up.

At the end of March, about 6 million people in England were waiting for treatment through the National Health Service. In more than 94,000 cases, patients had already been waiting longer than a year.

Canadians waited a median of 28.6 weeks from referral by a general practitioner to treatment by a specialist in 2025. And, contrary to Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-VT) statements, “Medicare for All” is not free. The average Canadian family of four paid $21,115 in hidden taxes to sit on a waiting list.

Canada offers another, darker warning about the incentives government-run healthcare can create. Medical assistance in dying has become remarkably common north of the border.

In 2024, 5.1% of people who died in Canada received MAID — roughly 1 in 20. The program now extends to some people whose conditions are not terminal.

The granddaughter of 83-year-old Brigitte Stegemann told Fox News in September that her grandmother had previously rejected assisted death. According to her family, Stegemann broke down two days before the procedure after learning that the scheduled “medicine” would kill her and said she had “made a mistake.” Two days later, she received MAID and died.

The incentives are uncomfortable. Canada’s Parliamentary Budget Officer estimated in 2020 that the expansion of MAID would reduce provincial healthcare costs by a net $62 million annually.

That’s the danger of charging the government with paying for care and setting the rules that govern access to it.

OPINION: MEDICARE FOR ALL REMAINS A DISASTER PROPOSITION

“Medicare for All” would put Washington in much the same position. As costs mounted, officials would inevitably face pressure to limit spending. The long waits in Britain and Canada show one way that pressure can affect patients. Canada’s rapid embrace of assisted death offers a more disturbing warning.

Americans should consider those consequences before embracing “Medicare for All.” The promise of universal coverage sounds appealing. The experience of other countries suggests otherwise.

Sally C. Pipes (@sallypipes) is president, CEO, and Thomas W. Smith fellow in health care policy at the Pacific Research Institute. Her latest book is The World’s Medicine Chest: How America Achieved Pharmaceutical Supremacy — and How to Keep It (Encounter 2025).
