Hoover Institution senior fellow Victor Davis Hanson discusses controversies surrounding a Smithsonian museum in Manhattan over the museum’s framing of American history on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

The Smithsonian Institution is sometimes called the nation’s attic. That description is inadequate. An attic stores things. The Smithsonian does something far more consequential: It helps Americans understand who we are.

That responsibility carries particular weight as the United States celebrates its 250th anniversary and the Smithsonian prepares for new leadership. The transition comes amid an intense debate over how the Smithsonian presents American history. A White House review criticized the National Museum of American History, arguing that ideological concerns have displaced an understanding of history as a shared national inheritance.

Smithsonian leaders and historians have defended the institution’s scholarly independence and warned against allowing political power to dictate how history is told. The answer cannot be choosing one of those impulses and ignoring the other.

TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED

Outgoing Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch recently said the Smithsonian must show both the light and the dark. He has also described America as an ideal as much as a place — an aspiration toward liberty, fairness, justice and equality.

People walk on the National Mall near the Smithsonian Castle in Washington, D.C., on May 10, 2021. (MANDEL NGAN/AFP via Getty Images)

But has the Smithsonian been telling the American story fairly?

SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PRAISES OUTGOING SMITHSONIAN LEADER WHO WAS UNDER PRESSURE FROM TRUMP ADMIN

The harder question is one of proportion: How should America’s national museums put the light and the dark together into an honest account of the country?

I have spent much of the past quarter-century helping govern museums and historic institutions in Virginia. That experience has convinced me that historical integrity requires more than factual accuracy. It requires proportion, context and perspective.

HISTORIAN BLASTS SMITHSONIAN'S ACTIVISM SHIFT AFTER FIRST VISIT IN OVER A DECADE: 'COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PLACE'

America’s national museums should tell our history honestly, including our shortcomings, contradictions and occasions when Americans failed to live up to the principles proclaimed at the nation’s founding.

But those failures should not become the organizing principle through which the American experience is understood.

SMITHSONIAN'S NATIONAL MUSEUM OF AMERICAN HISTORY PROMOTES 'EXTREME POLITICAL ACTIVISM,' WH REPORT ALLEGES

Viewed in proportion, the American story is extraordinary.

A collection of colonies declared that human beings possess rights governments do not grant. Americans then built an enduring constitutional republic around representative government, individual liberty and the rule of law. Those ideas changed human history.

The nation they produced survived civil war, expanded freedom and political participation, welcomed generations of immigrants, became an industrial and scientific power, defeated fascism and Soviet communism and put human beings on the moon.

America’s national museums should tell our history honestly, including our shortcomings, contradictions and occasions when Americans failed to live up to the principles proclaimed at the nation’s founding.

When America fell short of its founding principles, succeeding generations repeatedly returned to those principles to demand the nation do better.

There is an important distinction between examining America critically and teaching Americans to regard their country cynically. A great national museum should be capable of the former without succumbing to the latter.

Museums inevitably make choices: which objects to display, which stories to emphasize and which context visitors receive. Individual facts can be accurate while their cumulative presentation leaves a distorted impression.

LEGAL EXPERT CALLS FOR SMITHSONIAN LEADERSHIP OVERHAUL OVER ‘SELF-LOATHING’ PORTRAYAL OF HISTORY: ‘IT’S BILE’

The Smithsonian should resist any interpretive approach that begins with contemporary political or ideological categories and works backward through history to validate them. History should illuminate today’s debates, but the past deserves to be encountered on its own terms.

Nor can the answer be replacing one political orthodoxy with another.

WATCH: SMITHSONIAN DIRECTOR ADMITS SHE SEES HISTORY AS ‘TOOL’ OF ‘SOCIAL JUSTICE’ AFTER EXPLOSIVE HEARING

The Smithsonian has endured presidents and Congresses of both parties. Its credibility rests upon scholarship, independence and public trust. Americans should never believe exhibits in their national museums are rewritten whenever political power changes hands.

James Smithson envisioned an institution devoted to the "increase and diffusion of knowledge."

Two centuries later, the Smithsonian holds objects that belong to all of us: General George Washington’s uniform. President Abraham Lincoln’s hat. The Star-Spangled Banner. The Wright Flyer. Harriet Tubman’s hymnal. The Greensboro lunch-counter stools. The Apollo 11 command module.

They tell a remarkable story of aspiration, struggle, achievement and progress.

The Entertainment Nation exhibit at the Smithsonian National Museum of American history features late rapper Nipsey Hussle's chain, sweatshirt and songwriting notepad. It does not mention rapper's gang ties or songs promoting street violence and drug use. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

No curator owns that story. Neither does a president, political party, academic movement — or generation. We hold it temporarily in trust. That principle matters especially during America’s 250th anniversary. This milestone should invite reflection. But reflection is not national self-reproach.

Our semiquincentennial should not become a 250th-anniversary wake, principally devoted to cataloging America’s shortcomings while treating its achievements as qualifications or afterthoughts.

There is too much worth celebrating.

Visitors should leave the Smithsonian knowing America’s history more fully. They should understand our shortcomings and contradictions, but also our achievements. They should leave impressed by what Americans built, moved by what Americans sacrificed, grateful for what they inherited — and challenged to preserve and improve it.

They should even leave proud.

Pride in one’s country is not the enemy of historical understanding. Properly grounded in truth, it can be one of its products.

The Smithsonian need not tell Americans what to think about America. It should give them the artifacts, scholarship, context and perspective necessary to understand the inheritance that belongs to them.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Tell the hard stories. Tell the great ones, too. Trust Americans with both.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

After 250 years, the American story remains unfinished. The Smithsonian’s responsibility is to preserve it faithfully, interpret it honestly — and ensure the next generation understands why it remains a story worth celebrating.

David Botkins is a former chairman of the Science Museum of Virginia and current trustee of the Jamestown-Yorktown Foundation. He has more than 25 years of museum and historic preservation governance experience and is founder and CEO of Botkins Strategies, LLC.

Payback is a Tish.

A top adviser to ex-Gov. Andrew Cuomo blasted Attorney General Letitia James as the “biggest hypocrite in Albany” for releasing the personnel records of a whistleblower who accused her office of targeting President Trump.

Richard Azzopardi, who was senior adviser and communications director for Cuomo during his time leading the state, was accused of retaliation by Tish’s team for doing the same thing five years ago when records went public on a staffer who accused the governor of sexual harassment.

“AG James is probably the biggest hypocrite in Albany — and that’s a contest,” Azzopardi told The Post. “It’s galling that she’s doing the same thing and is expecting everyone to look the other way.”

“If what I did was retaliation, what is this?” said Azzopardi. “There’s no daylight between these two situations.”

Azzopardi said it was remarkable to see James’ office release some internal records and office emails of whistleblower Daniel Wiesenfeld, a prosecutor in the Investor Protection Bureau. Wiesenfeld has claimed his manager told him to keep pursuing an insider trading case against President Trump despite a lack of evidence of a crime.

Records first obtained from the AG’s office by the Times Union, via a Freedom of Information Law request, last week revealed that Wiesenfeld had been “counseled” for performance issues including failing to participate in meetings or answer to supervisors.

“The agency is specifically aware that you e-mailed privileged and/or confidential information related to the work of OAG to your personal e-mail account,” Jenna Moran, the attorney general’s human resources director, wrote in a letter to Wiesenfeld on Sept. 4, when she formally notified him that he was being terminated.

“Those e-mails and documents, as well as any records in your possession that may have been derived from such privileged and/or confidential information, must be destroyed or returned immediately,” the letter stated.

A prior June  performance review of Wiesenfeld — first hired by the AG’s  office in 2024 — noted that last year he was considered “hardworking, reliable (and) takes ownership of his cases.” That review also noted he had a “good attitude.”

Last week Wiesenfeld claimed he was being threatened by the AG’s office for refusing to delete evidence of the alleged corruption.

In an exchange of emails – copies of which were obtained by The Post from the AG’s office under Freedom of Information law — Wiesenfeld denied that the documents in question were “confidential and privileged information” as the AG claimed.

“These documents are simply evidence and your threats will not compel me to destroy such evidence,” he wrote. “If anything, carrying out your threats by bringing this to a legal forum will make this information public.”

Wiesenfeld claimed the push to dig dirt on Trump came directly from James.

“Tish was the boss and what Tish wanted, Tish got,” Wiesenfeld told The Post last week. “So we had to keep going.”

Trump, who has had legal fights with James, shared The Post’s exclusive interview with Wiesenfeld claiming he has ordered to target the president.

Wiesenfeld has been at odds with his boss since August, when he blasted an email to over 2,000 colleagues claiming he was forced investigate Trump, his family and his pals.

He was later fired.

James defended her office’s action in the Wiesenfeld disciplinary case and dismissed Azzopardi’s criticism as “disingenuous.”

“The Office of the Attorney General is duty bound to take disciplinary action when one of its attorneys violates the law, the New York Rules of Professional Conduct, or agency policy. Mr. Wiesenfeld was terminated for cause after it was determined that he committed such violations,” a spokesperson for AG James said.

“We remain committed to enforcing New York’s laws and defending the rights of all New Yorkers. Any suggestion otherwise is disingenuous.”

Wiesenfeld’s personnel files were released  to the media in accordance with the state FOIL and a review of his allegations that AG’s office was pushing another probe of Trump were not substantiated, the AG’s office said, adding that Wiesenfeld did not participate in the probe.

Azzopardi was involved in releasing the personnel records of Lindsey Boylan, a former executive chamber staffer who was the first of several women to accuse Cuomo of sexual harassment.

After Boylan tweeted in December 2020 that the governor “sexually harassed” her over her looks, Azzopardi sent several reporters — including one from The Post — “confidential files” detailing workplace complaints against Boylan, along with a formal statement denying the allegations.

He testified that the release of records had been cleared by legal counsel.

James’ investigative team hammered Azzopardi and others in Cuomo’s camp for releasing Boylan’s records.

“These actions also sent a chilling message to other would be complainants,” James’ bombshell report said, concluding that Cuomo, a Democrat, engaged in sexual misconduct.

“Regardless of the involvement of counsel, we find that the result of the Executive Chamber’s release of the Confidential Files related to Ms. Boylan constituted unlawful retaliation,” the James report said.

The devastating report triggered Cuomo’s resignation in 2021, though he continues to deny wrongdoing.

Democrat James, seeking re-election to a third-term, is facing off against Republican Saritha Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor.

Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Sean O’Kane, Rebeccan Bellan and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities.

Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried.

Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication.

“We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said.

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Sean O’Kane: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular.

There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. etc.

I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point.

This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber  was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip.

The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too.

So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now.

Rebecca Bellan: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco, which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years.

But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this.

Anthony Ha: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York. I believe it’s a one year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.]

So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.”

But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried.

It’s also noteworthy that Microsoft, earlier this year, made a similar announcement about not using NDAs. I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it. I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step.

Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right? This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc.

And I’m not trying to beat that horse, because we’re in the media and [we] think we’re still relevant. But we’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them. And that’s because, a lot of time, the [technological] ability’s not there, and in part because they’re just not explaining it well.

I wrote a story last week about how it’s been a year since we’ve really heard Tesla beating its own drum about building towards what it originally was calling “sustainable abundance” and is now “amazing abundance” as its mission statement. It’s just wild to me that we’re a year into that, and the company still doesn’t have a very good definition of it, especially considering that they released this whole multi-page PDF laying it out when they announced this, and even Tesla’s biggest fans criticized Elon Musk and Tesla for how unspecific it was. It read like LLM nonsense.

Anthony: One of the things this has made me think about is just the narrative and this sense that for a while, it really felt like it was being pushed down our throats — this idea of, “This is inevitable, this AI-driven future, and get on board or you’re just going to be left behind.”

Obviously that future is barreling ahead in a lot of ways, but in a few key ways, there have been these obstacles. What I’ve really liked about that is this sense of “No, you actually have to make the case for it.” You can’t just say, “This is the future, shut up.”

And then specifically about Tesla and the abundance thing, what was shocking to me is not so much that they haven’t come up with a definition of abundance, but that that was a promise that they were making in the first place. I think [that] speaks to how strange our relationship to Tesla, and particularly the people who are invested and ride-or-die for Elon, [has become.] It’s not about, is this company going to sell a lot of cars? It’s about this vision for remaking society. Or at least, that’s what they’re being sold.

Eligible Cash App users could soon begin receiving $2,500 in their pockets as part of a whopping $15 million law suit settlement over a data breach.

The mobile financial platform was slapped with a lawsuit after the alleged 2021 breach resulted in the “unauthorized public release of the personally identifiable information of 8.2 million current and former Cash App Investing customers,” USA Today reported, citing the class-action suit filed in 2022.

Cash App, its parent company Block Inc. and the lawsuit’s plaintiffs agreed to the settlement in March 2024 — but neither company admitted to any violations of the law, the publication reported.

Payments from the $15 million settlement are expected to be distributed sometime this month to users who filed a claim before the deadline two years ago, according to the settlement website.

Users who experienced authorized or fraudulent withdrawals or transfers from their Cash App accounts between Aug. 23, 2018 and Aug. 20, 2024 had to have filed a claim for damages before Nov. 18, 2024 to be eligible.

Impacted individuals could seek reimbursement for out-of-pocket losses of up to $2,500 — including loss of funds from transactions and lost time spent on the data breach, capped at up to three hours at $25/hour.

No claims filed after the November 2024 deadline will be accepted, according to the settlement website.

The $15 million settelment, while sizeable, covers legal fees and settlement administrative costs in addition to valid user claims.

Cash App, launched in 2013, is a mobile financial platform that works like a “digital wallet” for users to send a receive money, invest in Bitcoin and stocks, apply for loans and file taxes, according to USA Today.

While it is not a bank, the platform offers an interest-earning savings account and a Cash App debit card for users to make purchases and ATM withdrawals.

Mike Bloomberg-affiliated Everytown for Gun Safety responded to the ATF’s new guidelines for suppressor sales by calling ATF Director Robert Cekada a gun industry “puppet.”

Breitbart News spoke with Director Cekada Friday before the new guidelines were released and he told us the ATF/DOJ decided to broaden an August 5, 2026, district court ruling against suppressor registration so that it freed all law-abiding Americans from the cumbersome NFA requirements.

In the ruling, handed down in Silencer Shop Foundation v. ATF,  U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas Judge James Wesley Hendrix found registration requirements for suppressors and short-barreled rifles and shotguns “unconstitutional” and said the requirements could not be enforced against plaintiffs. Cekada announced Friday that the ATF/DOJ was applying the ruling to all law-abiding Americans, thereby crushing federal NFA registration requirements for suppressors and short-barreled rifles and shotguns.

Everytown was not happy. They responded to Cekada’s announcement with an Instagram post in which they wrote, “The federal agency tasked with enforcing our gun laws is now deciding not to. The National Firearms Act was enacted nearly a century ago to prevent criminals from getting their hands on weapons like short-barreled rifles and shotguns, and silencers.”

They added, “ATF Director Cekada’s decision to be a puppet for the gun industry will only put the safety of our communities at risk.”

In other news, suppressor sales are booming.

mary-peltola-slur-allegations:
Two former staffers of former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-AK) allege the Alaska Democrat repeatedly used the n-word in 2024, according to a report from the Alaska Landmine.

The two former aides worked in the Alaska Democrat’s House office and on her campaign. They spoke to the Landmine on the condition of anonymity, citing fear of retaliation. Both described separate episodes in 2024.

One instance allegedly followed an October 25, 2024 dinner honoring the roughly 4,000 African American soldiers who helped build the Alaska-Canada Highway during World War II. The event was promoted by Ed Wesley, an Army veteran, former commander of American Legion Post 34, and former president of the Anchorage NAACP.

Wesley pressured the campaign to buy tables and promised to fill them, according to a former aide. The campaign purchased eight tables at $1,000 each, the staffer said, and an October 18, 2024 FEC filing shows $8,000 paid to Eventbrite for tickets. The tables sat mostly empty. Peltola did not attend.

After staff told her about the turnout, the Senate candidate grew angry and called Wesley a “scammer,” the staffer alleged.

“I can’t believe that n****r,” Peltola said, according to the staffer.

The aide told the Landmine they had grown “numb” to such language, alleging they had previously heard Peltola use the slur “faggot” when referring to gay staffers.

A second staffer alleged the Alaska Democrat used the n-word multiple times during a spring 2024 campaign meeting. Staff conducting opposition research had discovered that her son, Job Nelson, ran a YouTube channel featuring self-produced rap music that frequently used the word. The channel was later deleted, the staffers said.

“It shocked everyone in the room,” the second staffer said, adding that no one confronted her out of fear.

The allegations come weeks after the New York Times published a report describing a pattern of angry outbursts, a shove, and slurs across Peltola’s years in office. Peltola is challenging Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) in a race that could decide control of the Senate.

The Peltola campaign did not respond to the Landmine before publication but afterward claimed the report was “an outright lie published by a right-wing gossip blogger.”

“Mary would never use this word, which is a vile slur with a painful, hateful history,” the campaign said.

Cloudflare announced Friday that it’s acquiring Deno, the startup behind the programming runtime of the same name.

According to Cloudflare’s Kenton Varda, Cloudflare will use this acquisition to improve its Workers programming model and platform, which allows customers to build and run software on Cloudflare’s network. (Varda is principal engineer for Cloudflare Workers.)

Deno — which was co-founded by Bert Belder and Node.js creator Ryan Dahl — recently launched celld, an open source implementation of Workers, which Varda wrote “delighted” the Cloudflare team. Varda argued that contrary to “a popular theory” that the company “made Cloudflare Workers work differently from other cloud platforms in order to create ‘lock-in,’” the company believes “being open source and giving people an escape hatch is good business.”

Dahl, meanwhile, wrote that his team is “joining Cloudflare to make the Workers programming model a mainstream way to build servers.”

The financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. Deno had raised a total of $26 million, including a Series A led by Sequoia.

Like many great plans, it was deceptively simple. Stillness. Balance. Patience. Concentration. No frills, no fast moves and no undue risks, just decisive action when needed.

Not for the first time at Test level, a burly Queenslander, a three-pound cleft of willow and a healthy dose of self-confidence was the difference between Australian success and failure.

That Matt Renshaw resurrected an Australian first innings which teetered near oblivion at 6-124 was the first point of order.

Of consequences further-reaching, the left-hander resurrected his entire Test career overnight in Durban, sweeping, clipping and crashing his way to 190 from 397 deliveries across 465 minutes of life-affirming Test batting.

Numerous records fell or threatened to. Renshaw's epic was the highest score by an Australian in Durban, the fourth highest overall by an Aussie against South Africa, and the best by a number-five of any nation at Kingsmead.

It was also a new Test personal best for Renshaw, usurping the 184 he made nine years ago as a boyish tyro against Pakistan in Sydney, back when the world was at his feet.

Renshaw is 30 now — a husband, a father of two children and an entirely different cricketer. He knows his own mind and understands his place in the scheme of things.

For a nation which has been crying out for big, important runs by someone not named Smith or Head, his Daddy hundred here was one for the ages.

Practically speaking, Renshaw helped Australia to a first-innings total of 390, which was at least 150 more than had seemed optimistic when he first took guard.

On a deeper level, it restored belief in the value of grinding out an innings of depth and character. It was the real deal — the proper Test match batting the Australian cricketing public has been craving.

No mistake should be made about the high degree of difficulty, either. When Renshaw began shepherding the tail a day earlier, Australia was at the mercy of a vigorous and versatile South African pace attack jagging the ball all over the place.

Waiting in the wings were the Proteas' twin spin options of Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer, with 1700+ first-class wickets between them.

Australia has struggled against left-arm spin in recent times. Last time they played a Test in Durban, Maharaj took nine wickets. And Australia's selection for this match — four left handers in the top six — was said to favour right-arm off-spinner Harmer even more.

Matt Renshaw blunted South Africa's spin attack with judicious use of the sweep and reverse sweep in Durban. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

So much for that, in the end. Renshaw swept, reverse-swept and paddled Maharaj into irrelevance and by the time Harmer finally removed the top-scorer for spin's first wicket of the game, the horse had well and truly bolted.

As it turned out, the sterner challenge was curbing the influence of the quicks, who'd posed constant difficulties for the rest of Australia's batters.

A microcosm came when Renshaw was on 130, yet still not able to relax. He was struck a scary blow to the grille of his helmet from an absolute snorter by Anrich Nortje, who bowled with genuine pace and accuracy in short, sharp spells.

Handling the wily and indefatigable Wiaan Mulder was no cinch either. Early on day two, the all-rounder scythed through Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc and threatened to blow the game open.

Wiaan Mulder (centre) took two wickets on day two and proved hard to play for Australia's batters. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

That he didn't was not exclusively a matter of Renshaw's dominance but of the rearguard partnerships which have so often saved Australia's bacon in recent times.

Renshaw shared stands of 86 across 32 overs with Pat Cummins and a monumental and possibly series-shaping 134 from 47 overs with Nathan Lyon.

Australia will not be looking too far ahead, but there was a blueprint here, not just of personnel but of general batting philosophy: know your game, make them bowl to you, stick around and wear them down.

Australia's total was the most obvious metric of success, but its innings duration of 137.2 overs will surely please Andrew McDonald and his analysts just as much.

In Australia's 35 Test innings in the two years before this match, they'd batted past the 100-over mark only six times, compared with 13 times in the 42 innings of the two-year period preceding.

That downward trend has, of course, coincided with a proliferation of the result pitches which characterise the World Test Championship era.

Concurrently, it is agreed by most involved in the Australian domestic scene, it has been difficult for Test batting candidates to put their best feet forward, or get in the habit of playing long innings, when the primary bloc of red-ball cricket occurs in spring, when Sheffield Shield pitches sometimes resemble Monty Don's perennial beds.

Without peering too far into the future or wishing disruption on a player who's just delivered something so special, one awkward talking point that will be aired soon enough is if and when Renshaw might move up to his normal position of opener.

The theory going into this game was that in batting down the order, he could blunt the influence of the spinners, which he assuredly did. But he would surely be just as assured against the new ball as he was here against the second new ball.

And yet, who'd be an opener these days? Late on day two, Ryan Rickelton provided a study in contrasts for the Proteas.

Having spent the better part of two days chasing leather in the field, and perhaps daydreaming that he was in Renshaw's shoes, he lasted only three deliveries before chasing Josh Hazlewood outside his off-stump and sending an edge to the cordon.

The more telling image of day two arrived an hour earlier, on the stroke of tea, when an exhausted Renshaw removed his helmet and trudged off for refreshments.

Appearing on the balcony of the player's area, Australian skipper Cummins peered down on the centurion with something like a look of love on his face.

Ray Illingworth once said a captain needs the patience of a saint, the diplomacy of an ambassador, the compassion of a social worker and the skin of a rhino. Colleagues who can bat for eight hours help, too.

ai-open-source-models-changing-debate:
Photo Illustration by Cheng Xin/Getty Images

A rising open-source American artificial intelligence (AI) industry seeks to challenge the prevailing narrative that companies and consumers must choose between closed, frontier labs and Chinese alternatives.

Politicians and experts have long focused on the competing spheres of AI development: open-source Chinese and closed, frontier AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI. Now, many leading tech companies are launching open-source AI models that give consumers and corporations the benefits of open AI — customization, lower cost and privacy — without relying on Chinese AI.

“We are dying for an American alternative,” Michael Frank, the CEO of Radiant Intel, an AI platform that does geopolitical risk analysis and a visiting AI fellow for the Wilson Center, told the Daily Caller News Foundation in an interview about the need for American open-source AI.

Open-source models are AI systems that can be altered and customized without having to request permission from the AI lab and are often free to use, according to IBM.

“The vast majority of AI deployments are going to be built on open source AI models, and the reason for that is because we’re headed towards the agentic era,” Frank continued, referring to AI “agents” that can perform tasks for the AI user, per IBM.

The growth of the American open-source AI industry may undermine calls for regulation that may ultimately protect the leading, closed-source frontier AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI, the Radiant Intel chief executive said. (RELATED: Beware The Beware-ers: Tech Lords Sounding Alarm On Their Own Tech Have Lots To Gain From Latest 180)

“That’s the problem with the framing: with China being seen as open source and American frontier AI being closed source, we feel like we have this duty to protect this nest egg, but we shouldn’t do that because that’s not where we’re headed in the long run, and it is not the government’s responsibility to give these guys a business model. We should let the market decide,” Frank explained.

“The reason why open source is important is because you need to be able to customize and configure. It’s just a pure economic calculus. Why are we going to pay a 3x markup for a model?” Frank said, referring to the higher cost of closed, frontier AI models.

Other experts believe American open AI may help businesses with lower cost solutions.

“A strong American open-source ecosystem finally gives businesses a real alternative. Open models cost a fraction of commercial models, but do not need to outperform every frontier model on every task,” Lauren Gil, the governing board member of the Tokenomics Foundation as well as the cofounder and president of Kimchi Coding, told the DCNF.

“You would not rent a Ferrari to bring home groceries. Likewise, a routine coding task does not automatically require the most expensive model,” Gil remarked.

“We recently launched Kimchi Coding to tackle this specific problem head-on. It automatically matches coding tasks to the right models, so developers can spend more time building without worrying about each request’s cost,” Gil added.

Gil added that open-source models allow corporations to better secure their most sensitive data than closed models.

“It is all about trust and security. Commercial models have a trust issue,” he explained. “We all know closed commercial-model companies use any training data they can get for their next release. As a result, some enterprises are reluctant to share their most sensitive intellectual property, data, and source code with service providers that may use that data for training, willingly or unwillingly. An American open-weight model gives enterprises the comfort of running it on-prem, air-gapped, on their own dedicated GPUs, or within a secure cloud environment they control.”

Open-source AI was once dominated by Chinese labs and their models experienced so much demand that the Trump administration considered banning or limiting access to them over the summer, the DCNF reported.

In July Moonshot AI, a Beijing-based startup, launched Kimi K3, an open-source model that threatened America’s lead in the global race on AI, according to Axios.

The Chinese open-source race became predominantly represented by Chinese labs such as Moonshot, DeepSeek, and Z.ai, according to Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. The advent of Kimi K3 made the Trump administration appear more interested in banning Chinese open-source AI over the summer, according to Axios.

Now, Reflection, an Nvidia-backed startup developing its own open-source AI model, enters the national dialogue.

Reflection’s open-source model, Beam, could rival the most expensive closed, frontier AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI and keep pace with Chinese open-source models, Axios reported this week.

Reflection CEO Misha Laskin has argued that owning and controlling how the AI operates may be more important than raw AI power.

“Once you’re spending that amount on intelligence, you want to move from renting it to owning it yourself. That’s kind of where open source is very powerful because it is customizable at every level,” Laskin told Axios in October.

“Our goal is to give end users control, sovereignty and continuity, at lower cost – and contribute to a growing open ecosystem, with multiple frontier labs pushing one another forward. The launch of Beam is just the start,” Eleanor Hawkins, a public policy communications official for Reflection, wrote in October on X.

Our goal is to give end users control, sovereignty and continuity, at lower cost – and contribute to a growing open ecosystem, with multiple frontier labs pushing one another forward. The launch of Beam is just the start. https://t.co/WrlmMUbEWb

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has long sought to combine high-end computing power with open-source AI models so that businesses could retain their own data, according to The Information.

An Nvidia spokesperson referred the DCNF to Huang’s comments in late September.

“I believe very deeply in advancing open intelligence,” he told CNBC at the time. “I think we ought to democratize intelligence. I think every company will become an AI company. And this platform really, really keeps that community thriving.”

There are other rising open-source AI models.

Nvidia in August announced a $1 billion investment in the AI startup Poolside to build its own open-source models that would compete against Anthropic and OpenAI, according to the Wall Street Journal. Poolside employees will help Nvidia develop the Nemotron project, which aims to develop its own open-weight models that the company released in 2023.

Thinking Machines Lab in July released its open-source model, Inkling, according to Forbes. The AI startup said, although its model is not the strongest, it is very customizable, according to a Thinking Machines Lab press release.

Thinking Machines Lab declined to respond to a DCNF comment request.

Together AI runs a cloud-based platform for running, fine-tuning and scaling open-weight AI models, per a blog post on its website. The AI startup did not respond to a comment request from the DCNF.

The Trump administration appears to be on board with open AI as well.

A Reflection spokesperson referred the DCNF to Laskin’s panel with White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross at the Black Hat conference in August.

“I think the role that open source plays is vital to this ecosystem,” Cairncross said at the Black Hat during the panel about how open-source AI plays a part in cybersecurity.

“We are extremely interested in looking at ways to build U.S. open source, making it competitive, making it the preferential adoption by planet Earth for U.S. open source,” he continued.

FILE - In April 2024, Alberto Plata-Hurtado helps a Benson Polytechnic High School Escalera senior with his FAFSA.

Tiffany Camhi / OPB

The Free Application for Federal Student Aid, or FAFSA, opens to college students around this time every year. The federal form determines how much financial aid students may receive and is a gateway to federal grants, student loans, scholarships and other aid programs.

But FAFSA makes an assumption that doesn’t work for everyone: that a student’s parents are still part of their life.

For most undergraduate students under the age of 24, FAFSA requires financial information from their parents. Without it, the application is incomplete.

“Not every single college student is someone who can ask their parents or ask someone else. Some of us are just completely dead in the water,” said Alexa, a 21-year-old Portland State University creative writing student.

Alexa said she became homeless after she came out as transgender and was kicked out of her home in North Carolina. Because of concerns about safety from an abusive family member, OPB is only using her first name.

She moved to Oregon last year, where someone she knew took her in. “I started trying to pull myself up, get on my feet again, and eventually I did,” she said.

Alexa found work as an in-home caregiver. She worked full time, six days a week, while supporting herself.

“I got into a position that was decent enough where I could start trying to look into going to school. And that’s where I ran into the issues with the FAFSA,” she said.

Under federal financial aid rules, being financially independent from your parents isn’t necessarily enough to qualify as an independent student. With some exceptions, undergraduate students must have their parents’ information to complete the form and be eligible for most aid.

Alexa was told by Portland State’s financial aid office to apply for a “dependency override.” That process required her to get a letter from her landlord and meet with a therapist to document that she came from an abusive home environment.

“They needed to know when the last time I talked to my parents was,” Alexa said. “And what exactly is stopping me from getting their information — which I had to go into detail — and that wasn’t really fun.”

Alexa has started attending classes but hasn’t yet heard whether she will receive financial aid. If she doesn’t receive aid, she said she will delay classes for another term while she earns enough money to pay for school.

Alexa’s experience isn’t uncommon among LGBTQ+ young adults. Research has found that LGBTQ+ young adults are more than twice as likely to experience homelessness as their heterosexual peers. A survey found that nearly half of LGBTQ+ young adults are estranged from at least one family member.

Rebecca Reilly works with LGBTQ+ young adults at New Avenues for Youth in Portland and said she frequently sees young people run into barriers with FAFSA.

“If you don’t have that parental buy-in, it’s almost impossible to really submit without that paperwork and information,” Reilly said.

Sometimes, she said, the application itself discourages young people from pursuing college.

“They see that it’s asking for this information they don’t have, so then they just don’t fill it out. It gets stopped before it’s even submitted,” she said.

For LGBTQ+ students, paying for college can be only one of several challenges. Reilly said young people she works with can also face mental health and substance use issues, as well as housing instability and a lack of family support.

Without a support system, students can struggle to stay enrolled. “If you don’t have family support, you end up feeling a little bit lost. It’s a lot of newness. It’s a lot of you on your own,” Reilly said.

And for queer and transgender students, the pressures can extend far beyond the classroom — to housing, health care and basic safety. Queer and transgender students often have to worry about their access to dorms, bathrooms, counseling and health services.

Kate Kyvik, an Oregon State University student studying fisheries, wildlife and conservation science, said they have to think about those concerns alongside their schoolwork.

“We don’t just have to sit there and worry about grades or can we afford it?” Kyvik said. “We’re also, daily, worrying about surviving in this country. We’re worrying about: Are we going to make it another day? Or what portions of our rights are we going to lose tomorrow?”

When Kyvik met their partner, who is transgender, one of their parents disowned them.

“That caused a lot of forks in the road or a lot of bumps in the journey in terms of mental health and being able to stay in school,” Kyvik said.

Kyvik found scholarships to fill their financial aid gaps, including one specific to LGBTQ+ students, the National Rainbow College Fund.

The scholarship offered more than financial support. “It validated my identity. It validated my family’s identity. It validated and encouraged me to just keep going,” Kyvik said.

Reilly said that kind of validation doesn’t always have to come in the form of money.

“They just need one person to see them and believe in them,” she said.

That person might be a friend, teacher or service provider — someone who can help a student navigate the paperwork and keep going when things get difficult.

“We do see it,” Reilly said. “As soon as one person is telling them they can do this, then young people are signing up for the FAFSA and they’re enrolling in college.”

Thousands of residents were forced to evacuate on Christmas Eve in 2018 after cracks were found in the building. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The Opal Tower apartment complex in Sydney's west has been declared defect-free at a ceremony.

Residents were forced to evacuate the complex on Christmas Eve in 2018 after cracks were found in the building.

The process of fixing the high-rise and securing compensation for owners has involved a class action, two legal cases, and has cost millions of dollars.

A ribbon-cutting ceremony has taken place at the once-plagued Opal Tower in Sydney's west to mark the building officially being declared defect-free.

The celebration brings an end to a saga, spanning close to eight years, that involved a class action, two legal cases, ongoing rectification work and relocations after cracks appeared on level 10 of the complex on Christmas Eve in 2018.

Fearing a collapse, thousands of people were forced to evacuate with the emergency response also shutting down the nearby train station and surrounding roads at Sydney Olympic Park.

Opal Tower was officially declared defect-free on Saturday. (ABC News)

At the time, police said the tower had moved "1 to 2 millimetres".

Days later, more cracks were discovered on other levels of the 36-storey high-rise.

Opal Tower Owners Corporation chairman Shady Eskander has been at the forefront of the fight to get the complex made up of 392 units repaired, and secure compensation for those affected.

"It's fantastic to announce that Opal Tower is defect-free."

Shady Eskander says the impact of the defects has been devastating for residents. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Mr Eskander told the ABC that a lot of work had taken place and millions of dollars had been spent to be able to declare "this building is the safest and best residential building in Australia".

"Everything that was done was done with the consultants, with the builder, with all of those involved in the design and construction of Opal Tower.

"We came alongside each other in a very collaborative manner."

Developer Ecove, backed by Japanese firm Kajina Corporation, engineers WSP, and builder Icon have been the other parties involved in the process.

An engineer's report commissioned by the NSW government concluded in 2019 that the cracks had been caused by a combination of "design and construction matters, in particular changes made after the original design".

In what Mr Eskander described as an Australian-first, the high-rise is now protected by a 20-year structural warranty.

A report concluded the defects were caused by a combination of "design and construction matters". (Supplied)

All owners have been fairly compensated, and all legal matters have been resolved.

"This is the greatest property comeback story in Australian history," Mr Eskander said in a statement.

Nutan Borkar was out of her unit for 11 months after the incident, and was glad there was finally "light at the end of the tunnel after a big struggle".

"It's great because a lot of time has been invested in getting the building back to the way it should've been," she said.

"I love being here. I wouldn't think of being anywhere else but here now. It's home."

Nutan Borkar says she "wouldn't think of being anywhere else". (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Building standards were lifted across the state, with the Coalition government at the time introducing the role of building commissioner and a suite of other reforms.

"The lesson that can be learnt from Opal Tower … is that quality needs to be there so that defects aren't," Mr Eskander said.

"And we need to ensure that defects don't occur in the towers that are being constructed over Sydney because builders and contractors will spend more on fixing the defect than building it right the first time."

A 56-year-old New York construction worker was killed when he became submerged during a water main break near Long Island’s largest mall on Friday morning.

Rafael Peralta, of Babylon, was working the line underneath Ring Road outside the Roosevelt Field mall in East Garden City when the water enveloped him at around 11:13 a.m., according to News12 and Nassau County police.

Peralta’s coworkers hoisted him out of the hole after he became submerged before first responders administered “life-saving measures” at the scene.

He was rushed to a local hospital where he was pronounced dead, police said.

Peralta was employed by a private contractor hired to work on a private water main and hydrant, News12 reported, citing the Town of Hempstead.

The water main is on the property of Roosevelt Field, who had hired Peralta’s company

“Losing a loved one is really hard. Knowing that they went out there to provide for their families,” New York resident Alice Lindow told News12 near the scene. “And I just want to pray for God’s comfort and strength for the family that is grieving a lost one, because it’s never easy.”

Police launched an investigation into Peralta’s death, shutting down Ring Road between Stewart Avenue and Zeckendorf Boulevard for several hours, the outlet reported.

Peralta’s death follows a similar incident where an Illinois worker died after being trapped in an underground vault during a water main break.

Village of Westmont public works employee Matthew Heiden was killed when water filled the area he was inside on Feb. 23, 2023, according to ABC7 Chicago.

The 20-year-old, the most junior full-time employee on the crew, was “knowingly and intentionally” sent underground, according to a lawsuit filed by Cooney and Conway law firm for Heiden’s estate in November 2023.

Heiden was sent into the confined space “to work on a non-isolated, fully energized, water main valve, without the most basic plan, training, safety equipment, support or supervision,” the suit claims.

The lawsuit sought damages against the village.

A panel of three judges reversed a trial judge’s ruling in March, allowing the lawsuit to proceed, after it was initially dismissed with prejudice.

Vice President JD Vance said Friday he will not watch the planned live-streamed execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan and doubts the broadcast will happen at all.

The vice president made the comments to reporters as seen on C-SPAN footage days after the Pentagon announced that Hasan’s December 3 execution by firing squad would be streamed for the public.

Vance, a Catholic who has said he supports the death penalty, was asked how he squared his faith with the decision to stream the killing. He said Hasan “brutally murdered” innocent people.

“If it’s ultimately live-streamed, I’m not going to be watching it,” Vance said.

The vice president also questioned whether the stream would occur. “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” he said. “Let’s sort of see.”

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth told Real America’s Voice the terrorist’s execution would be streamed for the public, framing it as a warning.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it. That it’s public,” Hegseth said. “Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” The execution is set for 1:00 p.m., the same hour Hasan opened fire at Fort Hood in 2009, shouting “Allahu Akbar.”

Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chairman Brendan Carr said Friday the matter sits outside his agency. Pressed on CNBC’s “Squawk Box” over whether the FCC would permit a broadcast, Carr said, “Ultimately, we’re going to defer to Secretary Hegseth and his decisions on how to move forward with this.”

Meta has barred live-streamed capital punishment on Facebook and Instagram since 2019, and a TikTok spokesperson pointed to a policy against depicting the moment of death. Meta, YouTube, and X did not answer questions about how they would treat the footage.

The United Nations and Amnesty International condemned the plan. The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops called it “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death.” Hillary Clinton called the idea “barbaric.”

President Donald Trump this week approved the execution and defended it Friday at a Columbus Day event. “We’re giving a man the death penalty … through firing squad, and he deserves it,” he said.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was convicted in 2013 of killing 13 people at the Soldier Readiness Processing Center. His execution would be the first by the United States military since 1961, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Global Voices is at a critical moment. Without the support of readers like you, we won’t be able to continue our 20-year legacy of ad-free multilingual journalism. Learn why »

Screenshot of the Internet Infrastructure Map in 2026, from kmcd.dev. Fair use

By Alli Armijo

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The internet has always been illusive. Stretching bodies of water, screens, and time zones, it exists in a plurality increasingly shaped by big tech. And the cables mediate this; the cables are its nervous system.

With over 600 active and planned underwater internet cables spanning over 1.5 million kilometers around the globe, the majority of subsea infrastructure is predominantly owned and operated by US tech monopolies, namely Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft.

This infrastructure is largely laid on trans-Atlantic slave ship and oil extraction routes, algorithmically bound by a legacy of colonial violence and exploitative labor practices.

Three years after the internet was made accessible to the public, the US government passed the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which incentivized independent companies and communications services to compete in the global market. Relaxed regulations and an end to the cap on radio station ownership created more opportunities for media conglomerates — the majority of which are funded by private tech companies — to own, operate, and influence public-facing content.

This is still true today, as Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft currently own roughly over 75 percent of subsea cables around the world. These companies control where information physically flows and the platforms through which this information, this data, circulates.

The growing importance of subsea cables in military and economic policy for major world powers like the US, Israel, and Saudi Arabia offers an entry point into understanding the corrosive, yet dependent, relationship between AI and oil infrastructure.

Earlier this year, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) announced the Communications and Technology Transparency Act as an update to the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019, expanding the “malicious technology and equipment from foreign adversaries” on the FCC’s control list to include China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran. This comes in response to Iran restricting access through the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial point for global oil shipping and subsea cable infrastructure in which the US has invested a significant amount.

We have not seen this kind of surge in subsea cable investment since the internet went public in 1993, effectively shifting the digital sphere from a privatized space for military communications into a public playground. Around this time, companies like Amazon and eBay came online alongside chatrooms, search engines, independent news outlets, and, in turn, the digital sphere entered the homes of those who could afford it.

Today, internet infrastructure policy is increasingly a topic of discussion in military strategy and policy decision-making. China has supposedly asked Iran to help defend against Houthi attacks along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, as Saudi Aramco oil exports, in which it has invested USD 4 billion, remain vulnerable. Chinese and US-based companies Alibaba, Amazon, IBM, Google, and Microsoft maintain some of the largest investments in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) having the most data center and cloud projects.

This internet infrastructure is deeply tied to oil infrastructure, as the natural gas systems increasingly used to keep data centers in America running are optimized by AI, effectively pillaging the physical and digital platforms through which local communities connect and express themselves. At the atomic level, crude oil is made almost entirely of hydrocarbons, which AI has been used to optimize in the form of wellbore drilling tools and environmental assessments.

In 2025, US President Donald Trump signed a $600 billion investment commitment in technological and defense systems with Saudi Arabia. In the same month, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) launched HUMAIN, a vertically integrated AI company developing an Arabic-first language learning model, with full computing infrastructure located in Saudi Arabia.

In March 2026, HUMAIN announced a partnership with Turing, an American AI cloud lab helping Fortune 500 companies scale and deploy AI agents. This move clarifies Saudi Arabia’s positioning as an AI exporter rather than strictly a consumer, reinforcing the feedback loop of US control over and investment in global AI infrastructure, specifically in the Gulf region.

And just 10 miles away sits the largest recipient of US foreign aid since cables first began being used strategically in warfare, in World War II. This colonial project hosts data centers owned and operated by Amazon, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle, companies that secured the $9 billion Joint Warfighting Cloud Capability (JWCC) contract with the Department of Defense (DoD).

Israel historically relies on oil imports, and the biggest resource they stole is the Leviathan Natural Gas field, the largest natural gas reservoir in the Mediterranean off the coast of the Gaza Strip. In this way, the colonial project’s energy policy is contingent on its ability to sustain US-backed AI infrastructure, and by extension, access to natural gas resources pillaged from land stolen from the Palestinian people.

Because jurisdiction over data belongs to the hosting country in which that data is located, the Palestinian people are constantly killed and robbed of not only their land, but their data and digital footprint. Heavily and forcibly reliant on Israel’s digital infrastructure, which is in turn heavily funded and supported by US interests, Palestinians are frequently left out of global conversations and decisions impacting their livelihood or killed with US-funded weapons before they get the chance.

On September 24, at the UN General Assembly in New York, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas spoke to the council from his office in Ramallah, after being denied entry into the country for the second year in a row. He spoke about the devastating effects of Israel’s ongoing genocidal war in Gaza, calling on the rest of the world to hold them accountable for their actions and end the ongoing occupation.

“We will not leave our homeland. We will not accept displacement. And we will not allow anyone to decide our future on our behalf.”

The Cornell student accusing seven frat brothers of gang raping her had worked with one of them to try to find the “rat” talking about them having sex at a party — claiming they needed to “grow up” and be more open-minded about what went on, according to a fresh batch of text messages.

Just four days after the Chi Phi fraternity party where the student now claims she was drugged and raped, Jane Doe texted student Matthew Ingalls in a panic claiming “everybody knows” about them having sex , leavin her “incredibly stressed out,” messages obtained by TMZ show.

Ingalls sympathized after the accuser complained about some  “random bitch” telling her friends.

“Dude I have no f—king idea, this sh-t is incredibly frustrating and I know how fast nonsense spreads at this school,” responded Ingalls, who later claimed he was the one assaulted while too drunk to consent.

“It’s fan behavior from everyone talking about it. Boring people who have nothing to do with their time,” texted Ingalls, who Doe later said instigated the alleged 2024 gang rape.

Doe said the rumors were “f—king RUINING my life” and that she wanted to sniff out “the rats.”

“My reputation is destroyed and i’m utterly ashamed. i’m f—king pissed because this many people shouldn’t know and i feel like i know who some of the rats in the room were,” she texted him.

She added that the rumors were not only spreading like wildfire but were growing “crazier every f—king day.”

“Stupid bitches like to yap, and the fact they’re doing it shows that they’re jealous of you for any number of reasons,” Ingalls shot back.

“The only shameful thing is how this spread and how much people won’t shut up about it — which just reflects poorly on them tbh,” he added.

Doe agreed that the gossips are “jealous” and threatened to beat up anyone who gives them “sh-t” about what happened while also opening up how she’s “open-minded” about sexuality.

“…but also like everyone needs to grow up cause sexuality and sex and sh-t is changing and stuff like this is going to become more common,” she said, while adding that she is “also really open minded tho.”

Doe later said she suspected of another Cornell fraternity brother she accused of partaking in the sexual assault, Jonathan Newell, of having loose lips.

“Jonathan def told people. I heard something today and i know he told people,” she texted Ingalls.

Ingalls denied Newell said anything, and suggested some upperclassman may have been spreading the word.

Doe responded that a female student who confronted her “wouldn’t tell me who she heard it from cause it’s one of her friends.”

Ingalls apologized and promised “these idiots will move on and it’ll be done with.”

More than a week later on November 7, Ingalls tells Doe that his ex-girlfriend told him he’s now been labeled a sexual abuser on campus — and asked if Doe had made those allegations against him.

Doe said she’s stayed mum but added  “people are changing the narrative because like in any sexual scenario w one woman and many men the woman was probably victim.”

“I know there are rumors I was gang banged,” she said.

That same day, Doe requested a rape kit at an emergency room and reported the alleged rape to campus police the following day, according to her lawsuit.

Ingalls and Newell were two of the seven fraternity brothers named in Doe’s lawsuit who were eventually expelled from the Ithaca, New York Ivy League school.

No criminal charges were brought at the time.
exclusive-viral-meme-mocking-maga:
Forbidden HQ

A grotesque, beer-guzzling caricature created to mock unquestioning MAGA influencers has become an unlikely mascot in conservative corners of the internet, and the anonymous creator behind it is himself a conservative who considers himself “America First,” he revealed to the Daily Caller News Foundation.

The creator of Forbidden HQ, a viral political satire account, spoke exclusively with the DCNF about the character widely known as “MAGAtard,” an exaggerated MAGA hardliner who reflexively rationalizes whatever new political talking point comes his way. The creator drew a distinction between the political principles he associates with America First and what he sees as an increasingly personality-driven MAGA culture — a divide that has become more visible as conservatives clash over issues including the Iran war. (RELATED: Megyn Kelly Guest Laughs Because ‘Democrats Don’t Know How To Meme’)

“My values are conservative,” the creator, who was granted anonymity due to privacy concerns, told the DCNF.

The DCNF independently verified the creator’s identity.

“Forbidden HQ is, it’s mostly satire. It’s entertainment,” he told the DCNF. “We take politics, internet culture, memes, public figures, politicians, celebrities, and turn all of that into basically ridiculous cinematic worlds. Nobody’s really safe from it, whether it’s left, right, establishment, anti-establishment.”

“If there’s something funny there, and there’s a discussion around it, we’ll make fun of it,” he said.

Conservative Inc influencers after the group chat sends out the new talking points: https://t.co/5X9716p0x8

In Forbidden HQ’s breakout video, the red-hatted character sits at his computer with a vacant grin, dutifully parroting defenses of everything from government surveillance and artificial intelligence data centers to the war in Iran.

The caption supplies the punchline: “Conservative Inc influencers after the group chat sends out the new talking points.”

The “MAGAtard” character was never supposed to represent every Trump voter, the creator told the DCNF.

“He’s a caricature. He’s intentionally absurd and exaggerated, and he’s what happens when an internet stereotype gets turned into, like, a recurring movie character,” he said. “He’s a fictional character, and that’s what makes him funny.”

The joke is aimed more narrowly at what the creator calls the online influencer class surrounding MAGA, particularly personalities he believes are willing to shift alongside the administration on issues ranging from the economy and tariffs to foreign policy.

LEAKED: Netanyahu’s private influencer briefing. Sources describe the meeting as productive, professional and occasionally hostile. https://t.co/GsfkWBv1FZ

“I’m absolutely America First to the core where I think, you know, Americans should always come first,” he said.

Trump built much of his political appeal by attacking the Republican establishment, questioning foreign wars and promising to “drain the swamp.” Forbidden HQ’s character targets what the creator sees as an establishment developing around the anti-establishment movement itself, complete with online personalities willing to defend the party line.

The creator’s videos repeatedly return to war, surveillance, Jeffrey Epstein, Israel, foreign lobbying and loyalty to Trump.

“I think it goes back to America First,” he said, arguing that “a lot of our elected officials put foreign governments, foreign-policy interests, and lobbying organizations before the American people.”

The running gag places MAGAtard in situations where a supporter might be expected to become angry with the government, only for the character to discover a reason to support what it is doing anyway.

The war in Iran provided one example of the tension Forbidden HQ targets. Trump faced opposition to the military campaign from prominent figures on the America First right after the U.S. launched Operation Epic Fury on Feb. 28, while other supporters rallied behind the administration’s case for the conflict.

Forbidden HQ’s character does not experience that internal debate. Whatever the administration does, he finds a way to support it.

Former MAGA influencer Ashley St. Clair alleged in a series of TikTok videos that prominent MAGA personalities were handed talking points from administration officials and congressional Republicans via private group chats.

St. Clair pointed to the online reaction following the shooting at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner as an example of what she alleged was coordinated messaging.

More than 100 right-wing influencers, politicians and commentators posted within roughly 24 hours about how the incident demonstrated the need for Trump’s proposed White House ballroom, according to a Washington Post analysis.

Then the people being mocked started claiming the character as their own.

Instead of rejecting the caricature, portions of the online MAGA world began treating the character as an ironic hero. The insult became a badge of honor, and the grotesque loyalist became something closer to a mascot.

“There are two ways I look at it. Part of me finds the commitment funny. But there’s also a serious point underneath the character,” the creator told the DCNF.

“For years, people on the right criticized the left for refusing to criticize its own side. The argument was basically: you don’t have to stop being a liberal to admit when your side is wrong.”

The creator said conservatives should hold themselves to the same standard.

“You can support Trump, be conservative, and still disagree with a war, complain about gas prices, demand transparency around Epstein, oppose an expanding surveillance state, or criticize the administration when you think it broke a promise,” he said.

“In fact, I think that’s healthy. Political commentators shouldn’t exist simply to validate politicians. If the people who elected an administration disagree with something it’s doing, they should be willing to say so publicly.”

Forbidden HQ does not limit that standard to MAGA.

FORBIDDEN STUDIOS PRESENTS: THE MAYOR A man of every principle, every position, every constituency, all at once. https://t.co/cv7IhqfDvr

The account has also turned its surreal style against the left. In “THE MAYOR,” Forbidden HQ mocked Democratic New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as “a man of every principle, every position, every constituency, all at once.”

The response helped illustrate another part of the creator’s argument.

Some followers, he said, were happy when Forbidden HQ mocked Trump or Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. When the account went after Mamdani, some announced they were done with it.

“I don’t want you people following me in the first place if this is how you’re going to be,” he recalled thinking. “Because when I’m making fun of Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu, you’re on board, but the second I make fun of the mayor of New York for being inconsistent and hypocritical, you want to get upset about it.”

“I’m pissing off both sides,” he said, “and there are people who appreciate that we’re willing to criticize everybody.”

Who gets mocked most can change with who holds power, he said. With Trump in the White House and conservatives controlling much of the federal government, the right supplies more material than it did during former President Joe Biden’s presidency.

“So it really depends on the current state we’re in,” he said.

Forbidden HQ’s creator also rejected the idea that describing the work as satire gives him license to do anything for a reaction.

“Satire and political commentary can absolutely coexist. Doxxing is different, and I don’t support it,” he said.

He described the account as a kind of “modern political cartoon,” where a point of view is unavoidable but cruelty is not the objective.

“My goal isn’t to add more division,” he said. “There’s already enough of that.”

“For me, the main line is that it has to work as satire. Even when the subject is serious, I’m not interested in mocking innocent victims or being gratuitously cruel. I want to make people think and laugh at the same time.”

He said there have been rare occasions when he decided a post crossed his own line and deleted it, even when it performed well.

“I don’t want the joke to cross over into being gratuitously personal or cruel,” he said.

The creator also said he believes political speech and satire should receive broad protections, including when they challenge powerful people or institutions.

“I believe very strongly in the First Amendment and in the broadest possible protection for political speech, satire, criticism, and controversial ideas,” he told the DCNF. “In America, people should be able to say what they believe, challenge powerful institutions, criticize public figures, and engage in uncomfortable conversations without fear of censorship or retaliation for lawful speech.”

“No public figure, government, political movement, ideology, institution, religion, or powerful organization should be treated as too sacred for satire, criticism, or scrutiny.”

Asked who he wants following Forbidden HQ, the creator did not answer Republicans, conservatives or even MAGA.

“My base is truth seekers,” he said.

He described them as people “that are not married to one idea, and one belief in politics” and are willing to “judge both sides accordingly. Or all sides accordingly.”

“Stepping out of the left-right paradigm, and really putting yourself on the side of the people,” he said.

Forbidden HQ did not initially settle on a name for its breakout character. Users called him “MAGA Chud,” “MAGAtard,” “Goyslob,” “Uncle Ham” and other variations, according to the creator.

Data centre operator Firmus was set to become Australia’s  biggest company, but has now cancelled its share float. Are investors starting to become wary of the industry’s circular financing? Watch this space.

Meanwhile, Donald Trump says, and I quote: “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

I am the enemy. And so are you.

Much was made of the parliamentary inquiry into AI and its public hearings this week, particularly the star appearances by representatives from Anthropic and OpenAI on Tuesday, but did we really learn anything?

OpenAI used AI to write an email — surprise! — but doesn’t know why Australians don’t trust AI. The company’s chief strategy officer Jason Kwon repeated their apology for hacking government websites and promised to do better in the future.

And as ABC News reported, Anthropic’s representatives said their company was “finalising a deal to let Australia's AI Safety Institute independently test its models”.

The Australian headlined the idea from Andrew Forrest’s non-profit Mindaroo of forcing AI giants to pay artists ($), while the AI companied bleated their usual whinge about having to pay for copyright.

But there doesn’t seem to have been much more than that.

To be fair I have yet to read the full Hansard transcript from Tuesday (PDF) or the rest of the hearings and all the other witnesses. Indeed, the fourth and final day is still in progress as I type these words. If anything significant happens I’ll let you know.

Meanwhile the South Australian government has announced the commissioners for its own AI Royal Commission.

The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) has opened an investigation into Shenzhen Qingcheng Future Technology Co Ltd.

According to the OAIC, the company’s HeyCyan app is used by a variety of low-cost smart glasses, ”including Kmart’s Anko branded smart glasses, glasses sold via Big W’s marketplace, and glasses sold via Amazon and other retailers”.

The OAIC has been asking privacy-related questions of various manufacturers and distributors of smart glasses, including Meta, Kmart, Google, and Shenzhen Qingcheng, since mid-August following a request from the attorney-general.

“In the absence of any response from Shenzhen Qingcheng to the OAIC’s preliminary inquiries, I have no assurance that it is protecting personal data of Australians as required by the Privacy Act,” said Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind.

Kind also wrote a blog post providing further background on this issue, including the OAIC’s position on smart glasses and the forthcoming “second tranche” Privacy Act reforms that we discussed last month.
