“The View” co-host Sunny Hostin predicted Thursday that voters will flip Texas blue in November for the first time in about 30 years as the panel discussed the tight race between Democratic candidate James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton for the US Senate.

“I think we will. I think we will see Texas go blue, actually. I really do,” Hostin remarked. “In September, not only one, but eight pollsters had Talarico ahead 51-45%. That is so significant given that a Democrat hasn’t won statewide office in 30 years.

“That same poll showed that he is leading Paxton among women, 56% to 40%. Among voters aged 18 to 29, 66% to 22%, and among Hispanics, 62% to 30%. We’re talking about Texas. He’s going to win this race.”

Co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin argued that Talarico’s edge in the Lone Star State was a referendum on President Trump’s administration.

“I mean, the fact that Texas is in play speaks to the moment right now that people are so frustrated with the current leadership,” she said.

“A Democrat hasn’t won statewide in Texas in over 30 years. I still think it could go either direction for Paxton or Talarico, but this is kind of a perfect storm, and it’s a mess of the president’s own making.”

Griffin agreed the state might flip blue, calling Talarico a good candidate. She argued that Sen. John Cornyn would’ve been a better Republican candidate over Paxton, who was endorsed by Trump and came out on top in the GOP primary.

A Fox News poll released in October found Talarico enjoying a net positive personal rating of 8 points among likely Texas voters (52% favorable vs. 44% unfavorable), compared to Paxton, who is underwater by 18 points (40% vs. 58%).

Republicans are six times more likely to view Paxton unfavorably (32%) than Democrats do Talarico (5%).

Likely Texas voters are split on control of the Senate: 49% prefer a Democratic Senate while 50% favor a Republican upper chamber. Eight percent of self-identified Republicans prefer the Democrats in power versus 1% of Democrats crossing over to pick the GOP.

All this gives Talarico a slim 2-point edge over Paxton (51-49%) in the poll among likely voters. These matchup results are within the margin of sampling error.

Co-hosts Whoopi Goldberg and Ana Navarro cast some doubt on the positive polling for the Democratic candidate.

“Two-thousand sixteen left me scared,” Navarro said.

“I have hope. People should have hope, but hope alone won’t win an election. People got to turn hope into vote. And I don’t think they, you know, relying on polls and just kind of sitting back and getting complacent is something that nobody can afford to do if they want to see change.”

Paxton’s campaign did not immediately return Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

Trump campaigned with Paxton in San Antonio, Texas, Wednesday.

They both pointed to Talarico’s absence from campaigning at the event. The Senate candidate’s campaign responded to the criticism, explaining Talarico has been sick with the flu and is expected to return to the campaign trail this weekend.

“Anyone taking seriously what Sunny Hostin and Alyssa Farah Griffin say about politics likely has a low enough IQ to qualify as a guest host on ‘The View,’” RNC spokesman Zach Kraft told Fox News Digital in a statement about the co-hosts’ remarks.

The two Ukrainian journalists detained in Austria on Oct. 8 are suspected of espionage, Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said at a press conference on Oct. 9.

Mykhailo Tkach, head of the media outlet Ukrainska Pravda's investigations team, has been released, while cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko is still in custody, Karner said, as cited by the Ausrian newspaper Kleine Zeituing.

"At 4 a.m. on Oct. 9, Mykhailo Tkach was released after being detained for more than 12 hours in Vienna," Sevhil Musayeva, Ukrainska Pravda's chief editor, wrote on Facebook. "However, his communication devices have still not been returned, so the editorial team is currently unable to contact him directly. Our colleague Yaroslav Bondarenko was injured during the detention and was hospitalized. Police did not begin questioning him until the early hours of the morning."

She added that the legal status of both journalists is unclear.

"The allegations made against our colleagues while they were detained are unlike anything our editorial team has encountered before and raise serious questions," Musayeva added. “We expect Austrian law enforcement authorities to explain the circumstances surrounding our colleagues’ detention, Yaroslav’s injury, and the reasons why both were held for so long. We also expect clarification of their legal status and the return of their communication devices.”

Musayeva said that Tkach had previously been detained in other countries and released within an hour to an hour and a half once the circumstances had been clarified.

"This is the first time they have been held for more than 12 hours," she argued. "The length of their detention, the nature of the allegations made against our colleagues, Yaroslav’s injury, and our inability to contact Mykhailo directly are all causes of serious concern.”

Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said on Oct. 9 that "Ukrainian diplomats and consular officials at the Ukrainian Embassy in Austria have been working with their Austrian counterparts to resolve the situation."

He said that Ukraine's Foreign Ministry is investigating the circumstances of Tkach's detention and trying to establish if Bondarenko has also been released.

zack-polanski-ethics-inquiry:
Labour and Tories claimed Green party leader breached London assembly ethics code over non-payment of tax

Zack Polanski has been cleared by an ethics inquiry looking into complaints that he did not pay council tax while living on a houseboat.

A report by the Greater London authority’s monitoring officer found that the circumstances of the Green party leader’s living arrangements were beyond its scope and he had therefore not breached the code of conduct for London assembly members.

The complaints from Labour and the Conservatives alleged that Polanski had breached the requirements of the ethics code because he had not paid council tax while living on a houseboat in east London from 2022.

Polanski, who previously apologised for the “unintentional mistake”, revealed in his evidence to the monitoring officer that it had still not been established whether any tax was due and that the site of the boat fell on the border of two local authorities. As part of the inquiry, he told the monitoring officer that he had “personal experience of financial hardship and housing insecurity”.

He previously said he had not been living at the marina full-time but at another address as a lodger, before it emerged that he had occupied the boat for a couple of years before moving to a house.

In his witness statement, Polanski said he had never had any intention to “evade council tax, avoid legal obligations or obtain any improper financial advantage” and it remained unclear whether he had actually failed to pay the proper tax.

“Any failure to appreciate the position arose solely from a misunderstanding of what was required in relation to an unusual and unconventional living arrangement,” he wrote.

“Having lived through periods of economic difficulty on a limited income, I understand first-hand the challenges faced by many Londoners,” he wrote in his statement. “My previous living arrangements reflected those circumstances rather than any attempt to avoid financial obligations.

“Whilst I accept that greater care could have been taken in understanding the practical implications of my unconventional housing arrangements, I strongly refute suggestions that my honesty or integrity should be called into question.”

Polanski also revealed that he had lived for five years as a property guardian, occupying an otherwise vacant building under licence in return for modest fees.

“This was one of the few affordable housing options available to me in London during a period marked by economic uncertainty, austerity measures and significant cost-of-living pressures,” he said.

“Under those property guardianship arrangements, I paid a licence fee to the relevant provider and, as was my understanding and experience throughout that period, utilities and council tax liabilities were managed and covered through those arrangements. Whilst unconventional, this became my normal experience of housing administration and associated household outgoings.”

He said that when he moved to the narrowboat in August 2022, he believed that council tax was included in the moorings fees “given the nature of the arrangement, my previous experience of property guardian accommodation”.

He added: “I readily acknowledge that I did not undertake further inquiries at the time regarding the specific council tax implications of living on a narrowboat. This is why I have already unreservedly apologised for that unintentional mistake.”

Polanski also raised concerns that the complaints were politically motivated and said they had been promoted under the guise of public interest yet appeared to aim to advantage his opponents.

The Green party said: “The monitoring officer for the Greater London Authority has conducted an independent inquiry into the complaints made against Mr Polanski and decided to take no further action. We therefore consider this matter closed.”

Neil Garratt, the Conservative assembly member who originally complained about Polanski, said his actions had shown a “cavalier attitude” to establishing whether tax was due.

Gov. Bob Ferguson submitted a letter to Trump asking him to unlock up to $42,500 for individuals.

Governor Bob Ferguson announced September 28 that he had submitted a letter to President Donald Trump asking for a federal major disaster declaration in the wake of a devastating wildfires across Eastern Washington in late July and early August.

The fires caused more than $188 million in damages, Ferguson said at a Monday press conference in Spokane. A major disaster declaration would open up an estimated $11.2 million in funds for individuals for Benton, Spokane, Stevens and Okanogan counties and the Spokane Tribe of Indians, and qualify the state for an additional $117.7 million in public assistance funds for debris cleanup and emergency costs across 11 counties. Now, the region waits for the president's decision.

A preliminary damage assessment by the Washington State Emergency Management Division, FEMA and local county jurisdictions showed that the fires had burned nearly 369,000 acres. Across the four counties, the fires destroyed 649 primary residences, with an additional 2,542 homes damaged, and forced more than 118,000 people to evacuate. About 70% of affected county residents and Spokane tribal members were insured, Ferguson said.

Ferguson credited Trump for “very quickly” granting the initial emergency declaration that allocated short-term federal resources for immediate response in the wake of the wildfires.

“But to be candid, the most significant request by far that any state has in a situation like this, that any community has in a situation like this, is the one that we're seeking today: a major disaster declaration,” he said.

Over the past five years, across both the Biden and Trump administrations, the president has taken an average of 43 days to approve a request for aid from Washington, according to a RANGE analysis of FEMA data. This encompasses seven approved state declarations and three from tribal nations in Washington.

Approval for the 2023 Gray and Oregon Fires took more than four months. The state's 2025 floods — the most recent major disaster declaration in Washington — took two and a half months to be officially approved.

“I want to emphasize that each disaster declaration request from different states can have its own timeline,” Ferguson said Monday.

Ferguson pointed to how the state had received a major disaster declaration for the historic flooding that more than a dozen counties experienced last December.

He described the federal administration as "tremendously helpful" in past situations.

“I have had multiple communications with folks at the federal level and the administration and deeply appreciate the assistance they provided to us up to this point," Ferguson said.

Jeremy Fagan and his wife Kittie Blansfield lost their home just a couple blocks from Rifle Club Road and are hoping for the funding to come through.

If the disaster declaration is approved, they’re planning to apply for FEMA funds. Ferguson’s request asks for the maximum amount of $42,500 to be made available for FEMA’s Individual Assistance Program.

“I have a whole house to rebuild, so I'll probably apply for the maximum,” Fagan said.

Ferguson’s request detailed that nearly 900,000 acres had burned in Washington this year as of September 2. So far, the state has invested more than $150 million for wildfire response and recovery in 2026 and distributed nearly $1 million in assistance to more than 600 households thus far, according to a press release from Ferguson’s office.

Since 2021, FEMA has committed more than $214 million in approved individual assistance and obligated hazard mitigation and public assistance funding to Washington as the state has grappled with disasters like severe storms, flooding and wildfires.

However, outlets like the New York Times and the Associated Press have reported increased approval times for disaster assistance nationwide in recent months.

Waymo is recalling nearly 4,000 robotaxis after its vehicles repeatedly failed to recognize freeway construction zones, in some cases driving past closure signs or between cones marking closed lanes.

A total of 3,871 vehicles equipped with Waymo’s fifth-generation Automated Driving System (ADS) are affected, and the interim workaround is to restrict freeway driving until a fix is available.

Six events were logged in Phoenix, Arizona, in April, during which vehicles drove past ramp-closure signs into pre-planned freeway construction zones. The response of Waymo's Field Safety Committee was to implement freeway driving restrictions.

There were seven incidents in May in the San Francisco Bay Area, where vehicles drove between cones designating a lane closure. According to the Safety Recall Report, this was "due to the ADS inappropriately prioritizing the avoidance of other freeway hazards and/or failing to recognize the construction zone."

The response was further freeway driving restrictions until the company could get to the bottom of the problem. On June 8, Waymo's Safety Board decided to conduct a recall.

Vehicles not capable of driverless operation on freeways are not affected and have not been recalled.

The recall comes a month after Waymo disclosed that flooding could confuse its vehicles on high-speed roads, prompting another software fix.

Waymo's vehicles operate in several US cities and have recently been sighted on the streets of London, albeit with a human ready to take control if needed.

wa_prisons_closing_the_gap:
September 21, 2026

Western Australia has the highest Aboriginal imprisonment rate of any state while expanding prison capacity. Yet shortages of stable housing can obstruct bail, parole and successful reintegration.

The Productivity Commission’s latest Closing the Gap figures should have caused a political shock. Instead, their release attracted remarkably little media attention. Target 10 requires Australia to reduce the rate of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adult imprisonment by at least 15 per cent by 2031. Yet, to date, the national rate has risen by almost 30 per cent since the 2019 baseline.

Western Australia exemplifies that failure. On the latest reported figures, it has the highest Aboriginal adult imprisonment rate of any state. The rate was 3,302 per 100,000 in 2019. If WA were moving steadily towards its commitment, it would now be near 3,013.2. Instead, it has reached a staggering 4,306.

Because imprisonment has risen rather than fallen, WA must now reduce the rate by almost 1,500 per 100,000 adults in only five years to meet its commitment. There is no published recovery plan showing how that will occur.

The rapid growth of remand is one of the clearest drivers of this worsening trajectory. Nationally, in 2025, 45.1 per cent of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults in prison were unsentenced. The number held on remand was 91 per cent higher than in 2019, while the number detained for more than a year had more than doubled. These people have not been sentenced; many have not been found guilty.

Remand is often presented solely as a response to risk. But risk is assessed through the material circumstances in which people live. Without a stable and acceptable address, a person may be unable to obtain bail. Without transport, legal assistance or culturally safe supervision, compliance becomes harder. Court delays then turn disadvantage into months – and sometimes more than a year – behind bars.

Housing is therefore not an issue that begins at release. Its absence can help move people into custody before trial, obstruct parole and make successful reintegration far less likely. For Aboriginal people, these pressures are compounded by poverty, racism, displacement from Country and a chronic lack of culturally safe place-based support.

The imbalance is visible in the south west where I live. Bunbury Regional Prison holds almost 600 men. However, there are only four transitional houses available, each with three single-occupancy bedrooms. One house is prioritised for women returning from prisons in Perth, leaving just nine beds for released men needing housing support.

Access to these houses is linked to parole, making them generally unavailable to those who complete their full sentence. Some Aboriginal men serve their entire sentence rather than accept parole conditions they experience as intrusive and difficult to satisfy. Others may be denied parole because they lack suitable accommodation, which is the very support they need to leave prison successfully. Either way, they can walk through the prison gate with nowhere stable to live.

People released from custody must then compete for scarce crisis, short-term and affordable accommodation. Through my work, I know men who have left prison only to couch-surf, armchair-ride, live under carports, camp in the bush or squat in abandoned buildings.

The latest national prison-health data show that one in four prison entrants had experienced homelessness in the preceding month, while about one in three people preparing for release expected to be homeless.

WA has reintegration services and homelessness programs, but its budget identifies no dedicated statewide pool of post-release housing, let alone culturally safe accommodation reserved for Aboriginal people leaving custody. Instead, assistance is bundled into broader programs, forcing former prisoners, already burdened by stigma, to seek shelter within a system overwhelmed by urgent need.

The contrast is a policy disgrace. The WA Government can build accommodation at scale – provided it is behind prison walls. An ABC report identifies 373 additional beds at Casuarina Prison, while the 2026–27 budget brings the Acacia Prison expansion to 480 beds. Together, these projects will add 853 beds at substantial public cost.

Within that response, the budget allocates $67.2 million to custodial expansion and $239.4 million to services required by a growing prisoner population. Yet there is no comparable, clearly identified commitment to the transitional housing needed to support successful release and return WA to the agreed Target 10 trajectory.

Redirecting expenditure outside the gate is not charity. It is sound public policy. Australian research comparing people given public housing after prison with those receiving private-rental assistance found that, after housing, police incidents fell 8.9 per cent a year and time in custody fell 11.2 per cent. Justice costs initially fell by almost $5,000 per person and then by another $2,040 each year. Public housing produced a net benefit rather than an additional cost.

Humane conditions inside prisons matter. But continuously building cells in response to unmanaged demand does not resolve overcrowding; it institutionalises it. Every new bed creates continuing staffing and operating costs while leaving the causes of imprisonment intact.

The WA Government should publicly justify every dollar of its prison expansion against Target 10. Funding earmarked for prison infrastructure beyond what is needed to remedy unsafe conditions should be redirected to Aboriginal community-controlled bail accommodation, transitional housing and permanent homes. Meeting Target 10 requires a targeted, at-scale housing program outside prison, delivered in community and for community.

Target 10 remains a commitment to reduce Aboriginal imprisonment: it is not permission to finance enough cells for its continued growth.

Western Australia must stop budgeting for failure and begin funding the conditions that make freedom possible.

She works with marginal Noongar peoples of the South West to implement preventative and interventionist strategies needed for reducing individuals and families who are vulnerable to engagement in the criminal justice system.

A combination of extreme heat and a risk of thunderstorms is forecast for Washington, D.C., on Sunday, potentially affecting plans around a major UFC Freedom 250 event being held as part of celebrations to mark the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, and on President Donald Trump's 80th birthday.

Forecasters are warning that hot, humid conditions could give way to scattered afternoon storms, with the potential for downpours, lightning and gusty winds across the Mid-Atlantic region.

While organizers have not indicated any changes to the event schedule, meteorologists say the timing of the weather system could intersect with outdoor activities.

According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Storm Prediction Center (SPC), parts of the Mid-Atlantic—including Washington, D.C., Baltimore and surrounding areas—face a “slight risk” of severe thunderstorms on June 14.

That designation means isolated severe storms are possible, with the primary hazards identified as damaging wind gusts.

In a forecast discussion, the SPC said: “scattered thunderstorms may develop… and pose a risk mainly for damaging gusts” as a cold front moves into a warm, moisture-rich air mass.

A broader swath of the Eastern U.S. is under a lower-level “marginal risk,” highlighting the potential for unsettled weather extending from the Southeast into the Northeast.

Separate forecasts point to high temperatures around 93°F in the capital, with “real feel” values approaching 102°F due to humidity, prompting a severe heat warning.

"Dangerously hot conditions with temperatures between 95 and 100 degrees F expected," says the NWS. "Peak heating days will be Sunday and Monday with a slight cool down on Tuesday. Overnight temperatures will remain elevated Sunday night into Monday morning, and Monday night into Tuesday morning."

Meteorologists say the day is expected to start hot and bright, with cloud cover building through the afternoon—conditions that can help fuel storm development later in the day.

There is currently a 55 percent chance of precipitation and roughly a one-in-three chance of thunderstorms, while wind gusts could reach around 34 mph in stronger cells. Forecasters are warning that lightning and brief heavy rainfall could disrupt outdoor activity.

While there is no certainty that the weather will cause problems for the UFC Freedom 250 event at the White House, many are watching closely. On prediction market site Polymarket, there is currently a 46 percent chance of a weather delay at the UFC event.

The combination of extreme heat and the potential for storms presents a dual challenge, particularly for large gatherings outdoors.

Heat indices above 100°F can increase the risk of heat-related illness, while even isolated thunderstorms can lead to temporary stoppages or safety delays if lightning is detected nearby.

At this stage, however, forecasts emphasize that storms are expected to be scattered rather than widespread, meaning impacts could vary significantly across short distances.

Forecasters say the key uncertainty is how quickly storms develop and where they track as the cold front approaches.

If storms form earlier in the afternoon, disruption risks increase. If development holds off until later in the evening, much of the day’s scheduled activity could proceed without interruption.

Weather conditions are expected to become clearer once the front moves through, with less humid air following into the next week.

Funding for Wales' controversial new farm subsidy scheme will exceed a billion pounds during this Senedd term, the Welsh government has announced.

Setting a budget spanning several years to help farmers plan ahead was one of Plaid Cymru's promises for its first 100 days in power.

Caryl Davies says her family have decided to join the SFS, and believes there are ways that farming and nature can work together

The protest-hit Sustainable Farming Scheme (SFS) was introduced earlier this year, after almost a decade in development.

Payments with a greener focus replace the subsidies farms had received before Brexit based on how much land they had.

Those who sign up have to agree to a checklist of requirements - including managing at least 10% of their land as habitat.

The budget announcement is being made on the opening day of the Royal Welsh Agricultural Show in Llanelwedd.

Caryl Davies, a beef and sheep farmer from Eglwyswrw, Pembrokeshire, said her family had decided to join the new scheme.

"There are ways that farming and nature can work together, it'll improve the soil and the crops we're growing," she said.

The fact that the budget was being ring-fenced over several years would "give people a bit more confidence they've made the right decision," she said.

"A three-year plan gives you some certainty about what you're going to get," agreed retired livestock auctioneer Alwyn Jones, showing his pedigree Welsh Black cattle.

But the money would not go far, he said, as costs have gone up and "everything has gone dearer".

While a three-year budget is welcome, "five years would be better and a bit more money obviously," added Stephen Roberts from Denbigh.

Alwyn Jones says a three-year plan would give farmers some certainty but warned the money might not go far

Figures show that about half of farmers applying for subsidies this year decided to opt into the new SFS.

The other half decided to stick with the old regime for now, meaning they will see a 40% cut in funding this year as those subsides are phased out.

However far more land is covered by the new arrangements - with 905,545 hectares being farmed by those in the SFS, and 384,399 hectares by those who remain in the legacy scheme.

The Welsh government said it would commit Â£340m per year to the SFS up to March 2030 and the next Senedd election.

It means Â£238m a year will be reserved for the entry-level payment - known as the scheme's universal layer.

A further Â£102m will go towards optional and collaborative layers - where farms can choose additional, more ambitious environmental work for extra cash.

Abi Reader, president of NFU Cymru, welcomes the announcement

NFU Cymru president Abi Reader said the industry would "really welcome the multi-annual funding".

"If we were still in the EU we would have a seven-year cycle so we're not quite there but at least we know for the next three years it's certain," she said.

Farmers' Union of Wales president Ian Rickman said recent years had brought significant financial uncertainty for the farming sector in Wales, making it "increasingly difficult for businesses to plan with confidence and make informed long-term financial decisions".

"The FUW has consistently called for a five-year funding framework, so today's commitment to provide certainty until March 2030 is a welcomed relief for the family farms of Wales," he said.

Environment groups said more funding would be needed to help farmers - who manage 90% of the Welsh landscape - restore nature and tackle climate change.

The charity, alongside the RSPB and National Trust, had called for a doubling of the current budget, she noted.

"Sticking with the same budget level is disappointing," she said, urging ministers to introduce full details of the scheme's optional and collaborative funding pots quickly.

Kosovo was finally cleared of landmines, Germany set a date for quitting fossil fuels, and a new cat species was discovered, plus more good news

Kosovo was finally cleared of landmines, Germany set a date for quitting fossil fuels, and a new cat species was discovered, plus more good news

Some 27 years after the Kosovo War ended, a humanitarian mission to clear the country of landmines has concluded.

The Halo Trust, a mine-clearance charity, announced this week that its work in the country was done, claiming the cleared land has “paved the way for Kosovo’s recovery”.

More than 800,000 people were displaced during the Kosovo War (1998-1999). When refugees returned home, they found a ravage landscape littered with mines. According to the Halo Trust, 150 people were killed or injured by mines in the first month alone.

Kosovo is a different place today. Cleared land has paved the way for agriculture and infrastructure projects, helping the country’s post-war economy to flourish. According to the World Bank, average life expectancy is now 78 – just one year less than it is in the US.

“Kosovo shows us that the real impact of removing landmines and cluster bombs is not measured in hectares cleared, but in what that land makes possible over time,” said Atholl Stewart, programme manager for Halo Kosovo.

Halo’s workers from Kosovo are now leading the charity’s operations in Syria and Ukraine.

Image: uskarp

The global goal to protect 30% of the planet by 2030 is within reach, but governments must accelerate action to achieve it.

That’s according to a major review of the policy, published this week. It found that around 20% of land and inland waters are already designated protected. Existing commitments, it adds, would increase that to 27% by 2030 – just shy of the target.

“Real progress is being made,” said Brian O’Donnell, director of Campaign for Nature. “Countries have expanded protected and conserved areas around the world – safeguarding critical ecosystems such as forests, wetlands, and mangroves.”

However, the Global Assessment 30×30 report warns that progress at sea is much slower. It finds that just 10% of the ocean is designated protected – a gap authors say could be closed by the High Seas Treaty (more on that below), which gives nations new powers to protect waters outside of their national boundaries.

Enforcing protected areas is another challenge. The report warns that bottom trawling and other damaging practices are still happening in many conservation zones.

O’Donnell called on governments to accelerate action and reframe the 30×30 target “not only as a conservation imperative, but as an investment in economic resilience, climate stability, food and water security, health, and long-term prosperity”.

Image: iStock

“The world is uniting around ocean protection even in divided times,” campaigners said this week, as the number of nations to ratify the High Seas Treaty reached 100.

Australia, Brunei, Canada, Germany, Papua New Guinea and Zimbabwe are the latest countries to ratify the treaty, which entered force in January. It provides the world’s first legal framework to conserve life on the high seas, which covers nearly half the planet’s surface. Currently, less than 1% of international waters are fully protected.

“In many cultures, the number 100 carries real weight – whether it is a marker for age, an anniversary, or a symbol of luck and prosperity. For the High Seas Treaty, it marks the real momentum of the world uniting around ocean protection, even in divided times,” said Rebecca Hubbard, director of the High Seas Alliance.

Hubbard called on more countries to ratify, and urged those that have done so to turn the “wave of support turns into real decisions”.

Forget the European summer lull: Startups can’t afford to stay still, and Brussels is following suit. In the middle of peak vacation time, the European Commission announced that the Scaleup Europe Fund was fully operational, with investments “expected in the coming weeks.” But its first deal was actually made public the very next day.

ICEYE, a Finnish satellite intelligence company now valued above $11 billion, is the first startup backed by this unique public-private vehicle, which co-led its Series F. Similar deals should follow soon; Scaleup Europe plans to deploy €5 billion ($5.7 billion) into growth-stage startups based in the EU or partnering countries and operating in strategic sectors.

“Space-based intelligence is becoming critical infrastructure for governments, and the Scaleup Europe Fund exists so companies like ours don’t have to leave Europe to compete globally,”  ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski (pictured above) wrote on LinkedIn.

Even in less critical sectors, helping Europe build scaleups and keep them is key for its competitiveness and tech sovereignty — and that’s also the fund’s raison d’être. With the conviction that Europe misses out when its deep tech talent lacks late-stage funding or only finds it abroad, the Commission took the matter into its own hands, but it also partnered up.

Unlike other programs that are managed directly by European institutions and handing out public monies, Scaleup Europe is backed by private investors and run by Swedish asset manager EQT, which was selected via an open call to “experienced fund managers.”

Other candidates reportedly included Eurazeo, Northzone, and Vitruvian Partners, with Atomico as final challenger. While it has offices across Europe, the firm may have been hindered by having its headquarters in London. But having pointed out the growth funding gap for years, still described Scaleup Europe as “urgent and necessary” when EQT was announced as the winner.

As for EQT, it described the initiative as a “big moment for Europe.” “Europe has proven its ability to create successful early-stage technology companies, the challenge is now to scale those businesses into becoming global leaders while maintaining their European roots,” EQT CEO and managing partner Per Franzén commented in a statement.

Notably, the Commission has given the fund manager some leeway as to where to invest — with a mandate “including but not limited to deep tech, life sciences, clean tech, advanced manufacturing, and digital technologies.” For EQT, this will overlap with the likes of AI, biotech, energy, robotics, semiconductors, and space — as shown by ICEYE.

With ties to the Wallenberg family, which was initially listed as a potential anchor investor of the fund, EQT was arguably a front runner to run Scaleup Europe. With more than $300 billion in assets under management, it will also be tasked with helping the fund reach its total fundraising target — starting with a “significant commitment” of its own capital.

It is unclear how much capital Scaleup Europe has raised so far, but its first closing was anchored by a €1 billion investment from the Commission (approximately $1.15 billion) investing alongside institutional investors from all across Europe, credited as “founding investors.”

According to public information, these founding investors include German insurance giant Allianz; APG, representing Dutch pension fund ABP; Spanish bank-affiliated funds CriteriaCaixa and Santander-owned Mouro Capital; Italy’s Fondazione Compagnia di San Paolo, Intesa Sanpaolo, and Fondazione Cariplo; and Denmark’s EIFO and Novo Holdings.

Scaleup Europe’s fundraising is expected to extend into 2027, with a second fundraising round described as potentially open to non-European investors, as long as these are aligned with Scaleup Europe’s objectives.

This might be a necessary compromise to raise the kind of capital Scaleup Europe is seeking. According to reports, the Commission suggested it could eventually expand to €25 billion ($28.9 billion). If it does, it would start belonging to the same category as Asian and U.S. growth funds.

As it stands, Scaleup Europe’s €5 billion target already makes it an outlier in the EU — VC firms in continental Europe typically manage millions, rarely billions. But with the EIF’s European Tech Champions Initiative actively backing growth-stage VC firms as a fund-of-funds, this could quickly change. In other words, Scaleup Europe may soon just be there to fill the gap.

This story was updated for a correction; EQT has more than $300 billion — and not millions — in assets under management.

Topic:Avian Influenza

Greater crested terns have been one of the species most severely affected by bird flu so far in Australia. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

In a matter of weeks, Australia has moved from its first mainland H5N1 bird flu detections to hundreds of confirmed cases and several wildlife mass mortality events from the disease.

A series of deaths off South Australia, including more than 1,000 terns, marked an important shift in Australia's encounter with H5N1 bird flu.

Federal authorities warn they will not be the last, although it is far too early to know what exactly comes next.

But what we do know is that these events are an increasing challenge for ecologists and wildlife managers.

Warning: This story contains images that some readers may find distressing.

Mass death events are sudden episodes in which unusually large numbers of animals die over a relatively short period, often near each other.

Disease is one cause. But they can also be triggered by heatwaves, drought, fire, floods, harmful algal blooms, starvation and other environmental extremes.

Besides bird flu deaths, there has recently been a mysterious mass death of pelicans at Menindee Lakes, NSW, and the disappearance of cuttlefish from the Upper Spencer Gulf, SA.

These events do not simply remove animals from ecosystems. They create masses of dead and decaying flesh (carrion), redistribute nutrients, attract scavengers and change interactions between species.

Yet despite their scale, we know surprisingly little about these events and their longer-term ecological consequences.

Mass death events are inherently difficult to study.

We rarely know when or where one will occur, making it difficult to collect the "before" data ecologists normally rely on.

Marine heatwaves, fires, droughts and other extreme events are already capable of killing wildlife on enormous scales.

Mass death events are expected to become more frequent as weather and climate extremes intensify.

A mass mortality event involving pelicans, which was not related to bird flu, was found at the Menindee Lakes earlier this month.
  (Damien Cook)

H5N1 bird flu adds another potential driver of mass mortality to Australian ecosystems.

By the time an event is detected, it may already be well underway, while events in remote areas may go unnoticed altogether.

Much of the attention understandably focuses on the animals that have died: how many, which species and why.

But the ecological effects of a mass mortality event do not end with those deaths.

A single carcass is a relatively small and temporary food resource.

But hundreds or thousands of carcasses arriving over a short period in close proximity can represent a substantial and concentrated pulse of food into an ecosystem.

The ecological impact of this sudden abundance of carrion will be different from the normal amount of dead animal flesh in an area.

When an animal dies in nature, there is usually something willing to eat it.

Flies and other invertebrates can find carcasses remarkably quickly. Birds and mammals often follow.

Some are familiar scavengers: ravens and other corvids, raptors, dingoes, and foxes. But scavenging is far more widespread than we often assume.

Dingoes are a species that will scavenge carcasses in the Australian landscape. (Supplied: Global Ecology Lab, Thomas Newsome, USYD)

Many animals we do not usually think of as scavengers will eat decaying flesh when the opportunity arises.

In our own work in Australia, for example, we've recorded brushtail possums frequently scavenging animal carcasses.

Other research has documented opportunistic scavenging across a huge diversity of vertebrates.

Most of the time this is an important ecological process. Scavengers consume dead animals, helping ecosystems cope with sudden increases in carcasses while returning nutrients and energy to the food web (a complex system of food chains).

But large amounts of carrion could shift where scavengers spend their time and how long they remain in an area.

Some species may dominate access to a large number of carcasses, changing opportunities for other scavengers.

It is also possible that scavenger communities are overwhelmed by too many carcasses and can't consume it all.

The effects do not necessarily stop at scavengers.

As carcasses decompose, large quantities of nutrients are released into the soil.

This can change soil chemistry and, in turn, vegetation. Depending on the size of the mortality event, those effects can persist long after the dead animals themselves have gone.

So mass mortality events do not simply remove animals from an ecosystem; they can temporarily restructure how energy and nutrients move through it.

But when the animals die from an infectious disease, another layer is added; each carcass may also be a potential source of exposure.

During a disease outbreak scavenging becomes more complicated.

With H5N1 bird flu, an infected animal can remain a source of infectious material after it has died.

Experimental work has shown the virus can persist in carcasses with environmental conditions, such as temperature, influencing for how long.

In one study, red foxes fed infected bird carcasses became infected and shed virus for several days.

This is particularly relevant because scavengers are mobile. A fox feeding on a seabird carcass isn't restricted to the beach where it found it. Raptors can cover large areas. Gulls routinely move between beaches, wetlands, rubbish tips, urban areas and agricultural landscapes.

Animals can also physically remove parts of carcasses and consume them somewhere else. This means a carcass can connect species and habitats that would otherwise have relatively little direct contact.

Topic:Animals

Topic:Animals

Topic:Avian Influenza

Topic:Marine Biology

Topic:Avian Influenza

However it is important to note that finding a virus in a scavenger does not automatically mean that animal is important in spreading it onwards.

Exposure, infection and onward transmission are separate things, and we still have major gaps in our understanding of each.

But this is why scavenging deserves more attention in Australia's H5N1 response.

For many scavenger species, we have little idea how susceptible they are to H5N1 bird flu, how often they will encounter infected carrion, or what happens when they do.

And we should not assume that scavenging automatically makes a disease outbreak worse.

In some circumstances, scavengers may actually help.

Efficient scavenger communities can rapidly remove carrion, potentially reducing how long carcasses and their associated risks persist in the landscape.

Australia knew H5 bird flu was coming for years.

While considerable work has gone into surveillance and response planning, there have also been warnings that major gaps remain in our ability to respond to its impacts on wildlife, particularly during mass death events.

Surveillance of living animals remains critical, as does protecting poultry, identifying outbreaks and preparing responses for threatened species.

There will not be one answer.

Removing every dead animal from the Australian environment would be impossible and probably undesirable.

Carrion is a natural part of ecosystems.

But during very large mortality events, carcass dispersal or removal may sometimes be warranted when carrion exceeds what scavenger communities can efficiently process.

This may be particularly important at breeding colonies, where infected carcasses can accumulate in a relatively small area, or where threatened species are at risk.

We need evidence to know when intervention helps and when it does not. Monitoring how long carcasses persist, what consumes them and where that material goes should therefore sit alongside disease surveillance from the beginning.

Dr Patrick Finnerty is a conservation ecologist at the University of Sydney and former participant in the ABC Top 5 science media residency.

By

Rachel Treisman

Construction has continued on the White House ballroom all summer, as seen on Wednesday.
                
                    
                    Tierney L. Cross/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

A federal appeals court ordered the Trump administration to halt construction on its White House ballroom, saying the project needs approval from Congress in order to continue.

"Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit wrote in a 136-page ruling issued Friday.

The three-judge panel issued a 2-1 ruling, but it says it will stay its order for two weeks to allow the Trump administration to appeal to the Supreme Court.

NPR has reached out to the White House for comment but did not hear back in time for publication.

President Trump slammed the decision within two hours, calling it "horrendous, politically motivated and unlawful." He wrote on Truth Social that his administration will appeal immediately. He pointed out that the two judges who sided against him in the ruling were appointed by Democratic presidents: Barack Obama and Joe Biden.

Trump also repeated his administration's argument that the ballroom is a matter of national security, and that Friday's ruling threatens it.

The decision "severely jeopardizes the lives and welfare of the people who work, and will be working, at the White House — including all future Presidents of the United States, and their families, as well as the lives of all those visiting, such as Heads of State and other Dignitaries, and all Americans who wish to visit the historic, beautiful Executive Mansion," Trump wrote.

The nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation, chartered by Congress, which brought the lawsuit late last year, celebrated the ruling.

"This is a great day for our country and for the American people's right to voice their opinions about the historic places they cherish, including the White House," Brent Leggs, its president and CEO, said in a statement shared with NPR.

Friday's ruling is the latest chapter in a saga that began in October, when the Trump administration started demolishing the East Wing of the White House to make way for Trump's long-held dream of a presidential ballroom.

The administration has said the ballroom will total roughly 90,000 square feet and seat 1,000 guests. The White House originally estimated the cost at $200 million, but the Washington Post reported in June — citing contractors' invoices — that the total cost could be at least $600 million.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued the administration in December, seeking to halt construction until the government completed the legally mandated review process, which includes obtaining approval from Congress.

"From the beginning, our position has been clear and consistent: the law states that only Congress can authorize the construction of a ballroom at the White House," Leggs said on Friday.

The Trump administration has argued that the case has no legal standing, and that stopping construction has implications for national security.

The legal fight has revealed new details about the mysterious bunker beneath the East Wing: Trump said the "military is building a big complex" under the would-be ballroom. The administration has pointed to high-profile threats in the months since — like the White House Correspondents' Dinner shooting — to paint the ballroom as a national security issue.

"The single, integrated project includes Bomb Shelters, State of the Art Hospital and Medical Facilities, Protective Partitioning, Top Secret Military Facilities, Structures and Equipment, Protective Missile Resistant Steel, Columns, Roofs, and Beams, Drone Proof Ceilings and Roofs, Military Grade Venting, and Bullet, Ballistic, and Blast Proof Glass. It is all tied together as one big, expensive, and very complex unit, which is vital for National Security and Military Operations of the United States of America!" Trump wrote on Friday.

Senate Republicans originally proposed adding $1 billion in taxpayer security funding for the ballroom as part of a sweeping immigration and border security package in May, but ultimately dropped that provision after significant bipartisan backlash.

In the meantime, Trump's efforts to put his mark on D.C. — and weaken federal protections for historic sites — continue. Several, such as his proposed triumphal arch, face legal challenges of their own.

Miguel Vargas hadn’t hit a home run since the sixth inning of an Aug. 21 game against the New York Mets.

The Chicago White Sox third baseman was stuck on 29 for the season. That changed in the first inning Friday against the Minnesota Twins when Vargas hit a solo home run to right-center field for his 30th of the year.

“It’s pretty awesome,” Vargas said. “I know how hard it is and I’ve been working very hard. (To) achieve one of these moments, it means a lot for me for sure.”

Shortstop Colson Montgomery joined him in the 30-homer club in the fourth inning with a two-run blast.

Photos: Chicago White Sox 4, Minnesota Twins 1

The Sox finished with three home runs in a 4-1 victory against the Twins in front of 25,616 at Rate Field.

Even with the win, the Sox saw the American League Central race tighten. The first-place Sox (74-67) have a 2½ game lead over the second-place Cleveland Guardians (72-70), who won both games of a doubleheader Friday against the Detroit Tigers in walk-off fashion.

According to STATS, Vargas and Montgomery are the first Sox teammates in franchise history to record their 30th home run of the season in the same game.

“It just goes back to offseason training and things like that,” Colson Montgomery said. “You dream of all this stuff and you try to prepare for all this stuff. Going out there and making it happen is not easy by any means. I think it’s just a lot of dedication to staying with your approach and process and stuff.

“Doing it on the same night and being able to share with Vargas is awesome.”

They are the first pair of Sox players to record 30-plus home runs since José Abreu (33) and Eloy Jiménez (31) in 2019.

“It’s really cool, a special season really by all our offense,” manager Will Venable said. “Sitting on 29, I’m sure they’re thinking about it a little bit. So great to see it. Now they can move past it and continue to hit.”

Vargas is the fifth primary third baseman in Sox history to hit 30 home runs in a season, joining Todd Frazier (40 in 2016), Robin Ventura (34 in 1996), Bill Melton (33 in 1970-71) and Joe Crede (30 in 2006).

Vargas, Ventura and Crede are the only primary third basemen in franchise history to record 30 doubles and 30 home runs in the same season. Vargas has 30 doubles.

Montgomery, 24, is the third player in Sox history at age 24 or younger to record 30-plus home runs and 80-plus RBIs in a season, along with Frank Thomas in 1991 (23 years old, 32 home runs, 109 RBIs) and Melton in 1970 (24 years old, 33 home runs, 96 RBIs). Montgomery has 81 RBIs.

The Vargas home run came with one out in the first inning on a 3-2 fastball from Twins starter Zebby Matthews. Braden Montgomery hit a solo home run in the second.

“We scored in the first two innings and have a little more comfort and go after guys,” Sox starter Erick Fedde said. “Breathing room is always nice. This team has done that for the most part all year.”

Colson Montgomery made it 4-0 with the two-run blast in the fourth on an 0-1 fastball.

“We all know how good Colson is and how important he is for the team,” Vargas said. “Doing this with him, it means a lot for me and I’m very glad to share that moment with him too.”

Matthews — who carried a perfect game into the sixth inning last weekend against the Sox at Target Field — allowed four runs on four hits with four strikeouts and one walk in five innings.

“The last time we faced him in Minnesota, we did a really good job — we got good barrels, good contact, good at-bats, just we didn’t get the result that we wanted,” Vargas said. “Today we came in with the same mentality, trying to be a little bit more aggressive and attacking a little bit more and we got a good result.”

The Sox took the opener of the three-game series thanks to the home runs and a strong outing from Fedde. The right-hander allowed three hits, struck out two and walked two in five scoreless innings.

“Just trying to make quality pitches no matter the count,” Fedde said. “These games are as important as they come, throwing every pitch like it’s the most important one of the year. And just kind of carrying that mentality pitch to pitch and it’s had success.

“When I go out there right now, I’m feeling as good as I’ve felt all year.”

who_is_in_cabinet:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced his new cabinet after taking office following the resignation of Sir Keir Starmer.

Tap or click on a person in our interactive guide below to learn more about them and their role in government.

Andy Burnham is the prime minister, after winning the backing of 379 of Labour's 403 MPs as the best person to replace Sir Keir Starmer.

He has pledged to shift power away from Whitehall, introduce "greater public control" of the water and energy sectors and to build more council houses - while keeping Labourâs election pledge not to raise the main rates of income tax or National Insurance.He also promised to provide "breathing space" for households struggling with the cost of living.

Born in Aintree in 1970, Burnham was inspired by the minersâ strike to join the Labour Party in his teens and first became an MP in 2001.

The former health secretary had twice failed to become party leader - losing to Ed Miliband in 2010 and Jeremy Corbyn in 2015 - and after leaving Parliament, served as Greater Manchester mayor. He returned as Makerfield MP in June and succeeded Sir Keir Starmer a month later.

A life-long Everton fan and talented sportsman, he was part of Labour's Demon Eyes FC football team when Tony Blair was PM, and regularly featured in the Labour MPs vs Lobby journalists match while in Parliament.

John Healey returned to the cabinet as chancellor of the exchequer, less than two months after quitting as defence secretary.

A former Treasury minister, Healey had recently attacked what he called a "Treasury orthodoxy that's a dead hand on dynamic government" that viewed defence as "a drain rather than a driver of growth".

Senior figures in government say he shares Burnham's ambitions for reindustrialisation and devolution. He now faces the task of making the government's spending plans add up.

It is a surprise appointment for the MP for Rawmarsh and Conisbrough in South Yorkshire, with many speculating the role would go to Ed Miliband or Shabana Mahmood.

Healey was parliamentary private secretary to Chancellor Gordon Brown from 1999 to 2001, before serving as adult skills, Treasury, local government and housing minister between 2001 and 2010.

Louise Haigh has become chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, first secretary of state and Cabinet Office minister.

Haigh, one of Andy Burnhamâs closest allies, will run the Cabinet Office, the department that supports the prime minister and co-ordinates the governmentâs policies to deliver its agenda.Her appointment as first secretary of state underlines her senior status in government and cements her place at the heart of Burnham's administration, after she was among a small group of trusted allies involved in preparations for the transition to power.

After entering parliament as MP for Sheffield Heeley in 2015, Haigh was named the hardest-working new MP in 2016 due to the number of her Commons speeches and questions, and praised by then-Speaker John Bercow for her "terrier-like intensity".

In 2025, the former special constable and Unite union shop steward became the first person to resign from Sir Keir Starmerâs cabinet as transport secretary after it emerged that she had admitted a fraud offence in 2013.

On the backbenches she emerged as a crucial power broker on Labour's "soft left", and was at the heart of the huge rebellion that scuppered the government's welfare cuts in 2025.

Ed Miliband is the foreign secretary, after moving from the energy and net zero brief he had held since Labour returned to power.

He had been touted as a possible chancellor, but opinion was divided between supporters who pointed to his experience in the Treasury, and opponents who distrusted his views, particularly on energy.

Since the election he has spoken out against those urging the government to drop its net zero ambitions and insisted the party's green power transition will help secure social justice and national security.

Miliband has been the MP for Doncaster North since 2005 but has been at the centre of Labour politics for even longer - working for Labour MPs before the 1997 election win and as a special adviser to Gordon Brown when he became chancellor.

He is best known as a former Labour leader - having beaten his brother David, a former foreign secretary, among others, in the leadership contest that followed the partyâs 2010 general election defeat - but also co-hosted the Reasons to be Cheerful podcast for several years.

Shabana Mahmood remains home secretary, the position she has held since September 2025.

Mahmood, who has a reputation among Labour MPs as a hardliner on immigration, is responsible for that brief in the role, along with national security and for policing in England and Wales.

When first appointed as home secretary, she announced sweeping changes to the UKâs asylum system, describing the previous system as "out of control".

Her plans include making it harder for migrants already in the UK to settle permanently, which was criticised by more than 100 Labour MPs, peers and union leaders - and former deputy leader Angela Rayner, who is now back in the cabinet, described it as "un-British".

The Birmingham Ladywood MP claims to be the first female Muslim MP - although she was elected in 2010 alongside Yasmin Qureshi and Rushanara Ali - because, she says, her count was the first completed on the night.

Wes Streeting is the defence secretary, having replaced former soldier Dan Jarvis who had only been in the role for a matter of weeks.

Streeting, who resigned as health secretary in May saying he had lost confidence in Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, eventually decided to back Andy Burnham rather than launch his own leadership bid.

The former National Union of Students president and London councillor is widely seen as one of the partyâs most skilled communicators.

He has written an autobiography about growing up in a council flat in Londonâs East End, visiting his bank robber grandfather in jail, growing up as a gay Christian and about being diagnosed and treated for kidney cancer at the age of 38.

The Ilford North MP has said his upbringing left him "quite cynical" of the role of the state compared with many Labour colleagues, aware of its failings as well as its potential to enable opportunity.

Yvette Cooper remains in cabinet but became health and social care secretary, having most recently served as foreign secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government and home secretary before that.

She will face numerous challenges in the role, including getting NHS waiting lists in England down, improving relations with senior doctors and making progress on social care - one of Andy Burnham's priorities.

The former journalist was first elected as an MP in 1997 and went to serve as the first female chief secretary to the Treasury, later becoming work and pensions secretary in the Labour government under Gordon Brown.

Among other firsts in her political career, the Pontefract, Castleford and Knottingley MP became the first minister to take maternity leave, and she was one half of the first married couple in the cabinet - alongside her husband, former education secretary and Strictly Come Dancing contestant, Ed Balls.

Lucy Powell in now the education secretary and says there is "no more important job" than making sure young people have the best education and opportunities they can.

Powell had been leader of the House of Commons - responsible for delivering the government's legislative programme - until she was sacked by Sir Keir Starmer in the reshuffle that followed Angela Rayner's resignation from the cabinet.

She went on to replace Rayner as deputy leader of the party, winning an election of Labour members.

Powell, who joined the Labour Party at 15, has been an MP since winning a by-election in Manchester Central in 2012 and has held several shadow cabinet roles, including stints leading on education, housing and culture.

She led Ed Miliband's successful campaign to become Labour leader in 2010, helping him defeat Andy Burnham among others, and was then Miliband's chief of staff for two years. However, as a Manchester MP she has also worked closely with Burnham for many years.

Pat McFadden remains work and pensions secretary, the role he has held since September 2025.

He took over the department months after the party was forced to U-turn on extensive changes designed to reduce the welfare bill and has pledged to reform the welfare system "in a way that is fair and sustainable".

As the partyâs national campaign co-ordinator McFadden was one of the masterminds behind Labourâs historic 2024 election victory, constantly stressing the need for message discipline ahead of the election and warning activists and MPs alike to ignore the opinion polls.

A former adviser to Sir Tony Blair, the Glasgow-born MP has represented the Wolverhampton South East constituency since 2005, serving as a business minister under Gordon Brown and in several shadow ministerial roles since then.

McFadden has also held the post of chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, responsible for running the Cabinet Office - the department that supports the prime minister and co-ordinates the governmentâs policies to deliver its agenda.

Angela Rayner returned to the cabinet as secretary of state for housing, communities and local government, months after settling her tax affairs with HM Revenue and Customs.

She quit as Sir Keir Starmerâs deputy PM and housing secretary after the then prime ministerâs independent ethics adviser found that she had broken the ministerial code by underpaying stamp duty when she bought a flat in May 2025.

As housing secretary, Rayner will be a key figure in delivering Burnham's plans to devolve power from Westminster and oversee a large-scale expansion of council house building.

Born in Stockport, Greater Manchester, in 1980, Rayner grew up on one of the area's poorest council estates and from an early age, was caring for her mother, who had bipolar disorder and suffered from depression.

She left school with no qualifications but, after having her first child at 16, Rayner studied part-time at college, gained a vocational qualification in social care.

As she worked as a care worker in Stockport, she also rose quickly through the ranks of the union Unison, and she credits the union movement for encouraging her to enter politics. She became MP for Ashton-under-Lyne in 2015 and is a powerful figure on Labour's "soft left".

Jonathan Reynolds has become secretary of state for business, innovation, science and trade.

It is a return to the business department he led until September 2025 but the role has been expanded to take in science and innovation, which were in a separate department.

The son of a fireman, Reynolds grew up in Sunderland - and still supports the cityâs football club - but he went to university in Manchester, where he joined the Labour Party and chose to remain after graduating.

Reynolds, who has described himself as a Christian socialist, has been the MP for Stalybridge and Hyde in Greater Manchester since 2010 - he had been an assistant to the constituencyâs previous MP James Purnell.

Bridget Phillipson remains in the cabinet as women and equalities minister but will no longer be education secretary. She was also appointed Labour Party chair.

Before becoming an MP she managed a refuge for women and children who were fleeing domestic violence.

Raised by her mother in a small terrace council house with rotting window frames and no upstairs heating in a former mining town near Sunderland, she was bullied at school and received free school meals.

But Phillipson credits "amazing teachers" for encouraging her to apply to Oxford, where she studied modern history.

She had joined Labour aged 15 and became its MP for Houghton and Sunderland South in 2010, aged 26.

Former Labour leadership challenger Lisa Nandy remains digital, culture, media and sport secretary.

In the role she has held negotiations with the BBC about how it will be funded in the future and has said she is thinking "quite radically and creatively" about alternatives to the "deeply regressive" licence fee.

Nandy stood against Sir Keir Starmer in the 2020 leadership race and was described as ârefreshingly untribalâ by one Tory MP who thought she was Labourâs best choice.

She finished third but her reward was to become shadow foreign secretary. 
                        Nandy later shadowed Levelling Up Secretary Michael Gove before moving to international development.

As co-founder of the Centre for Towns think tank, Nandy has been a vocal champion of places like Wigan, which she has represented since 2010, arguing they have been overlooked in discussions on regional development and devolution.

Miatta Fahnbulleh is the energy security and net zero secretary, after replacing Ed Miliband who has become foreign secretary.

She had been working on policy ideas for a potential Burnham government since resigning as a junior communities minister in the aftermath of Labour's disastrous local election results in May.

Born in Liberia, she was brought to the UK as a five-year-old by her parents who were fleeing the countryâs civil war in 1986 - the family were granted asylum in the late 1980s.

A trained economist, she is a former civil servant and also ran the New Economics Foundation think tank before becoming MP for Peckham in London in 2024.

She is seen as being part of Labourâs "soft left" faction.

Former Home Office minister Alex Norris is the justice secretary and Lord Chancellor.

The former Trade Union organiser and Nottingham City councillor was first elected to Parliament in 2017.

In the Home Office he was responsible for border security and asylum.

The Nottingham North and Kimberley MP, who was born in Manchester, describes himself as a keen runner and Manchester City supporter.

Heidi Alexander remains transport secretary, the role she has held since November 2024.

The former Lewisham MP has previously been in charge of transport in London â having quit parliament in 2018 to become deputy mayor of London for transport.

She has spoken of her pride at helping to bring the Elizabeth line into service and of keeping the cityâs transport network running during the pandemic.

Alexander returned to parliament as MP for Swindon South in July and was serving as a justice minister before taking on the transport brief.

She had been shadow health secretary under Jeremy Corbyn but quit the role in 2016 describing the shadow cabinet as âentirely dysfunctionalâ.

Dame Angela Eagle is the secretary of state for environment, food and rural affairs.

She was previously a minister in the Home Office and Cabinet Office and has been on the Labour front bench since the last Labour government.

Eagle is perhaps best known for challenging the leadership of Jeremy Corbyn in 2016 - but withdrawing to back rival Owen Smith days later.

She has been MP for Wallasey since 1992 and was joined in the Commons in 1997 by her identical twin sister Maria Eagle.

Sir Chris Bryant is the secretary of state for Northern Ireland, replacing Hilary Benn.

He moved from the Department for Business and Trade.

It is Sir Chrisâs first cabinet position, although he held a number of shadow frontbench roles under Sir Keir Starmer and Jeremy Corbyn.

A former Anglican priest, he was awarded a knighthood in 2023 in recognition of his campaigning work around acquired brain injury and melanoma - a type of skin cancer.

He was elected as the MP for Rhondda and Ogmore (previously Rhondda) on 7 June 2001.

Douglas Alexander stays in the cabinet as Scotland secretary, having previously been in the cabinets of Keir Starmer, Gordon Brown and Tony Blair.

A former secretary of state for international development and for transport, Alexander lost his Paisley and Renfrewshire South seat to the SNP in one of the biggest shocks of the 2015 general election.

He was re-elected to parliament in 2024 as MP for Lothian East and was tipped for an immediate return to cabinet, but Sir Keir Starmer initially appointed him as a trade and economic security minister.

Alexander is one of the few Scottish Labour MPs who knows Andy Burnham - from their time working together in the Blair and Brown governments - and is seen as experienced and smart.

He has been robust in his dealings with SNP ministers, who say his original appointment marked a significant deterioration in Scottish and UK government relations after a period of better co-operation in the early days of the Starmer government.

Stephen Kinnock is the secretary of state for Wales.

He had been the care minister since Labour won the general election in 2024.

The son of former Labour leader Neil Kinnock, he joined the Labour Party aged 15 during the miners' strike and has been MP since 2015.

He is married to the former prime minister of Denmark Helle Thorning-Schmidt.

Emma Reynolds is chief secretary to the Treasury, working under Chancellor John Healey.

She was previously secretary of state for environment, food and rural affairs and had served in Labourâs shadow cabinet as shadow secretary of state for housing and planning and shadow secretary of state for communities and local government).

She trained as a solicitor and worked in public policy before entering parliament.

She was elected as MP for Wycombe in 2024, having previously served as MP for Wolverhampton North East from 2010 to 2019.

Anneliese Midgley, one of the key figures in Andy Burnham's leadership campaign, is in the cabinet in the role of chief whip.

She has only been the MP for Knowsley, not far from Makerfield, since 2024 but she has been an influential force in the Labour movement for much longer than that, working for both Sir Keir Starmer and Jeremy Corbyn in opposition, following stints at the TUC.

She has spoken about how, when she was growing up, her familyâs life was changed by the "secure, well-paid, unionised job" her father got at a car factory.

Before her political career, music lover Midgey ran club nights in Liverpool, worked in record shops and helped bands including Pulp with press.

She was briefly married to Bob Stanley, a member of indie group Saint Etienne, and has told how the couple shared their first kiss on hearing that Tory grandee and TV personality Michael Portillo had lost his seat in the 1997 election.

Ellie Reeves has been appointed attorney general and will attend cabinet.

The sister of former chancellor Rachel Reeves, Ellie has previously attended cabinet as minister without portfolio and Labour Party chair.

She had been solicitor general since September 2025.

The former employment rights lawyer, who joined the Labour Party at the age of 15, represents Lewisham West & East Dulwich and has been an MP since 2017.

Sir Alan Campbell remains the leader of the House of Commons.

In the role, he is responsible for delivering the governmentâs legislative programme, by working closely with the chief whip to manage Commons business, like motions and debates.

He was previously chief whip, responsible for making sure MPs vote in line with party policy.

Sir Alan has been MP for Tynemouth since 1997 and was Sir Keir Starmerâs opposition chief whip, but he also has experience in the Government Whipsâ Office under Sir Tony Blair.

The former history teacher was knighted in 2019.

Baroness (Angela) Smith of Basildon remains leader of the House of Lords.

The role, which she shadowed in opposition, sees her responsible for delivery of the governmentâs legislative programme in the Upper House.

She was an MP for Basildon throughout the last Labour government from 1997 to 2010, serving as a minister under Sir Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.

She became a life peer in the 2010 Dissolution Honours List and is also patron of an animal welfare charity.

Hamish Falconer is the minister for intergovernmental relations & European relations attending cabinet in the Foreign Office and the Cabinet Office.

He will be responsible for intergovernmental and European relations.

He entered the House of Commons as an MP after the 2024 general election and was promoted to the front bench, as a Foreign Office under-secretary, less than a year later.

He is the son of Baron (Charlie) Falconer who served as Lord Chancellor under former Labour PM Tony Blair.

Before becoming MP for Lincoln, he had worked for the Foreign Office and for the Institute for Public Policy Research and Labour Together think tanks.

Kanishka Narayan is the minister for artificial intelligence, and attends cabinet.

Born in India and raised in Cardiff, Narayan worked in government and business before entering Parliament in 2024 as the MP for the Vale of Glamorgan.

He was previously the minister for AI and online safety under Sir Keir Starmer, where he was part of the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), which has been abolished.

Narayan, who went to Eton College and Oxford, and holds an MBA from Stanford University, has frequently championed AI and its power to transform society, while noting its risks.

Credited as having a deep knowledge of the AI sector, his becoming a cabinet-level AI minister has been broadly welcomed - but DSIT's axing alongside this has also caused some concern.

Matthew Pennycook continues as housing minister in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government but now attends cabinet.

A former Labour councillor in the London Borough of Greenwich, Pennycook became an MP in 2015.

Before that he had worked in the charity and voluntary sector, with a particular focus on child poverty and low pay.

whsmith-restructuring:
The owner of TG Jones, WH Smith's former High Street business, has won approval for a sweeping restructuring which will see up to 150 shops close as well as steep rent cuts on most of the remaining stores.

Modella Capital bought the chain stores last year and they were then rebranded under the name TG Jones.  There are currently 451 stores employing 4,700 workers.

WH Smith travel stores, in railway stations and airports, weren't part of the deal and the business kept the rights to the historic brand name.

But less than a year later, Modella announced a radical restructuring plan blaming "challenging retail conditions".

As well as store closures, some 120 landlords will receive no rent for up to three years; and rent will be cut on hundreds of other stores by between 15% and 75%.

Modella says the plans are vital for the survival of the business and will use some of the cost savings to invest in stores as part of its turnaround strategy.

The High Court heard this week that the retailer was on the brink of insolvency and was facing a cash shortfall of nearly Â£8m by the end of this week, unless the rescue deal was approved.

Tom Smith KC, for TG Jones, told the hearing that the business is "highly distressed" and "running on fumes at the moment".

He said the business would have run out of cash in April had it not been for a Â£10m loan from Modella and a deferral in liabilities including a large tax bill from HMRC.

Modella said some of the problems were due to serious underinvestment in stores by the chain's previous owners, saying long-term sales had declined.

But it also blamed its current poor trading on "challenging retail conditions" and its inability to keep the WH Smith brand name.

There was considerable opposition to the plans, led by property owner British Land who described them as "fundamentally unfair". Modella sweetened the deal with several concessions, which convinced British Land to drop its opposition.  Many suppliers are also taking a big financial hit.

The restructuring plan forecasts the business will end up with 302 stores depending on how many landlords exercise their rights to terminate the lease instead of accepting reduced rents.

The judge, Mr Justice Hildyard, had to decide if the restructuring was fair â whether creditors would be no worse off under than plan than if the retailer were to go into administration.

Mr Justice Hildyard gave the green light to Modella's plans this morning.

In a summary of his judgement he described the plans as "complex in their terms and far-reaching in their effect".

He said he'd been most concerned about the potential financial impact on landlords, but was persuaded the rescue deal was "objectively, the lesser of two evils" resulting from the company's "trading failures and financial predicaments".

Alex Willson, TG Jones chief executive, welcomed the court's approval.

He said: "This decision allows us to move ahead with our turnaround strategy.

"The plan protects the substantial core of the store estate and makes TG Jones a stronger, more sustainable business.

"We are incredibly grateful to all the colleagues, partners and stakeholders who engaged constructively throughout the process, and to Modella Capital for its continued financial commitment."
